subjects.name: Hematology
subjects.description: Comprehensive hematology and hemostasis principles, cellular physiology, anemias, leukocyte disorders, hematologic malignancies, hemostasis, coagulation testing, and instrumentation from Rodak's Hematology, 6th Edition.

topics.name: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
topics.description: Principles of statistical quality control, reference intervals, delta checks, preanalytical and postanalytical variables, and QA management in hematology.

topics.name: Cellular Structure and Function
topics.description: Ultrastructure of hematopoietic cells, organelles, cell cycle regulation, signal transduction, and apoptosis mechanisms.

topics.name: Hematopoiesis
topics.description: Embryonic, fetal, and adult hematopoiesis, stem cell differentiation, bone marrow microenvironment, and regulatory cytokines.

topics.name: Erythrocyte Production and Destruction
topics.description: Normoblastic erythropoiesis, maturation stages, erythropoietin kinetics, and extravascular versus intravascular red blood cell destruction.

topics.name: Erythrocyte Metabolism and Membrane Structure and Function
topics.description: Erythrocyte glycolytic pathways (Embden-Meyerhof, hexose monophosphate shunt, Rapoport-Luebering, methemoglobin reductase) and membrane architecture.

topics.name: Hemoglobin Metabolism
topics.description: Heme synthesis, globin gene regulation, hemoglobin tetramer assembly, oxygen dissociation curve, and abnormal hemoglobin derivatives.

topics.name: Iron Kinetics and Laboratory Assessment
topics.description: Dietary iron absorption, transferrin transport, ferritin and hemosiderin storage, hepcidin regulation, and clinical laboratory assays.

topics.name: Leukocyte Development, Kinetics, and Functions
topics.description: Granulopoiesis, monocytopoiesis, lymphopoiesis, neutrophil kinetics, marginating and circulating pools, and phagocytic destruction mechanisms.

topics.name: Platelet Production, Structure, and Function
topics.description: Megakaryocytopoiesis, endomitosis, platelet ultrastructure, receptor glycoproteins, and primary hemostatic plug formation.

topics.name: Manual, Semiautomated, and Point-of-Care Testing in Hematology
topics.description: Microhematocrit, manual WBC/RBC counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), reticulocyte counts, and point-of-care hematology testing.

topics.name: Automated Blood Cell Analysis
topics.description: Electrical impedance, optical light scatter, radiofrequency, flow cytometry cytochemical staining, and automated flagging algorithms.

topics.name: Examination of the Peripheral Blood Film and Correlation With the Complete Blood Count
topics.description: Wedge smear preparation, Romanowsky staining, systematic smear examination, WBC differential, and CBC parameter correlation.

topics.name: Bone Marrow Examination
topics.description: Bone marrow aspiration and core biopsy indications, specimen processing, M:E ratio determination, iron staining, and diagnostic evaluation.

topics.name: Body Fluid Analysis in the Hematology Laboratory
topics.description: Cerebrospinal fluid, serous fluids (pleural, peritoneal, pericardial), synovial fluid, bronchoalveolar lavage, and crystal analysis.

topics.name: Anemias: Red Blood Cell Morphology and Approach to Diagnosis
topics.description: Morphologic classifications (normocytic, microcytic, macrocytic), kinetic approach, RDW evaluation, and diagnostic algorithms for anemia.

topics.name: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
topics.description: Iron deficiency anemia, anemia of chronic disease/inflammation, sideroblastic anemias, porphyrias, and lead poisoning.

topics.name: Anemias Caused by Defects of DNA Metabolism
topics.description: Megaloblastic anemias, vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, pernicious anemia, nonmegaloblastic macrocytic anemias, and nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony.

topics.name: Bone Marrow Failure
topics.description: Acquired and inherited aplastic anemias (Fanconi, dyskeratosis congenita), pure red cell aplasia, and myelophthisic processes.

topics.name: Introduction to Increased Destruction of Erythrocytes
topics.description: Pathophysiology of hemolytic anemias, laboratory findings of extravascular vs intravascular hemolysis, and clinical compensatory responses.

topics.name: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
topics.description: Hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, stomatocytosis, G6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency, and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).

topics.name: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Nonimmune Causes
topics.description: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (TTP, HUS, DIC), macroangiopathic hemolysis, infectious agents (malaria, babesiosis), and chemical/thermal injury.

topics.name: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Immune Causes
topics.description: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA), cold agglutinin disease (CAD), paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH), and drug-induced immune hemolysis.

topics.name: Hemoglobinopathies (Structural Defects in Hemoglobin)
topics.description: Sickle cell anemia (Hb SS), hemoglobin C, SC disease, unstable hemoglobins, and clinical manifestations of abnormal globin chain variants.

topics.name: Thalassemias
topics.description: Pathophysiology and genetic mutations of alpha- and beta-thalassemias, clinical phenotypes, hemoglobin electrophoresis, and HPLC interpretation.

topics.name: Nonmalignant Leukocyte Disorders
topics.description: Qualitative and quantitative neutrophil abnormalities (Pelger-Huët, Chediak-Higashi, May-Hegglin, Alder-Reilly), reactive lymphocytosis, and infectious mononucleosis.

topics.name: Introduction to Hematologic Neoplasms
topics.description: Etiology, clonal evolution, cytogenetic abnormalities, proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and WHO classification of hematologic malignancies.

topics.name: Flow Cytometric Analysis in Hematologic Disorders
topics.description: Principles of multicolor flow cytometry, fluorochromes, gating strategies, immunophenotypic markers (CD markers), and minimal residual disease analysis.

topics.name: Molecular Diagnostics in Hematopathology
topics.description: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR), RT-PCR, next-generation sequencing (NGS), and molecular clonality testing in hematopathology.

topics.name: Cytogenetics/Cytogenomics
topics.description: Conventional karyotyping, G-banding, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and chromosomal rearrangements in hematologic neoplasms.

topics.name: Acute Leukemias
topics.description: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), WHO diagnostic criteria, blast identification, and cytochemical staining.

topics.name: Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
topics.description: Chronic myeloid leukemia (BCR-ABL1), polycythemia vera (JAK2), essential thrombocythemia, and primary myelofibrosis.

topics.name: Myelodysplastic Syndromes
topics.description: Clonal cytopenias, dyserythropoiesis, dysgranulopoiesis, dysmegakaryocytopoiesis, WHO subgroups, and progression risk in MDS.

topics.name: Mature Lymphoid Neoplasms
topics.description: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL), follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, hairy cell leukemia, and plasma cell neoplasms.

topics.name: Normal Hemostasis and Coagulation Regulation
topics.description: Primary and secondary hemostasis, vascular endothelium, coagulation cascade, cell-based model of hemostasis, and fibrinolysis.

topics.name: Hemorrhagic Coagulation Disorders
topics.description: Hemophilia A (factor VIII) and B (factor IX), von Willebrand disease types, factor deficiencies, vitamin K deficiency, and trauma-induced coagulopathy.

topics.name: Qualitative Platelet Disorders and Vasculopathies
topics.description: Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, storage pool deficiencies, drug-induced platelet dysfunction, and vascular purpuras.

topics.name: Thrombocytopenia and Thrombocytosis
topics.description: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), drug-induced thrombocytopenia, thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP/HUS), and essential thrombocythemia vs reactive thrombocytosis.

topics.name: Thrombotic Disorders and Antithrombin Deficiencies
topics.description: Factor V Leiden (APC resistance), prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin deficiency, protein C and S deficiencies, antiphospholipid syndrome, and D-dimer testing.

topics.name: Antithrombotic Therapies and Monitoring
topics.description: Heparin (UFH and LMWH), warfarin (Coumadin) and INR, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), antiplatelet therapies, and laboratory monitoring.

topics.name: Coagulation and Hemostasis Laboratory Testing
topics.description: Specimen collection and preanalytical variables, PT/INR, APTT, thrombin time, fibrinogen assays, mixing studies, factor assays, and platelet aggregometry.

topics.name: Coagulation Instrumentation and Point-of-Care Testing
topics.description: Mechanical, photo-optical, and chromogenic clot detection methodologies, automated analyzers, platelet aggregometers, viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM), and POC devices.

topics.name: Hematology and Hemostasis in Selected Populations
topics.description: Pediatric hematology reference intervals, hematogones, physiologic anemia of infancy, geriatric hematology, and physiologic hematologic changes in pregnancy.

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: What procedure is NOT employed to validate a new assay?
choices: Comparison of assay results to a reference method
questions.explanation: Validation of a new clinical laboratory assay requires documenting precision (reproducibility), accuracy through comparison to an established reference method (EP09), analytical measurement range/linearity (EP06), analytical specificity, and reference intervals. In contrast, moving average algorithms (such as the Bull algorithm for red blood cell indices) are used for ongoing quality control monitoring of patient data during active testing, not for initial assay validation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 9, PDF p. 22; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: You validate a new assay using linear regression to compare assay calibrator results with the distributor’s published calibrator results. The slope is 0.99 and the y intercept is +10%. What type of error is present?
questions.explanation: In linear regression analysis (y = mx + b), the slope (m) reflects proportional systematic error, while the y-intercept (b) reflects constant systematic error. A slope of 0.99 is close to 1.0 (indicating minimal proportional error), but a positive y-intercept of +10% indicates that the new method consistently measures 10% higher than the comparison method across all concentrations, representing constant systematic error. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book pp. 10–11, PDF pp. 23–24; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: Which is a statistical test that compares means?
questions.explanation: The Student t-test is a parametric statistical test designed specifically to compare the means of two groups (or paired data) to determine if a statistically significant difference exists. Bland-Altman plots assess paired bias and limits of agreement; ANOVA compares variance across three or more groups; Pearson r measures linear correlation, not equality of means. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 11, PDF p. 24; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: The acceptable hemoglobin control value range is 13 ± 0.4 g/dL. The control is assayed five times and produces the following five results: 12.0 g/dL, 12.3 g/dL, 12.0 g/dL, 12.2 g/dL, 12.1 g/dL. These results are:
questions.explanation: The acceptable target interval is 12.6 to 13.4 g/dL (13 ± 0.4 g/dL). All five assayed values (12.0, 12.3, 12.0, 12.2, 12.1 g/dL) are tightly clustered around a mean of 12.12 g/dL with a small standard deviation, demonstrating high precision (reproducibility). However, all five values fall completely below the acceptable target interval, demonstrating poor accuracy. Therefore, the results are precise but not accurate. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 12, PDF p. 25; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: A WBC count control has a mean value of 6000/µL and an SD of 300/µL. What is the 95.5% confidence interval?
questions.explanation: In a Gaussian (normal) distribution, the 95.5% confidence interval encompasses the mean ± 2 standard deviations (mean ± 2 SD). With a mean of 6000/µL and an SD of 300/µL: 2 SD = 2 × 300 = 600/µL. The 95.5% confidence limits are 6000 - 600 = 5400/µL and 6000 + 600 = 6600/µL (5400 to 6600/µL). Mean ± 1 SD (68.2%) would be 5700 to 6300/µL; mean ± 3 SD (99.7%) would be 5100 to 6900/µL. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 12, PDF p. 25; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: The ability of an assay to distinguish the targeted analyte from interfering substances within the specimen matrix is called:
questions.explanation: Analytical specificity is the ability of an assay to detect and measure only the targeted analyte without cross-reacting with or being affected by interfering substances in the specimen matrix (such as hemolysis, icterus, lipemia, or cross-reactive proteins). Analytical sensitivity is the limit of detection (lowest measurable concentration). Clinical specificity is the ability to correctly identify patients who do not have the target condition. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 14, PDF p. 27; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: The laboratory purchases reagents from a manufacturer and develops an assay using a protocol published in a volume of the Methods in Molecular Biology series. How would the FDA classify this assay?
questions.explanation: An assay designed, developed, validated, and performed within a single laboratory using non-FDA-cleared protocols, in-house reagents, or analyte-specific reagents is classified by the FDA as a Laboratory-Developed Test (LDT). Cleared assays are commercially packaged systems with 510(k) clearance; Research Use Only (RUO) reagents cannot be used for clinical reporting without full validation as an LDT. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 14, PDF p. 27; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: What process ensures comparability in multi-site validation?
choices: Distribution of proficiency materials to all sites
Publication of individual site reference intervals
questions.officialAnswer: Distribution of proficiency materials to all sites
questions.explanation: CLSI guideline EP31 emphasizes that when an assay is performed across multiple testing sites within a single health network, comparability is established by distributing identical split patient samples or proficiency materials to all participating sites and demonstrating statistical concordance among instruments. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 15, PDF p. 28; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: A laboratory scientist measures prothrombin time for plasma aliquots from 15 healthy men and 15 healthy women. She computes the mean and 95.5% confidence interval and notes that they duplicate the manufacturer’s statistics within 5%. This procedure is known as:
questions.explanation: Under CLSI guideline EP28-A3c, a laboratory can adopt a manufacturer's published reference interval through transference (verification) by assaying a small group of healthy reference donors (e.g., 20–30 subjects) and confirming that the local donor values replicate the published interval within acceptable statistical tolerance (≥90% to 95% of donor values within limits). Establishing a new RI de novo requires at least 120 reference subjects. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 16, PDF p. 29; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: You purchase a preserved whole blood specimen from a distributor who provides the mean values for several complete blood count analytes. What is this specimen called?
questions.explanation: A preserved specimen whose matrix closely mimics patient specimens and has established target means and acceptable standard deviation ranges provided by a manufacturer for multiple parameters is a control. Controls are analyzed alongside patient specimens to verify ongoing analytical system performance and stability. Calibrators are used to establish instrument response curves and set baseline measurement values. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 17, PDF p. 30; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: You perform a clinical efficacy test and get the following results: Among individuals unaffected by the disease, the assay is negative in 40 and positive in 10; among individuals affected by the disease, the assay is negative in 5 and positive in 45. What is the number of false-negative results?
questions.explanation: A false-negative result occurs when a patient who is truly affected by the disease or condition yields a negative test result. In the clinical efficacy contingency table: affected patients who test negative = 5 (false negatives); affected patients who test positive = 45 (true positives); unaffected patients who test negative = 40 (true negatives); unaffected patients who test positive = 10 (false positives). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 20, PDF p. 33; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).
questions.promptAfterReferences: What is the number of false-negative results?

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: What agency provides external quality assurance (proficiency) surveys and laboratory accreditation?
choices: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS)
questions.explanation: The College of American Pathologists (CAP) is the premier peer-based organization that provides external quality assurance proficiency testing (surveys) and inspects and accredits clinical medical laboratories under deemed status from CMS. CMS is the federal regulatory body enforcing CLIA '88; CLIAC is an advisory committee; TJC accredits healthcare organizations. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 19, PDF p. 32; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: What agency provides continuing medical laboratory education?
choices: American Society for Clinical Laboratory Science (ASCLS)
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS)
questions.officialAnswer: American Society for Clinical Laboratory Science (ASCLS)
questions.explanation: The American Society for Clinical Laboratory Science (ASCLS) is the primary professional organization dedicated to providing continuing medical laboratory education through its Professional Achievement Continuing Education (P.A.C.E.) program, conferences, and webinars. CMS and CLIAC are governmental and advisory bodies; CAP focuses on accreditation and surveys. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 19, PDF p. 32; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: Regular review of blood specimen collection quality is an example of:
questions.explanation: The preanalytical phase encompasses all processes that occur before testing begins, including test ordering, patient identification, phlebotomy technique, anticoagulant-to-blood ratio, specimen transport, and rejection of hemolyzed or clotted samples. Monitoring blood collection quality is a core preanalytical quality assurance activity. Analytical QC monitors the testing process itself; postanalytical QA monitors result reporting and delivery. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 22, PDF p. 35; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: Review of laboratory report integrity is an example of:
questions.explanation: The postanalytical phase begins once analytical results are generated and encompasses review of report formatting, reference range flags, delta checks, critical value notifications, electronic health record interface transmission, and clinician communication. Verifying report integrity and delivery is a postanalytical quality assurance responsibility. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 23, PDF p. 36; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: When performing a receiver operating curve analysis, what parameter assesses the overall efficacy of an assay?
questions.explanation: In Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, sensitivity (true-positive rate) is plotted against 1 - specificity (false-positive rate) across all possible decision thresholds. The overall diagnostic efficacy and discriminative power of the assay is quantified by the Area Under the Curve (AUC). An AUC of 1.0 indicates perfect discrimination, while an AUC of 0.5 indicates performance no better than random chance. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 21, PDF p. 34; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Quality Assurance in Hematology and Hemostasis Testing
questions.prompt: You require your laboratory staff to annually perform manual lupus anticoagulant profiles on a set of plasmas with known values. This exercise is known as:
questions.explanation: Distributing characterized specimens with known values to laboratory testing personnel to assess their testing proficiency, technical competence, and procedural adherence is internal proficiency testing (competency assessment). External quality assessment involves surveys sent by third-party accrediting agencies; assay validation is the one-time evaluation prior to clinical implementation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 2, Book p. 19, PDF p. 32; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The organelle involved in packaging and trafficking of cellular products is the:
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus (Golgi complex) is a system of stacked membranous cisternae that receives newly synthesized proteins and lipids from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies them (e.g., glycosylation, phosphorylation), sorts them, and packages them into secretory vesicles or lysosomes for intracellular trafficking or exocytosis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 36, PDF p. 49; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The glycocalyx is composed of membrane:
questions.explanation: The glycocalyx is the carbohydrate-rich outer coat surrounding the exterior leaflet of the cell membrane. It is composed of oligosaccharide chains covalently bound to membrane proteins (glycoproteins) and lipids (glycolipids), functioning in cell-cell recognition, antigen expression (such as ABO blood group antigens), and cell protection. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 32, PDF p. 45; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The “control center” of the cell is the:
questions.explanation: The nucleus is the control center of eukaryotic cells because it houses the genetic material (DNA), directs cellular replication, regulates cell division, and orchestrates protein synthesis through transcriptional regulation and messenger RNA synthesis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 33, PDF p. 46; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The nucleus is composed largely of:
questions.explanation: The nucleus is composed primarily of chromatin, which consists of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) complexed with basic histone proteins and non-histone chromosomal proteins, enclosed within a double-membrane nuclear envelope. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 33, PDF p. 46; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The site of protein synthesis is the:
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are macromolecular complexes of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and proteins that translate genetic instructions from messenger RNA into polypeptide chains, serving as the universal site of cellular protein synthesis. Ribosomes may exist free in cytoplasm or bound to rough endoplasmic reticulum membranes. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 35, PDF p. 48; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The shape of a cell is maintained by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Cell shape, structural stability, mechanical deformability, and intracellular transport are maintained by the cytoskeleton, an intricate network composed of microfilaments (actin filaments), intermediate filaments, and microtubules (tubulin polymers). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 37, PDF p. 50; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Functions of the cell membrane include all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Transport of specific molecules into the cell
questions.explanation: The plasma membrane functions as a selectively permeable barrier, regulates molecular transport via pumps and channels, provides receptor sites for extracellular signal transduction, and facilitates cell-cell adherence. Protein synthesis is an intracellular process performed exclusively by ribosomes, not by the cell membrane. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book pp. 31–32, PDF pp. 44–45; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The energy source for cells is the:
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are the metabolic powerhouses of eukaryotic cells, generating the vast majority of cellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) through oxidative phosphorylation, the citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle), and the electron transport chain. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 36, PDF p. 49; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Ribosomes are synthesized by the:
questions.explanation: The nucleolus is a non-membrane-bound dense subnuclear structure responsible for transcribing ribosomal RNA (rRNA), processing rRNA precursors, and assembling rRNA with imported ribosomal proteins into small and large ribosomal subunits before export to cytoplasm. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 34, PDF p. 47; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Euchromatin functions as the:
questions.explanation: Euchromatin represents uncoiled, dispersed, genetically active chromatin that is readily accessible to RNA polymerase and transcription factors for RNA transcription. Heterochromatin is tightly coiled, condensed, and transcriptionally inactive. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 33, PDF p. 46; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The cell cycle is regulated by:
questions.explanation: Progression through cell cycle checkpoints (G1 to S, G2 to M, metaphase to anaphase) is tightly regulated by cyclins (regulatory subunits) and their catalytic partners, cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), which phosphorylate target proteins to drive cell cycle progression. Protooncogenes and growth factors stimulate cycle entry, while apoptosis eliminates cells, but the direct biochemical clockwork is mediated by cyclins and CDKs. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 38, PDF p. 51; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The transition from the G1 to S stage of the cell cycle is regulated by:
questions.explanation: The transition across the G1 restriction point into S phase (DNA replication) is driven by the Cyclin E/CDK2 complex (along with Cyclin D/CDK4/6), which hyperphosphorylates the retinoblastoma protein (pRb), releasing E2F transcription factors. Cyclin B/CDK1 controls entry into mitosis (G2 to M); Cyclin A/CDK2 regulates progression through S phase. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 38, PDF p. 51; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Apoptosis is morphologically identified by:
questions.explanation: Apoptosis is morphologically characterized by cell shrinkage, cytoplasmic blebbing, and nuclear chromatin condensation (pyknosis) and fragmentation (karyorrhexis), culminating in the formation of intact apoptotic bodies phagocytized without inflammation. Cellular swelling and membrane rupture are characteristic hallmarks of necrosis, not apoptosis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 40, PDF p. 53; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Regulation of the hematopoietic microenvironment is provided by the:
questions.explanation: The hematopoietic inductive microenvironment (marrow niche) is provided by bone marrow stromal cells (endothelial cells, reticular adventitial cells/fibroblasts, adipocytes, osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and macrophages) and the growth factors and extracellular matrix proteins they secrete to support stem cell self-renewal, differentiation, and trafficking. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book p. 41, PDF p. 54; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements is FALSE concerning cellular signal transduction?
choices: Membrane-permeable ligands can directly bind to intracellular receptors.
A transmembrane receptor can transmit a signal into the cell through its intracellular domain when ligand binds its extracellular domain.
The binding of membrane receptors to fixed ligands such as extracellular matrix can transmit intracellular signals.
The binding of soluble ligands to membrane receptors is not able to induce changes in gene expression.
questions.officialAnswer: The binding of soluble ligands to membrane receptors is not able to induce changes in gene expression.
questions.explanation: Statement D is false. The binding of soluble extracellular ligands (such as erythropoietin, cytokines, and hormones) to cell surface transmembrane receptors activates intracellular signaling cascades (such as JAK-STAT, MAPK, or PI3K/Akt) that translocate transcription factors to the nucleus and directly induce changes in gene expression. Statements A, B, and C are true principles of signal transduction. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 3, Book pp. 32–33, PDF pp. 45–46; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The process of formation and development of blood cells is termed:
questions.explanation: Hematopoiesis is the continuous, regulated process of blood cell production, differentiation, and development from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow. Hematemesis is vomiting of blood; hematocytometry is cell counting; hematorrhea is free hemorrhage. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 45, PDF p. 58; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: During the second trimester of fetal development, the primary site of blood cell production is the:
questions.explanation: During intrauterine development, hematopoiesis progresses through three phases: the mesoblastic (yolk sac) phase during the first 2 months, the hepatic phase during the second trimester (with the fetal liver serving as the primary site of hematopoiesis, supplemented by the spleen), and the medullary (myeloid) phase in the bone marrow beginning around the fifth month and becoming dominant by the third trimester and throughout postnatal life. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 48, PDF p. 61; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following organs is responsible for the maturation of T lymphocytes and regulation of their expression of CD4 and CD8?
questions.explanation: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ where lymphoid progenitor cells from the bone marrow migrate to undergo proliferation, selection, and maturation into immunocompetent T lymphocytes. In the thymic cortex and medulla, thymocytes undergo positive and negative selection, regulating the sequential surface expression of CD4 and CD8 co-receptors. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 4, Book pp. 50–51, PDF pp. 63–64; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The best source of active bone marrow from a 20-year-old would be:
questions.explanation: By age 20 (adulthood), hematopoiesis is largely restricted to the central axial skeleton and proximal ends of long bones (pelvis/iliac crest, sternum, vertebrae, skull, and ribs) due to retrogression of red marrow to fatty yellow marrow in distal appendicular bones (such as tibia, radius, and shafts of long bones). The posterior superior iliac crest provides the most abundant, safe, and accessible volume of active red marrow for diagnostic marrow aspirates and core biopsies. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 4, Book pp. 45–46, PDF pp. 58–59; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Physiologic programmed cell death is termed:
questions.explanation: Apoptosis is genetically programmed, physiologic cell death characterized by cellular shrinkage, chromatin condensation, DNA fragmentation, and membrane blebbing into apoptotic bodies phagocytosed by macrophages without inciting inflammation. Necrosis represents accidental traumatic cell lysis; angiogenesis is new blood vessel formation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 56, PDF p. 69; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which organ is the site of sequestration of platelets?
questions.explanation: Under normal physiologic conditions, approximately one-third (30% to 35%) of total circulating platelets are sequestered within the red pulp cords and sinuses of the spleen as a readily exchangeable reserve pool, while the remaining two-thirds circulate in the peripheral blood. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 4, Book p. 49, PDF p. 62; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following morphologic changes occurs during normal blood cell maturation?
questions.explanation: General morphologic changes during normal hematopoietic maturation include progressive reduction in overall cell diameter, progressive condensation and clumping of nuclear chromatin, disappearance of visible nucleoli, reduction in the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N:C) ratio, and loss of cytoplasmic basophilia (as ribosomal RNA degrades and lineage-specific proteins or granules accumulate). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 4, Book pp. 59, 72, PDF pp. 72, 85; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following cells is a product of the common lymphoid progenitor?
questions.explanation: The pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell diverges into the common myeloid progenitor (CMP) and common lymphoid progenitor (CLP). The CLP gives rise to T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, natural killer (NK) cells, and lymphoid dendritic cells. In contrast, megakaryocytes, erythrocytes, granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils), and monocytes arise from the CMP. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 4, Book pp. 53–54, PDF pp. 66–67; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What growth factor is produced in the kidneys and is used to treat anemia associated with kidney disease?
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin (EPO) is a glycoprotein cytokine synthesized primarily (85% to 90%) by renal peritubular interstitial fibroblasts in response to tissue hypoxia. Recombinant human EPO is widely administered as an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent to treat normocytic anemia resulting from impaired EPO synthesis in chronic kidney disease. TPO stimulates megakaryocytes; G-CSF stimulates granulocytes; KIT ligand (stem cell factor) acts early on primitive stem cells. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 4, Book pp. 57–58, PDF pp. 70–71; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following cytokines is required very early in the differentiation of a hematopoietic stem cell?
questions.explanation: Early-acting (primitive) hematopoietic cytokines, such as FLT3 ligand, KIT ligand (stem cell factor), and thrombopoietin (TPO), work synergistically to maintain dormancy, survival, self-renewal, and initial multilineage commitment of primitive hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and multipotent progenitors. Lineage-specific cytokines such as EPO, IL-2, and IL-8 act much later on committed precursors. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 4, Book pp. 54–57, PDF pp. 67–70; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: When a patient has severe anemia and the bone marrow is unable to effectively produce red blood cells to meet the increased demand, one of the body’s responses is:
choices: Extramedullary hematopoiesis in the liver and spleen
Decreased production of erythropoietin by the kidney
Increased apoptosis of erythrocyte progenitor cells
Increased proportion of yellow marrow in the long bones
questions.officialAnswer: Extramedullary hematopoiesis in the liver and spleen
questions.explanation: When medullary bone marrow hematopoiesis is destroyed, fibrotic, or overwhelmed by severe hemolytic or chronic anemia, the spleen and liver can revert to their fetal hematopoietic capacity to generate blood cells outside the marrow cavity, a compensatory process known as extramedullary hematopoiesis (often leading to hepatosplenomegaly). In severe anemia, kidney EPO production increases (not decreases), apoptosis decreases, and yellow marrow converts to active red marrow. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 4, Book pp. 45, 48–49, PDF pp. 58, 61–62; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Hematopoietic stem cells produce all lineages of blood cells in sufficient quantities over the lifetime of an individual because they:
choices: Have the ability of self-renewal by asymmetric division
Are present in large numbers in the bone marrow niches
Have a low mitotic potential in response to growth factors
questions.officialAnswer: Have the ability of self-renewal by asymmetric division
questions.explanation: Pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) maintain lifelong hematopoiesis through the capacity for self-renewal, primarily via asymmetric division: one daughter cell retains stem cell identity within the marrow niche to replenish the stem cell reserve pool, while the other daughter cell enters differentiation toward multipotent progenitor pathways. HSCs are rare in number (not present in large numbers) and are multipotent/pluripotent (not unipotent). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 4, Book pp. 52–53, 59, PDF pp. 65–66, 72; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an erythroid progenitor?
questions.explanation: Hematopoietic differentiation distinguishes between early, committed progenitor cells (burst-forming unit-erythroid [BFU-E] and colony-forming unit-erythroid [CFU-E]), which are morphologically indistinguishable lymphoblast-like cells identified by in vitro colony assays, and morphologically identifiable erythroid precursors (pronormoblast, basophilic normoblast, polychromatic normoblast, orthochromic normoblast, reticulocyte, and mature RBC). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 5, Book pp. 63–64, PDF pp. 76–77; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most mature normoblast?
questions.explanation: In normoblastic erythroid maturation, the sequential developmental stages from earliest to most mature nucleated precursor are: (1) pronormoblast (proerythroblast/rubriblast), (2) basophilic normoblast (prorubricyte), (3) polychromatic normoblast (rubricyte), and (4) orthochromic normoblast (metarubricyte). The orthochromic normoblast is the final nucleated stage prior to nuclear extrusion, after which the enucleated cell becomes a reticulocyte (polychromatic erythrocyte). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 5, Book pp. 64–67, PDF pp. 77–80; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What erythroid precursor can be described as follows: The cell is of medium size compared with other normoblasts, with an N:C ratio of nearly 1:1. The nuclear chromatin is condensed and chunky throughout the nucleus. No nucleoli are seen. The cytoplasm is gray-blue.
questions.explanation: The polychromatic normoblast (rubricyte) is 10 to 12 µm in diameter with an N:C ratio of approximately 4:1 to 1:1. Its nuclear chromatin is distinctly condensed, clumped, and chunky with visible parachromatin (and no nucleoli). Its cytoplasm is characteristically murky, gray-blue or lilac because the pink staining of accumulating hemoglobin blends with the blue staining of residual ribosomal RNA. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 5, Book pp. 65–66, PDF pp. 78–79; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: At which normoblastic stage does globin production begin?
questions.explanation: Globin mRNA transcription and globin polypeptide chain production begin at the pronormoblast (proerythroblast) stage, the earliest morphologically recognizable erythroid precursor, along with the onset of heme synthesis. However, the accumulation of hemoglobin only becomes morphologically visible under light microscopy at the polychromatic normoblast stage when cytoplasm takes on a gray-blue hue. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 5, Book pp. 64–65, PDF pp. 77–78; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Hypoxia stimulates RBC production by:
choices: Inducing more pluripotent stem cells into the erythroid lineage
Stimulating EPO production by the kidney
Increasing the number of RBC mitoses
Stimulating the production of fibronectin by macrophages of the bone marrow
questions.officialAnswer: Stimulating EPO production by the kidney
questions.explanation: Renal peritubular interstitial cells detect diminished tissue oxygen tension via oxygen-sensing prolyl hydroxylase enzymes and hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1/HIF-2). Hypoxia stabilizes HIF-2α, which translocates to the nucleus and upregulates transcription of the erythropoietin (EPO) gene, stimulating the kidneys to synthesize and release EPO into the circulation to rescue erythroid progenitors from apoptosis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 5, Book pp. 70–71, PDF pp. 83–84; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Erythropoietin can increase the production of RBCs by:
choices: Promoting early release of reticulocytes from bone marrow
questions.officialAnswer: Promoting early release of reticulocytes from bone marrow
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin (EPO) promotes erythrocyte production and delivery through multiple concerted mechanisms: (1) rescuing CFU-E and early normoblasts from apoptosis (by downregulating Fas and upregulating anti-apoptotic Bcl-xL), (2) shortening the marrow transit time between cell divisions, (3) reducing the total number of mitotic divisions, and (4) accelerating egress and premature release of young polychromatic erythrocytes (shift reticulocytes) into the peripheral circulation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 5, Book pp. 71–72, 75, PDF pp. 84–85, 88; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: In the bone marrow, erythroid precursors are located:
choices: Adjacent to megakaryocytes along the adventitial cell lining
Surrounding fat cells in apoptotic islands
In the center of the hematopoietic cords
questions.explanation: In normal bone marrow, normoblasts mature in specialized anatomical niches termed erythroid islands. Each island consists of a central "nurse" macrophage surrounded by a rosette of maturing erythroblasts. The macrophage provides critical cytokines, anchors cells via adhesive molecules, transfers ferritin iron, and phagocytoses extruded normoblast nuclei. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 5, Book pp. 73–74, PDF pp. 86–87; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following determines the timing of egress of RBCs from the bone marrow?
choices: Stromal cells decrease production of adhesive molecules over time as RBCs mature.
Endothelial cells of the venous sinus form pores at specified intervals of time, allowing egress of free cells.
Periodic apoptosis of pronormoblasts in the marrow cords occurs.
Maturing normoblasts slowly lose receptors for adhesive molecules that bind them to stromal cells.
questions.officialAnswer: Maturing normoblasts slowly lose receptors for adhesive molecules that bind them to stromal cells.
questions.explanation: Normoblast retention in hematopoietic cords is mediated by interactions between surface adhesive receptors (such as VLA-4 and VLA-5 integrins) and extracellular matrix ligands (such as fibronectin and vascular cell adhesion molecules) produced by stromal cells. As erythroid cells mature into reticulocytes, they progressively downregulate and lose these adhesive receptors, detach from the stromal matrix, and squeeze through endothelial fenestrations/pores into venous sinus lumens. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 5, Book pp. 73–74, 75, PDF pp. 86–87, 88; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What single feature of normal RBCs is most responsible for limiting their life span?
choices: Increased flexibility of the cell membrane
questions.explanation: Mature erythrocytes lack a nucleus and ribosomes, which completely deprives them of the ability to synthesize new proteins, enzymes, or membrane lipids. Over their ~120-day circulating lifespan, metabolic enzymes slowly degrade without replacement, membrane pump activity falters, lipids peroxidize, and cells become dehydrated, spheroidal, and rigid, ultimately sealing their fate in the splenic microcirculation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 5, Book pp. 74–75, PDF pp. 87–88; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Extravascular hemolysis occurs when:
choices: RBCs extravasate from blood vessels into the tissues
RBCs are trapped in blood clots outside the blood vessels
questions.explanation: Approximately 90% of normal red cell destruction occurs via extravascular (macrophage-mediated) hemolysis, wherein senescent, rigid RBCs traveling through the hypoxic, acidic, hypoglycemic red pulp cords of the spleen become unable to deform through the narrow endothelial slits into the sinusoids, prompting their phagocytosis and catabolism by splenic and hepatic macrophages. Mechanical rupture in circulation represents intravascular hemolysis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 5, Book pp. 74–75, PDF pp. 87–88; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which RBC process does not require energy?
choices: Preventing the peroxidation of proteins and lipids
questions.explanation: Oxygen transport by hemoglobin is a passive physicochemical process of reversible, cooperative binding and release driven entirely by ambient oxygen partial pressures (PO₂) and allosteric effectors, requiring zero ATP or metabolic energy consumption. In contrast, maintaining cation gradients (via Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and Ca²⁺-ATPase), cytoskeletal protein phosphorylation for deformability, and regenerating reduced glutathione to prevent peroxidation all consume ATP and NADPH. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 6, Book p. 79, PDF p. 92; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What pathway anaerobically generates energy in the form of ATP?
questions.explanation: The Embden-Meyerhof pathway (EMP) is the anaerobic glycolytic pathway that catabolizes glucose into pyruvate and lactate, generating 90% to 95% of the red blood cell's ATP. It consumes 2 ATP molecules and produces 4 ATP molecules per molecule of glucose, yielding a net gain of 2 ATP. The hexose monophosphate shunt produces NADPH; the Rapoport-Luebering shunt produces 2,3-BPG and bypasses ATP synthesis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 6, Book pp. 79–81, PDF pp. 92–94; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which is true concerning 2,3-BPG?
choices: The least abundant of RBC organophosphates
questions.explanation: 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG), generated via the Rapoport-Luebering shunt, binds in the central cavity of deoxygenated hemoglobin tetramers between the beta globin chains, stabilizing the low-affinity T (tense) quaternary structure and shifting the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, thereby promoting and enhancing oxygen release to peripheral tissues. It does not generate ATP (it bypasses the phosphoglycerate kinase ATP step) and is the most abundant organophosphate in erythrocytes. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 6, Book pp. 81–82, PDF pp. 94–95; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What hexose-monophosphate shunt products participate in the detoxification of peroxides?
questions.explanation: The hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt / pentose phosphate pathway metabolizes ~5% to 10% of RBC glucose via glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) to generate NADPH. NADPH serves as the essential reducing cofactor for glutathione reductase to reduce oxidized glutathione (GSSG) back into reduced glutathione (GSH). GSH is then used by glutathione peroxidase to neutralize dangerous hydrogen peroxide and reactive oxygen radicals into water, protecting membrane lipids, cytoskeletal proteins, and hemoglobin from oxidative damage. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 6, Book pp. 80–81, PDF pp. 93–94; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following helps maintain RBC shape?
questions.explanation: The biconcave discoid shape, structural stability, and extraordinary deformability of the erythrocyte are maintained primarily by a two-dimensional submembranous meshwork of peripheral cytoskeletal proteins—predominantly α- and β-spectrin tetramers linked to short actin filaments, protein 4.1R, and ankyrin—anchored to integral transmembrane proteins. Disruption of these cytoskeletal linkages leads to poikilocytic shape alterations such as spherocytes and elliptocytes. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 6, Book pp. 83–87, PDF pp. 96–100; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The glycolipids of the RBC membrane:
choices: Attach the cytoskeleton to the lipid layer
questions.explanation: Membrane glycolipids make up approximately 5% of external surface lipids on the outer bilayer leaflet. Their carbohydrate side chains extend into the surrounding plasma, functioning as major blood group antigens, including the ABH, Lewis, P, and Ii blood group systems. Ion channels and cytoskeletal attachment complexes are mediated by integral and peripheral transmembrane proteins, not glycolipids. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 6, Book p. 83, PDF p. 96; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: RBC membranes block passage of most large molecules, such as proteins, but allow passage of small molecules such as the cations Na⁺, K⁺, and Ca²⁺. What is the term for this membrane property?
questions.explanation: A semipermeable (or selectively permeable) membrane is a biological barrier that permits the passive or controlled diffusion of water and specific small solutes (such as anions via Band 3 and cations through specialized pumps and channels) while completely barring the transit of large macromolecules, colloidal proteins, and hemoglobin. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 6, Book pp. 82–83, 88, PDF pp. 95–96, 101; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: RBC membrane phospholipids are arranged:
choices: In chains beneath a protein cytoskeleton
In two layers whose composition is asymmetric
So that hydrophobic portions are facing the plasma
questions.officialAnswer: In two layers whose composition is asymmetric
questions.explanation: The RBC lipid bilayer is composed of two asymmetric phospholipid leaflets: choline-containing phospholipids (phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin) are localized predominantly in the outer, plasma-facing leaflet, whereas amino-phospholipids (phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylserine) are restricted to the inner, cytoplasm-facing leaflet by ATP-dependent flippase enzymes. Hydrophobic fatty acyl tails face inward toward each other, while polar hydrophilic heads face the aqueous plasma and cytoplasm. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 6, Book pp. 82–83, PDF pp. 95–96; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: RBC membrane cholesterol is replenished from the:
questions.explanation: Mature erythrocytes lack the enzymatic machinery and mitochondria required for de novo cholesterol or fatty acid synthesis. Membrane cholesterol exists in a continuous, passive, non-energy-dependent dynamic equilibrium with unesterified (free) cholesterol in circulating blood plasma, regulated by plasma lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) activity. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 6, Book p. 83, PDF p. 96; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Hemoglobin iron may become oxidized to Fe³⁺ by several pathologic mechanisms. What portion of the Embden-Meyerhof pathway reduces iron to Fe²⁺?
questions.explanation: When ferrous heme iron (Fe²⁺) is oxidized to ferric iron (Fe³⁺), nonfunctional methemoglobin is formed, which cannot bind oxygen. The methemoglobin reductase pathway (an essential offshoot of the Embden-Meyerhof glycolytic pathway) utilizes NADH generated by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPD) and the enzyme cytochrome b5 reductase (methemoglobin reductase) to reduce Fe³⁺ back to active Fe²⁺, maintaining methemoglobin levels below 1% of total hemoglobin. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 6, Book pp. 81, 88, PDF pp. 94, 101; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of a transmembrane or integral membrane protein?
questions.explanation: Red blood cell membrane proteins are categorized into integral/transmembrane proteins that span the lipid bilayer (such as Band 3 [anion exchanger 1], Glycophorin A, B, and C, and Glut-1) and peripheral/cytoskeletal proteins localized on the cytoplasmic surface of the lipid bilayer (such as α- and β-spectrin, ankyrin, protein 4.1R, and actin). Glycophorin A is a prototypical single-pass transmembrane sialoglycoprotein carrying MN blood group antigens. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 6, Book pp. 83–85, PDF pp. 96–98; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Abnormalities in the horizontal and vertical linkages of the transmembrane and cytoskeletal RBC membrane proteins may be seen as:
questions.explanation: Structural defects in red blood cell membrane protein linkages produce characteristic hereditary poikilocytic shape changes: defective vertical linkages between the lipid bilayer and cytoskeleton (involving ankyrin, spectrin, Band 3, or protein 4.2) cause uncoupling of the bilayer, lipid loss, reduced surface-area-to-volume ratio, and hereditary spherocytosis; defective horizontal linkages within the hexagonal cytoskeletal lattice (involving spectrin dimer-dimer self-association or the spectrin-actin-protein 4.1 junction) cause mechanical shear destabilization, resulting in hereditary elliptocytosis and poikilocytosis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 6, Book pp. 86–87, 88, PDF pp. 99–100, 101; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: A hemoglobin molecule is composed of:
choices: One heme molecule and four globin chains
Ferrous iron, protoporphyrin IX, and a globin chain
Protoporphyrin IX and four globin chains
Four heme molecules and four globin chains
questions.officialAnswer: Four heme molecules and four globin chains
questions.explanation: A complete hemoglobin tetramer is composed of four individual heme moieties (each containing a protoporphyrin IX ring chelating one central ferrous iron atom, Fe²⁺) and four polypeptide globin chains (two alpha-like and two non-alpha globin chains). Each heme group binds one molecule of O₂, allowing a single hemoglobin molecule to transport up to four O₂ molecules. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 7, Book p. 91, PDF p. 104; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Normal adult Hb A contains which polypeptide chains?
questions.explanation: Normal adult hemoglobin A (Hb A) is composed of two alpha (α) chains and two beta (β) chains (α₂β₂), comprising >95% of normal adult hemoglobin. Hb A₂ is composed of α₂δ₂ (<3.5%), Hb F is composed of α₂γ₂ (1%–2%), and embryonic hemoglobins incorporate zeta (ζ) and epsilon (ε) chains. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 7, Book p. 91, PDF p. 104; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: A key rate-limiting step in heme synthesis is suppression of:
questions.explanation: The initial and principal rate-limiting regulatory enzyme in heme biosynthesis is delta-aminolevulinate synthase (ALAS), which catalyzes the condensation of succinyl-CoA and glycine to form delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) in the mitochondria. Excess free heme suppresses ALAS through negative feedback inhibition. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 7, Book pp. 93–94, PDF pp. 106–107; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following forms of hemoglobin molecule has the lowest affinity for oxygen?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin exists in two allosteric quaternary conformations: the T (tense or taut) state, which represents deoxygenated hemoglobin with low oxygen affinity stabilized by salt bridges and 2,3-BPG; and the R (relaxed) state, which represents oxygenated hemoglobin where salt bridges are broken and oxygen affinity is high. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 7, Book pp. 95–96, PDF pp. 108–109; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Using the normal hemoglobin-oxygen dissociation curve for reference, predict the position of the curve when there is a decrease in pH.
choices: Shifted to the right of normal with decreased oxygen affinity
Shifted to the left of normal with increased oxygen affinity
Shifted to the right of normal with increased oxygen affinity
Shifted to the left of normal with decreased oxygen affinity
questions.officialAnswer: Shifted to the right of normal with decreased oxygen affinity
questions.explanation: A decrease in blood pH (acidosis / increased H⁺ concentration) produces the classic Bohr effect: H⁺ ions bind to specific amino acid residues on deoxyhemoglobin, stabilizing the tense (T) quaternary structure. This shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, decreasing hemoglobin's oxygen affinity and facilitating the unloading of oxygen to tissues. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 7, Book pp. 96–97, PDF pp. 109–110; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The predominant hemoglobin found in a healthy newborn is:
questions.explanation: Fetal hemoglobin (Hb F, α₂γ₂) is the predominant hemoglobin in neonates at birth, accounting for 60% to 80% of total circulating hemoglobin in a healthy full-term newborn, with Hb A (α₂β₂) comprising the remainder (20% to 40%). Hb F is gradually replaced by adult Hb A over the first 6 months of life. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 7, Book pp. 92, 100, PDF pp. 105, 113; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What is the normal distribution of hemoglobins in healthy adults?
choices: 80% to 90% Hb A, 5% to 10% Hb A₂, 1% to 5% Hb F
80% to 90% Hb A₂, 5% to 10% Hb A, 1% to 5% Hb F
>95% Hb A, <3.5% Hb A₂, 1% to 2% Hb F
>90% Hb A, 5% Hb F, <5% Hb A₂
questions.officialAnswer: >95% Hb A, <3.5% Hb A₂, 1% to 2% Hb F
questions.explanation: In healthy adults past 1 to 2 years of age, normal hemoglobin distribution consists of >95% Hb A (α₂β₂), <3.5% Hb A₂ (α₂δ₂), and 1% to 2% residual Hb F (α₂γ₂). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 7, Book pp. 92, 101, PDF pp. 105, 114; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a description of the structure of oxidized hemoglobin?
choices: Hemoglobin carrying oxygen on heme; synonymous with oxygenated hemoglobin
Hemoglobin with iron in the ferric state (methemoglobin) and not able to carry oxygen
Hemoglobin with iron in the ferric state so that carbon dioxide replaces oxygen in the heme structure
Hemoglobin carrying carbon monoxide; hence oxidized refers to the single oxygen
questions.officialAnswer: Hemoglobin with iron in the ferric state (methemoglobin) and not able to carry oxygen
questions.explanation: Oxidized hemoglobin is methemoglobin, wherein heme iron is oxidized from the functional divalent ferrous state (Fe²⁺) to the trivalent ferric state (Fe³⁺). Ferric heme cannot reversibly bind oxygen, rendering methemoglobin incapable of oxygen delivery to tissues. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 7, Book pp. 98–99, PDF pp. 111–112; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: In the quaternary structure of hemoglobin, the globin chains associate into:
choices: α Tetramers in some cells and β tetramers in others
A mixture of α tetramers and β tetramers
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin A quaternary structure consists of two identical αβ dimers (α₁β₁ and α₂β₂) that assemble into a complete tetramer ((αβ)₂). Strong hydrophobic contact areas stabilize the α₁β₁ interfaces, while sliding polar contacts at the α₁β₂ interface allow allosteric rotation during oxygenation and deoxygenation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 7, Book pp. 92, 95, PDF pp. 105, 108; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: How are the globin chain genes arranged?
choices: With α genes and β genes on the same chromosome, including two α genes and two β genes
With α genes and β genes on separate chromosomes, including two α genes on one chromosome and one β gene on a different chromosome
With α genes and β genes on the same chromosome, including four α genes and four β genes
With α genes and β genes on separate chromosomes, including four α genes on one chromosome and two β genes on a different chromosome
questions.officialAnswer: With α genes and β genes on separate chromosomes, including two α genes on one chromosome and one β gene on a different chromosome
questions.explanation: Globin gene clusters reside on two separate autosomes: the alpha gene cluster is on the short arm of chromosome 16 and contains two duplicate functional α-globin genes (α1 and α2) per haploid genome (four total per diploid cell). The beta gene cluster is on the short arm of chromosome 11 and contains a single β-globin gene per haploid genome (two total per diploid cell). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 7, Book pp. 92–93, PDF pp. 105–106; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The nature of the interaction between 2,3-BPG and hemoglobin is that 2,3-BPG:
choices: Binds to the heme moiety, blocking the binding of oxygen
Binds simultaneously with oxygen, helping it to bind more tightly
Binds to amino acids of the globin chain, contributing to a conformational change that inhibits oxygen from binding to heme
Binds to the alpha chains only, keeping them apart
questions.officialAnswer: Binds to amino acids of the globin chain, contributing to a conformational change that inhibits oxygen from binding to heme
questions.explanation: 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) binds via salt bridges to positively charged amino acid residues (histidine, lysine) in the central pocket between the two beta chains of deoxyhemoglobin. This stabilizes the deoxygenated tense (T) conformation, lowering oxygen affinity and prompting oxygen release. When hemoglobin binds O₂, the central cavity contracts and expels 2,3-BPG. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 7, Book pp. 96, 101, PDF pp. 109, 114; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Iron is transported in plasma via:
questions.explanation: Apotransferrin is the plasma transport glycoprotein synthesized by hepatocytes. When it binds up to two atoms of ferric iron (Fe³⁺), it becomes transferrin, safely carrying iron through circulation between sites of absorption (enterocytes), storage (macrophages and hepatocytes), and utilization (erythroblasts). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book pp. 105–106, PDF pp. 118–119; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What is the major metabolically available storage form of iron in the body?
questions.explanation: Ferritin is the primary, water-soluble, metabolically active storage form of iron in humans, composed of a spherical apoferritin protein shell capable of housing up to 4500 ferric iron atoms. In contrast, hemosiderin is an insoluble, partially degraded ferritin aggregate that releases iron much more slowly. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book pp. 104–105, PDF pp. 117–118; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) of the serum is an indirect measure of which iron-related protein?
questions.explanation: Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) measures the maximum amount of ferric iron that serum transferrin can bind when completely saturated. Because virtually all circulating iron is carried on transferrin, TIBC directly reflects the concentration of circulating transferrin in serum (TIBC ≈ Serum Transferrin × 1.4). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book p. 111, PDF p. 124; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: For a patient with screening iron study values that are equivocal for iron deficiency, which of the following tests would be most helpful in determining whether iron deficiency is present or not?
questions.explanation: Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) levels rise specifically in cellular iron deficiency but remain unaffected by systemic acute or chronic inflammation. When ferritin is equivocal (e.g., falsely elevated as an acute-phase reactant during inflammation or infection), measuring sTfR or calculating the sTfR/log ferritin index reliably identifies true underlying iron deficiency. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book pp. 112–113, PDF pp. 125–126; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What membrane-associated protein in enterocytes transports iron from the intestinal lumen into the enterocyte?
questions.explanation: Divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) is the apical/luminal membrane transport protein in duodenal enterocytes responsible for importing nonheme divalent cations, specifically ferrous iron (Fe²⁺), after dietary ferric iron is reduced by apical cytochrome b (DCYTB). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book pp. 106–107, PDF pp. 119–120; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Iron is transported out of macrophages, hepatocytes, and enterocytes by what membrane protein?
questions.explanation: Ferroportin (SLC40A1) is the sole known cellular iron exporter in mammals. Located on the basolateral surface of duodenal enterocytes and on the plasma membranes of reticuloendothelial macrophages and hepatocytes, it transports intracellular ferrous iron into the extracellular fluid and plasma. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book pp. 107–108, PDF pp. 120–121; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt:
Following are several of the many steps in the process from absorption and transport of iron to incorporation into heme. Place them in proper order.
i. Transferrin picks up ferric iron.
ii. Iron is transferred to the mitochondria.
iii. DMT1 transports ferrous iron into the enterocyte.
iv. Ferroportin transports iron from enterocyte to plasma.
v. The transferrin receptor transports iron into the cell.
questions.explanation: The sequential physiological path of iron is: (iii) DMT1 transports ferrous iron from the intestinal lumen across the apical enterocyte membrane; (iv) ferroportin exports iron across the basolateral membrane into plasma; (i) hephaestin oxidizes it to Fe³⁺, and transferrin picks up ferric iron in plasma; (v) transferrin binds transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) on the erythroblast membrane and enters via endocytosis; and (ii) acidified endosomes release iron, which is transported into mitochondria for incorporation into protoporphyrin IX by ferrochelatase. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book pp. 106–110, PDF pp. 119–123; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What is the fate of the transferrin receptor when it has completed its role in the delivery of iron into a cell?
choices: It is recycled to the plasma membrane and released into the plasma.
It is recycled to the plasma membrane, where it can bind its ligand again.
It is catabolized and the amino acids are returned to the metabolic pool.
It is retained in the endosome for the life span of the cell.
questions.officialAnswer: It is recycled to the plasma membrane, where it can bind its ligand again.
questions.explanation: After receptor-mediated endocytosis of the transferrin-TfR1 complex into clathrin-coated vesicles, endosomal proton pumps acidify the lumen to pH ~5.5, triggering release of ferric iron while apotransferrin remains bound to TfR1. The apotransferrin-TfR1 complex is then recycled via exocytic vesicles back to the cell surface, where neutral extracellular pH (~7.4) causes apotransferrin to dissociate into plasma, freeing the surface receptor to bind another transferrin molecule. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book p. 109, PDF p. 122; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The transfer of iron from the enterocyte into the plasma is REGULATED by:
questions.explanation: Hepcidin is the master systemic peptide hormone regulating iron homeostasis, synthesized by hepatocytes. Hepcidin binds to the iron exporter ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages, inducing its internalization, ubiquitination, and lysosomal degradation, thereby shutting off iron export into plasma. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book pp. 107–108, PDF pp. 120–121; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What is the percent transferrin saturation for a patient with total serum iron of 63 µg/dL and TIBC of 420 µg/dL?
questions.explanation: Transferrin saturation (%) = (Serum Iron ÷ TIBC) × 100. Calculating: (63 µg/dL ÷ 420 µg/dL) × 100 = 0.15 × 100 = 15%. Normal transferrin saturation is 20% to 50%; values below 16% to 20% indicate iron-deficient erythropoiesis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book p. 111, PDF p. 124; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Referring to Figure 8.6, into which quadrant of a Thomas plot would a patient’s results fall with the following test results: Soluble transferrin receptor: increased above reference interval; Ferritin: decreased below reference interval; Hemoglobin content of reticulocytes: within the reference interval?
questions.explanation: In the Thomas plot diagnostic matrix (Figure 8.6), the x-axis assesses iron stores via the sTfR/log ferritin ratio (soluble transferrin receptor divided by log ferritin), while the y-axis assesses functional iron supply to reticulocytes via reticulocyte hemoglobin equivalent (Ret-He / CHr). When iron stores are depleted (elevated sTfR / low ferritin) but reticulocyte hemoglobin content remains within the reference interval, the patient falls into Quadrant 2: latent iron deficiency. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book pp. 113–114, PDF pp. 126–127; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

stimulus.alt: Figure 8.6 Thomas Plot diagnostic quadrants
stimulus.caption: Figure 8.6 Thomas plot illustrating the four quadrants of iron status assessment based on reticulocyte hemoglobin content and sTfR/log ferritin ratio.
