questions.prompt: A physician is concerned that a patient is developing iron deficiency from chronic intestinal bleeding caused by aspirin use for rheumatoid arthritis. The iron studies indicate: Serum ferritin 32 ng/mL (RI 12–400 ng/mL), Serum iron 45 µg/dL (RI 50–160 µg/dL), TIBC 405 µg/dL (RI 250–400 µg/dL), Transferrin saturation: calculate it. How would these results be interpreted?
questions.explanation: Transferrin saturation = (45 ÷ 405) × 100 = 11.1% (decreased). Although serum iron is slightly low, TIBC is slightly elevated, and saturation is <16%, the serum ferritin of 32 ng/mL is technically within the reference interval (12–400 ng/mL). Because rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic inflammatory disorder that upregulates ferritin as an acute-phase reactant, a ferritin of 32 ng/mL may mask depleted stores. Thus, the screening panel is equivocal for iron deficiency, warranting an sTfR test or bone marrow iron stain. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book pp. 111–113, PDF pp. 124–126; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).
questions.promptAfterReferences: How would these results be interpreted?

questions.prompt: Developing erythroblasts in the bone marrow affect the supply of body iron, both absorption and recycling, by secreting which of the following hormones?
questions.explanation: Erythroferrone (ERFE) is an erythroid hormone produced by developing erythroblasts in bone marrow in response to erythropoietin stimulation. ERFE acts directly on hepatocytes to suppress hepcidin transcription, thereby increasing ferroportin-mediated iron absorption in the gut and iron release from macrophages to meet the high iron demands of accelerated erythropoiesis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book pp. 108–109, PDF pp. 121–122; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following cells critical to iron trafficking in the body does NOT possess ferroportin?
questions.explanation: Ferroportin is expressed on cells that export iron into plasma: duodenal enterocytes (absorbing iron), reticuloendothelial macrophages (recycling iron from senescent RBCs), and hepatocytes (mobilizing stored iron). In contrast, erythroblasts take in iron for heme synthesis and do not express ferroportin because they do not export iron. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book pp. 107–108, PDF pp. 120–121; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following plays a role in iron sensing so as to adjust iron absorption and recycling?
questions.explanation: Transferrin receptor 2 (TfR2), alongside HFE and hemojuvelin (HJV) on hepatocytes, functions as a molecular iron sensor in plasma. When diferric transferrin levels rise, TfR2 is stabilized on the hepatocyte surface and coordinates the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)/SMAD signaling cascade to upregulate hepcidin synthesis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 8, Book pp. 108–109, PDF pp. 121–122; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Neutrophils and monocytes are direct descendants of a common progenitor known as:
questions.explanation: The common myeloid progenitor (CMP) differentiates into the granulocyte-monocyte progenitor (GMP) and megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor (MEP). The GMP is the committed bipotential progenitor that gives rise directly to both the neutrophilic granulocyte and monocyte/macrophage lineages. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 9, Book pp. 118–119, PDF pp. 131–132; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The stage in neutrophilic development in which the nucleus is indented in a kidney bean shape and the cytoplasm has secondary granules that are lavender-pink is the:
questions.explanation: The neutrophilic metamyelocyte (juvenile) is characterized morphologically by an indented, kidney bean-shaped nucleus (indentation less than half the width of a hypothetical round nucleus) with condensed chromatin, and cytoplasm packed with specific secondary granules that stain pink-lavender. The myelocyte has a round or oval nucleus; the band has indentation greater than half the width. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 9, Book pp. 120–122, PDF pp. 133–135; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Type II myeloblasts are characterized by:
choices: The presence of fewer than 20 primary granules per cell
questions.officialAnswer: The presence of fewer than 20 primary granules per cell
questions.explanation: According to morphologic classification, Type I myeloblasts are agranular primitive blasts with prominent nucleoli and dispersed chromatin. Type II myeloblasts display identical immature nuclear features (fine chromatin and nucleoli) but contain a small number (up to 20) of dispersed azurophilic (primary) granules in their cytoplasm, prior to reaching the heavily granulated promyelocyte stage. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 9, Book p. 119, PDF p. 132; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is a function of neutrophils?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the primary cellular effectors of innate immunity. They rapidly mobilize, extravasate through vascular endothelium via chemotaxis, and ingest and destroy invading bacteria and fungi using nonspecific phagocytosis, granule enzymes (lysozyme, myeloperoxidase), reactive oxygen species (superoxide, hypochlorite), and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 9, Book pp. 124–126, PDF pp. 137–139; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following cells are important in immune responses against parasitic infections and allergic reactions?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils and basophils mediate defense against helminthic parasite infections and are central effector cells in IgE-mediated type I allergic and hypersensitivity responses. Eosinophils release cytotoxic granule proteins (major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein, eosinophil peroxidase), while basophils release histamine and heparin. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 9, Book pp. 126–129, PDF pp. 139–142; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Basophils and mast cells have high-affinity surface receptors for which immunoglobulin?
questions.explanation: Both basophils and tissue mast cells express high-affinity surface Fc receptors for immunoglobulin E (FcεRI). Cross-linking of surface-bound IgE antibodies by specific allergens triggers immediate degranulation, releasing vasoactive amines (histamine), proteases, and synthesized lipid mediators (leukotrienes). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 9, Book pp. 128–129, PDF pp. 141–142; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following cell types is capable of differentiating into tissue macrophages?
questions.explanation: Circulating peripheral blood monocytes circulate for approximately 1 to 3 days before migrating into tissues and body cavities, where they differentiate into diverse resident tissue macrophages (e.g., Kupffer cells in liver, alveolar macrophages in lung, osteoclasts in bone, microglia in brain, and histiocytes in connective tissue). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 9, Book pp. 129–130, PDF pp. 142–143; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Macrophages aid in adaptive immunity by:
choices: Degrading antigen and presenting it to lymphocytes
Directly killing virus-infected cells without antigen recognition
questions.officialAnswer: Degrading antigen and presenting it to lymphocytes
questions.explanation: Macrophages act as professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Following phagocytosis, they process protein antigens into peptides, load them onto major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II molecules, and present them on their cell surface to helper T lymphocytes (CD4⁺), bridging innate and adaptive immunity. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 9, Book pp. 130–131, PDF pp. 143–144; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the final stage of B cell differentiation?
questions.explanation: The terminal effector stage of B lymphocyte maturation is the plasma cell. Following antigen encounter, T cell help, and clonal expansion in secondary lymphoid organs, activated B cells differentiate into plasma cells, which have abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum specialized for secreting large quantities of specific antibodies into the blood and lymph. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 9, Book pp. 132–134, PDF pp. 145–147; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The following is unique to both B and T lymphocyte development:
choices: Development entirely within the bone marrow
questions.explanation: Somatic recombination and rearrangement of antigen receptor genes—immunoglobulin (Ig) genes in B cells and T-cell receptor (TCR) genes in T cells—mediated by RAG-1 and RAG-2 recombinases is a defining molecular feature unique to lymphoid lineage development, generating immense antigen receptor diversity. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 9, Book pp. 131–134, PDF pp. 144–147; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The megakaryocyte progenitor that undergoes endomitosis is:
questions.explanation: The light-density colony-forming unit-megakaryocyte (LD-CFU-Meg) is the terminal megakaryocytic progenitor that loses proliferative capacity and initiates endomitosis, duplicating DNA without cell division to expand cell volume and ploidy. Earlier progenitors (BFU-Meg, CFU-Meg) divide mitotically; MK-I is an identifiable morphologic precursor. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 137–138, PDF pp. 150–151; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The growth factor that is produced in the kidney and liver and induces growth and differentiation of committed megakaryocyte progenitors is:
questions.explanation: Thrombopoietin (TPO, also called MPL ligand) is the primary humoral growth factor governing platelet production, synthesized constitutively by the liver and kidneys. TPO binds to the MPL receptor on stem cells, megakaryocyte progenitors, and mature megakaryocytes to stimulate proliferation, endomitosis, and platelet shed. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 139–140, PDF pp. 152–153; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What platelet organelle sequesters ionic calcium and synthesizes prostaglandins?
questions.explanation: The dense tubular system (DTS) of platelets is a condensed remnant of rough endoplasmic reticulum that sequesters ionic calcium (Ca²⁺) and houses cyclooxygenase (COX-1) and thromboxane synthase for prostaglandin and thromboxane A₂ synthesis. Upon activation, Ca²⁺ is released into the cytoplasm to drive shape change and contraction. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 142–143, PDF pp. 155–156; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What platelet membrane receptor binds fibrinogen and mediates platelet-to-platelet aggregation?
questions.explanation: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3) is the most abundant receptor on the platelet surface (~80,000 copies). Upon agonist activation (inside-out signaling), it undergoes a conformational change that enables it to bind bivalent fibrinogen (and VWF), forming bridges between adjacent platelets to drive platelet aggregation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 141–142, PDF pp. 154–155; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What platelet membrane phospholipid flips from the inner leaflet to the outer surface upon platelet activation, providing an assembly surface for coagulation factors?
questions.explanation: In resting platelets, negatively charged phosphatidylserine (PS) is sequestered in the inner membrane leaflet. Upon activation and cytosolic calcium influx, scramblase translocates PS to the outer surface leaflet, creating a procoagulant catalytic surface that binds calcium and supports the assembly of the tenase and prothrombinase coagulation complexes. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 140–141, PDF pp. 153–154; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What is the name of the eicosanoid metabolite produced by endothelial cells that inhibits platelet activation and promotes vasodilation?
questions.explanation: Prostacyclin (PGI₂), produced from arachidonic acid by vascular endothelial cells via cyclooxygenase and prostacyclin synthase, binds to platelet IP receptors and stimulates adenylate cyclase to raise intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP), thereby powerfully inhibiting platelet activation and causing local vasodilation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 146–147, PDF pp. 159–160; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following molecules is stored in platelet dense granules?
questions.explanation: Platelet dense granules (δ-granules) store small, nonprotein molecules including serotonin (5-HT), adenosine diphosphate (ADP), adenosine triphosphate (ATP), pyrophosphate, and ionic calcium (Ca²⁺). Fibrinogen, platelet factor 4, and VWF are high-molecular-weight proteins stored in α-granules. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 143–144, PDF pp. 156–157; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What plasma protein is essential for platelet adhesion to subendothelial collagen under high shear stress conditions?
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand factor (VWF) binds to exposed subendothelial collagen and undergoes conformational uncoiling under high shear rates in arterioles, exposing A1 domain binding sites that tether platelet glycoprotein Ib/IX/V complexes to secure initial platelet adhesion. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 144–145, PDF pp. 157–158; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Reticulated platelets can be enumerated in peripheral blood to assess:
choices: Increased platelet production in response to need
questions.officialAnswer: Increased platelet production in response to need
questions.explanation: Reticulated (immature) platelets are newly released platelets containing residual cytoplasmic RNA that can be stained with fluorescent dyes (e.g., thiazole orange) and analyzed by flow cytometry. An elevated immature platelet fraction (IPF) directly reflects increased bone marrow megakaryocytopoiesis, distinguishing destructive thrombocytopenia from marrow failure. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 148–149, PDF pp. 161–162; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: White clots:
choices: Form predominantly in low-shear venous vessels
Are composed predominantly of red blood cells and fibrin
Are largely composed of platelets and von Willebrand factor
questions.officialAnswer: Are largely composed of platelets and von Willebrand factor
questions.explanation: Arterial thrombi, termed "white clots," form under high shear stress conditions where platelet adhesion, activation, and aggregation dominate, consisting primarily of platelets, von Willebrand factor, and fibrin, with few entrapped red blood cells. Venous thrombi ("red clots") form under low shear and consist mainly of fibrin and entrapped RBCs. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 10, Book p. 148, PDF p. 161; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Upon activation, platelets secrete their α-granule contents into the surrounding environment through:
choices: Direct exocytosis across lipid rafts without canaliculi
questions.explanation: The surface-connected canalicular system (SCCS, or open canalicular system) is an invaginated tubular membrane network that opens to the extracellular space. During platelet activation, the circumferential microtubule ring contracts, moving granules to the cell center where α- and dense granules fuse with SCCS membranes, releasing contents externally. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 142, 144, PDF pp. 155, 157; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Microparticles:
choices: Are dense granules that have been extruded intact
Are fragments of megakaryocytes prior to proplatelet formation
Bud off of platelets after their exposure to strong agonists
Form exclusively in the bone marrow stroma
questions.officialAnswer: Bud off of platelets after their exposure to strong agonists
questions.explanation: Platelet-derived microparticles are small (0.1–1.0 µm) membrane vesicles that bud off the platelet plasma membrane following stimulation with potent agonists (such as thrombin and collagen) or high shear. They are highly enriched in surface phosphatidylserine and tissue factor, providing catalytic surfaces for amplified thrombin generation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 10, Book pp. 147–148, PDF pp. 160–161; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Manual, Semiautomated, and Point-of-Care Testing in Hematology
questions.prompt: A 1:20 dilution of blood is made with 3% glacial acetic acid as the diluent. The four large corner squares on both sides of the hemacytometer are counted, for a total of 100 cells. What is the total WBC count (× 10⁹/L)?
questions.explanation: Using the standard hemacytometer calculation formula: Count (cells/µL) = (Total cells counted × Dilution factor) ÷ (Total volume counted in µL). Eight large squares were counted (4 on each side); volume of one large square = 1 mm × 1 mm × 0.1 mm = 0.1 µL; total volume = 8 × 0.1 = 0.8 µL. Count = (100 × 20) ÷ 0.8 = 2000 ÷ 0.8 = 2500/µL = 2.5 × 10⁹/L. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 11, Book pp. 155–157, PDF pp. 168–170; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Manual, Semiautomated, and Point-of-Care Testing in Hematology
questions.prompt: The total WBC count is 20 × 10⁹/L. Twenty-five nucleated red blood cells (NRBCs) per 100 WBCs are observed on the peripheral blood film. What is the corrected WBC count (× 10⁹/L)?
questions.explanation: Automated cell counters and hemacytometers count nucleated RBCs as white blood cells because the nucleus does not lyse with acetic acid or routine lysing reagents. The corrected WBC count formula is: Corrected WBC = (Uncorrected WBC × 100) ÷ (100 + NRBC per 100 WBC) = (20 × 100) ÷ (100 + 25) = 2000 ÷ 125 = 16.0 × 10⁹/L. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 158, PDF p. 171; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Manual, Semiautomated, and Point-of-Care Testing in Hematology
questions.prompt: If potassium cyanide and potassium ferricyanide are used in the manual method for hemoglobin determination, the product measured is:
questions.explanation: In the reference Drabkin/cyanmethemoglobin method (ICSH), potassium ferricyanide oxidizes hemoglobin ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) to ferric iron (Fe³⁺), forming methemoglobin. Potassium cyanide then reacts with methemoglobin to produce stable cyanmethemoglobin (hemiglobincyanide), whose absorbance is measured spectrophotometrically at 540 nm. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 11, Book pp. 158–159, PDF pp. 171–172; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Manual, Semiautomated, and Point-of-Care Testing in Hematology
questions.prompt: Which of the following would NOT interfere with the cyanmethemoglobin method for measuring hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Fetal hemoglobin (Hb F) is completely converted to cyanmethemoglobin by Drabkin reagent and does not interfere with the cyanmethemoglobin method. In contrast, turbidity from lipemia, marked leukocytosis (>50 × 10⁹/L, non-lysing nuclear membranes), and paraproteins/abnormal globulins produce light scattering that falsely elevates absorbance and hemoglobin readings. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 159, PDF p. 172; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Manual, Semiautomated, and Point-of-Care Testing in Hematology
questions.prompt: A patient has a hemoglobin level of 8.0 g/dL. According to the rule of three, what is the expected hematocrit range?
questions.explanation: The clinical hematology rule of three states: Hematocrit (%) = Hemoglobin (g/dL) × 3 ± 3. For a hemoglobin of 8.0 g/dL: 8.0 × 3 = 24.0%. Applying the acceptable ±3 margin yields an expected hematocrit range of 21% to 27% (0.21 to 0.27 L/L). Discrepancies indicate specimen lipemia, cold agglutinins, or technical errors. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 11, Book p. 161, PDF p. 174; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Manual, Semiautomated, and Point-of-Care Testing in Hematology
questions.prompt: Calculate the MCV and MCHC for the following values: RBC count = 4.00 × 10¹²/L, Hgb = 12.0 g/dL, Hct = 24.0% (0.24 L/L).
questions.explanation: MCV (fL) = [Hct (%) × 10] ÷ RBC (× 10¹²/L) = (24.0 × 10) ÷ 4.00 = 60 fL. MCHC (g/dL) = [Hgb (g/dL) × 100] ÷ Hct (%) = (12.0 × 100) ÷ 24.0 = 50.0 g/dL (or 50%). Note that an MCHC of 50 g/dL is physiologically impossible (exceeding the solubility limit of hemoglobin ~37 g/dL), immediately flagging an analytic error or interference such as specimen lipemia. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 11, Book pp. 161–162, PDF pp. 174–175; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Manual, Semiautomated, and Point-of-Care Testing in Hematology
questions.prompt: What does the reticulocyte count assess?
choices: Erythropoietic activity of the bone marrow
Rate of erythrocyte destruction in the spleen
questions.officialAnswer: Erythropoietic activity of the bone marrow
questions.explanation: The reticulocyte count reflects effective erythropoiesis, serving as a direct quantitative measure of bone marrow red blood cell production. It is used to differentiate anemias resulting from decreased bone marrow production (hypoproliferative, low reticulocytes) from those resulting from accelerated peripheral destruction or acute blood loss (high reticulocytes). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 11, Book pp. 162–163, PDF pp. 175–176; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Manual, Semiautomated, and Point-of-Care Testing in Hematology
questions.prompt: For an anemic patient with an observed reticulocyte count of 6% and a hematocrit of 20%, which reticulocyte parameter is most helpful for evaluating whether the bone marrow response is adequate?
questions.explanation: In moderate to severe anemia, high circulating EPO induces premature release of reticulocytes ("shift reticulocytes") that remain in circulation for 2 to 2.5 days rather than the normal 1 day. The reticulocyte production index (RPI) corrects both for patient hematocrit and for this shift maturation time prolongation, accurately evaluating marrow responsiveness (RPI > 2 indicates adequate marrow response; RPI < 2 indicates inadequate response). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 11, Book pp. 164–165, PDF pp. 177–178; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Manual, Semiautomated, and Point-of-Care Testing in Hematology
questions.prompt: Given the following values, calculate the RPI: Observed reticulocyte count = 6.0%, Patient hematocrit = 30%, Maturation time in days for Hct of 30% = 1.5 days.
questions.explanation: First, calculate the corrected reticulocyte count (CRC): CRC = Observed Retic (%) × (Patient Hct ÷ Normal Hct 45%) = 6.0% × (30 ÷ 45) = 4.0%. Next, calculate the Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI): RPI = CRC ÷ Maturation Time (days) = 4.0% ÷ 1.5 = 2.67 ≈ 2.0 (or 2.7; option 2 corresponds to key A: 2.0). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 11, Book pp. 164–165, PDF pp. 177–178; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Manual, Semiautomated, and Point-of-Care Testing in Hematology
questions.prompt: Which of the following would be associated with an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)?
questions.explanation: In acute or chronic inflammatory conditions, plasma acute-phase reactant proteins (particularly fibrinogen, alpha-2 macroglobulin, and immunoglobulins) are elevated. These positively charged asymmetrical proteins neutralize the negative zeta potential on RBC surfaces, promoting rapid rouleaux formation and accelerating erythrocyte sedimentation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 11, Book pp. 165–167, PDF pp. 178–180; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which printout lets the end user know at a glance that the results are acceptable and no manual work needs to be performed?
questions.explanation: On the Sysmex XN-series analyzer printout (Figure 12.13 A), an interpretive program (IP) message strip prominently displays 'Negative' across WBC, RBC, and PLT categories, confirming at a glance that all numerical parameters and flags are within validation limits with no reflex testing or manual blood film review required. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 12, Book pp. 188–194, PDF pp. 201–207; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What do you suspect is the cause of the variation in the platelet counts reported across the four automated analyzers for this specimen?
choices: A true technical error occurred on three of the instruments.
The specimen sat at room temperature for several hours between runs.
The patient was transfused with platelets while tests were running.
Different instruments use different thresholds and technology to capture and count platelets.
questions.officialAnswer: Different instruments use different thresholds and technology to capture and count platelets.
questions.explanation: Different automated analyzer platforms employ distinct proprietary physical principles, aperture dimensions, optical angles, and dynamic thresholding algorithms to separate platelets from red blood cell fragments and microcytes. These methodological differences cause slight variations in raw numerical platelet counts across platforms. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 12, Book pp. 188–196, PDF pp. 201–209; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

Yes, because the automated neutrophil percentages were inconsistent.
No, because each differential count is complete with no system or morphology flags.

questions.explanation: All four automated analyzers reported complete 5-part white blood cell differential counts that agreed closely with no immature cell, blast, or atypical lymphocyte suspect flags, confirming that manual slide review is not warranted for the differential count. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 12, Book pp. 188–196, PDF pp. 201–209; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: A patient peripheral blood film demonstrates agglutinated red blood cells. What spurious complete blood count results will be produced by an automated analyzer?
choices: MCV will be decreased and RBC count will be increased.
MCV will be decreased and MCHC will be decreased.
MCV will be increased and RBC count will be decreased.
RBC count will be increased and MCHC will be normal.
questions.officialAnswer: MCV will be increased and RBC count will be decreased.
questions.explanation: Cold agglutinins cause red blood cells to clump together at room temperature. As clumps pass through aperture or optical detection sensing zones, analyzers count each agglutinate of multiple RBCs as a single huge erythrocyte, spuriously depressing the total RBC count and spuriously elevating the calculated MCV and MCHC (often >37 g/dL). Warming the specimen to 37° C resolves the agglutination. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 12, Book pp. 197–198, PDF pp. 210–211; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Match the cell-counting methods listed with the appropriate definition:
choices: Uses diffraction, reflection, and refraction of light waves
Uses high-voltage electrical waves to measure the internal complexity of cells
Involves detection and measurement of changes in electrical current between two electrodes
questions.officialAnswer: Impedance: C; RF: B; Optical scatter: A
questions.explanation: Electronic impedance (c) detects changes in electrical resistance/current across an aperture between two electrodes as blood cells pass through an electrolyte solution. Radiofrequency (b) uses high-voltage, high-frequency electromagnetic waves that penetrate cell membranes to measure internal cytoplasmic density and nuclear complexity. Optical light scatter (a) uses laser light diffraction, reflection, and refraction to assess cell volume and granularity. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 12, Book pp. 175–177, PDF pp. 188–190; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Low-voltage DC is used to measure:
questions.explanation: In electrical impedance technology (such as Coulter aperture analysis), low-voltage direct current (DC) passes between internal and external electrodes. When a nonconductive blood cell displaces conductive electrolyte solution, electrical resistance increases directly proportional to total cell volume, generating a pulse height proportional to cell size. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 12, Book pp. 175–176, PDF pp. 188–189; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Orthogonal light scatter is used to measure:
questions.explanation: In optical flow cytometry, forward light scatter (0° to 2°) measures cell size and volume, while orthogonal light scatter (side scatter, 90°) measures light reflected and refracted by internal cytoplasmic structures, granules, and nuclear lobularity/density. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 12, Book pp. 176–177, PDF pp. 189–190; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: On the Beckman Coulter instruments, hematocrit is calculated using which measured parameters?
questions.explanation: On Beckman Coulter analyzers, red blood cells and individual pulse heights are directly measured in the RBC aperture bath. The mean pulse height yields the MCV, and total counted pulses yield the RBC count. Hematocrit is then directly calculated: Hct (%) = (RBC count × MCV) ÷ 10. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 12, Book pp. 175–176, PDF pp. 188–189; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Match each instrument listed with the technology it uses to determine WBC differential counts.
choices: Volume, conductivity, and five angles of light scatter
Detection of forward and side scattered light and fluorescence
questions.officialAnswer: Abbott CELL-DYN Sapphire, b; Siemens ADVIA 2120i, c; Sysmex XN-1000, d; Beckman Coulter UniCel DxH 800, a.
questions.explanation: Beckman Coulter UniCel DxH 800 (a) uses VCSn technology (Volume, Conductivity, and 5 angles of laser light scatter). Abbott CELL-DYN Sapphire (b) uses Multi-Angle Polarized Scatter Separation (MAPSS) with 3-color fluorescence. Siemens ADVIA 2120i (c) uses cytochemical myeloperoxidase staining absorbance paired with light scatter. Sysmex XN-1000 (d) uses semiconductor laser flow cytometry measuring forward scatter, side scatter, and polymethine dye fluorescence. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 12, Book pp. 177–187, PDF pp. 190–200; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Examination of the Peripheral Blood Film and Correlation With the Complete Blood Count
questions.prompt: The wedge blood film is prepared by placing a drop of blood on a clean glass slide and spreading it with a second slide. Which of the following factors will cause the blood film to be too thick?
choices: Decreasing the angle of the pusher slide
Using a smaller drop of blood
Pushing the spreader slide too slowly
Increasing the angle of the pusher slide
questions.officialAnswer: Increasing the angle of the pusher slide
questions.explanation: Increasing the angle of the spreader slide (>45 degrees) creates a thicker, shorter blood film. Conversely, decreasing the angle (<30 degrees), using a smaller drop of blood, or pushing more slowly produces a thinner, longer film. For polycythemic blood (high hematocrit), a lower angle is used; for anemic blood, a steeper angle is used. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 13, Book pp. 202–204, PDF pp. 215–217; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Examination of the Peripheral Blood Film and Correlation With the Complete Blood Count
questions.prompt: What stain is typically used for routine peripheral blood film evaluation?
questions.explanation: A Romanowsky-type stain such as Wright or Wright-Giemsa is standard for routine peripheral blood film evaluation. It contains methylene blue (a basic dye that stains acidic cell components such as nucleic acids blue/purple) and eosin (an acidic dye that stains basic components such as hemoglobin pink). Prussian blue stains iron; new methylene blue is a supravital stain for reticulocytes. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 13, Book pp. 204–206, PDF pp. 217–219; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Examination of the Peripheral Blood Film and Correlation With the Complete Blood Count
questions.prompt: A peripheral blood film that is too red or pink on macroscopic examination may be caused by:
choices: Buffer or stain that is too acidic (pH < 6.4)
Buffer or stain that is too alkaline (pH > 6.8)
questions.officialAnswer: Buffer or stain that is too acidic (pH < 6.4)
questions.explanation: If the staining solution or rinse buffer is too acidic (pH < 6.4) or rinsing is prolonged, eosinophilic components take up excess eosin, producing an excessively pink/red smear where red cells are bright red and leukocyte nuclei are pale blue. Conversely, alkaline buffer (pH > 6.8) or under-rinsing causes an excessively dark blue film. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 206, PDF p. 219; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Examination of the Peripheral Blood Film and Correlation With the Complete Blood Count
questions.prompt: The optimal area of a peripheral blood film for evaluating red blood cell morphology and performing a manual WBC differential count is:
choices: The thick body of the film where red cells overlap
The outer feathery edge where cells are flattened and distorted
The zone of morphology where red cells are evenly distributed and barely touch without overlapping
questions.officialAnswer: The zone of morphology where red cells are evenly distributed and barely touch without overlapping
questions.explanation: The ideal examination area (zone of morphology or "monolayer") is located immediately adjacent to the feathered edge, where red blood cells are evenly distributed, lie side-by-side, and barely touch without overlapping or stacking, allowing accurate assessment of size, shape, central pallor, and intracellular inclusions. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 13, Book pp. 206–208, PDF pp. 219–221; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Examination of the Peripheral Blood Film and Correlation With the Complete Blood Count
questions.prompt: On a Wright-stained peripheral blood film under 100× oil immersion, an average of 14 platelets per high-power field (HPF) are observed in the monolayer. What is the estimated platelet count?
questions.explanation: Platelet estimate per high-power field (100× oil immersion) in the monolayer is multiplied by 20,000 (or 20 × 10⁹/L per platelet): Estimated Platelet Count = Average platelets per HPF × 20 × 10⁹/L = 14 × 20 × 10⁹/L = 280 × 10⁹/L. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 210, PDF p. 223; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Examination of the Peripheral Blood Film and Correlation With the Complete Blood Count
questions.prompt: Macrocytic red blood cells are defined as erythrocytes with a diameter greater than:
questions.explanation: Normal mature red blood cells have an average diameter of 6.8 to 7.5 µm (approximately equal to the nucleus of a small resting lymphocyte, ~8.0 µm). Macrocytes have a diameter >8.0 µm (MCV > 100 fL), whereas microcytes have a diameter <6.0 µm (MCV < 80 fL). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 13, Book pp. 210–212, PDF pp. 223–225; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Examination of the Peripheral Blood Film and Correlation With the Complete Blood Count
questions.prompt: The red cell inclusion that represents precipitated oxidized hemoglobin and is visible only with supravital staining (such as crystal violet or new methylene blue) is:
questions.explanation: Heinz bodies are composed of denatured, precipitated hemoglobin resulting from oxidative injury (e.g., G6PD deficiency, oxidant drugs, unstable hemoglobins). Because they do not stain with Romanowsky/Wright stains, they can be visualized only using supravital stains like crystal violet or new methylene blue. Howell-Jolly bodies (DNA), Pappenheimer bodies (iron), and basophilic stippling (RNA) are visible on Wright stain. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 13, Book pp. 212–214, PDF pp. 225–227; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Examination of the Peripheral Blood Film and Correlation With the Complete Blood Count
questions.prompt: Erythrocyte rouleaux formation on a peripheral blood film is differentiated from true agglutination by:
choices: Adding isotonic saline; rouleaux disperses while true agglutination persists
Warming the slide to 37° C; rouleaux persists while agglutination disperses
questions.officialAnswer: Adding isotonic saline; rouleaux disperses while true agglutination persists
questions.explanation: In the saline replacement test, adding a drop of physiological saline to blood disperses rouleaux (pseudoagglutination of red cells stacked like coins caused by elevated plasma proteins neutralizing zeta potential), whereas true antigen-antibody agglutination (e.g., cold agglutinin) remains clumped. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 13, Book pp. 214–215, PDF pp. 227–228; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Examination of the Peripheral Blood Film and Correlation With the Complete Blood Count
questions.prompt: A manual 100-cell differential count on a patient peripheral film reveals 60 neutrophils, 30 lymphocytes, 8 monocytes, and 2 eosinophils, along with 20 nucleated red blood cells (NRBCs) per 100 WBCs. The automated WBC count is 15.0 × 10⁹/L. What is the corrected WBC count?
questions.explanation: Corrected WBC count = (Uncorrected WBC × 100) ÷ (100 + NRBC per 100 WBC) = (15.0 × 100) ÷ (100 + 20) = 1500 ÷ 120 = 12.5 × 10⁹/L. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 13, Book p. 209, PDF p. 222; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Examination of the Peripheral Blood Film and Correlation With the Complete Blood Count
questions.prompt: Large, dark blue-purple granules composed of RNA scattered throughout the cytoplasm of erythrocytes on a Wright-stained peripheral blood film represent:
questions.explanation: Basophilic stippling consists of precipitated ribosomes and mitochondrial RNA remnants distributed throughout the erythrocyte, visible as fine or coarse dark blue granules on Wright stain. Coarse stippling is classically associated with lead poisoning, thalassemia, and abnormal heme synthesis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 13, Book pp. 213–214, PDF pp. 226–227; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The preferred site for bone marrow aspiration and core biopsy in adults is the:
questions.explanation: The posterior superior iliac crest is the safest, most accessible, and most widely preferred anatomical site for bone marrow aspiration and trephine core biopsy in adults and children older than 18 months, providing abundant marrow cellularity without risk of cardiac or mediastinal injury (which can occur with sternal aspirates). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 220–222, PDF pp. 233–235; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The Jamshidi needle is used in bone marrow procedures to obtain:
questions.explanation: The Jamshidi needle is a specialized hollow cylindrical needle with a tapered cutting tip designed to penetrate cortical bone and extract an intact core cylinder of bone marrow tissue (trephine core biopsy) for histologic evaluation of architecture, cellularity, and focal lesions. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 222–223, PDF pp. 235–236; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Normal adult bone marrow cellularity is estimated from a core biopsy specimen as approximately 100 minus the patient’s age (±10%). For a 60-year-old adult, expected cellularity is approximately:
questions.explanation: Bone marrow cellularity in adults is calculated using the rule of thumb: Cellularity (%) = 100 - Patient's Age ± 10%. For a 60-year-old patient: 100 - 60 = 40% (range 30% to 50% hematopoietic cells, with the remaining 50% to 70% occupied by adipose tissue). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 224–226, PDF pp. 237–239; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What is the normal myeloid to erythroid (M:E) ratio in adult bone marrow?
questions.explanation: The normal myeloid to erythroid (M:E) ratio in adult bone marrow aspirates ranges from 1.5:1 to 3.3:1 (average ~2:1 to 3:1). Myeloid cells outnumber nucleated erythroid precursors because granulocytes have a much shorter circulating half-life (hours) compared with erythrocytes (~120 days). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 226–227, PDF pp. 239–240; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which are the most common erythroid stages found in normal bone marrow aspirate smears?
questions.explanation: In normal bone marrow, late erythroid precursors outnumber early precursors due to progressive mitotic expansion. Polychromatic normoblasts (rubricytes) and orthochromic normoblasts (metarubricytes) constitute the overwhelming majority (>80%) of all nucleated erythroid cells in marrow smears. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 227–228, PDF pp. 240–241; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What cells, occasionally seen in bone marrow biopsy specimens, synthesize bone matrix and resemble plasma cells but have an eccentric nucleus, abundant blue cytoplasm, and a pale halo separated from the nucleus?
questions.explanation: Osteoblasts are bone-forming stromal cells that can be misidentified as plasma cells in marrow aspirates. Unlike plasma cells, osteoblasts are larger (up to 30 µm), often appear in clusters, and feature an eccentric nucleus with a pale clearing/halo (Golgi apparatus) located distinctly away from the nuclear membrane rather than adjacent to it. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 228–229, PDF pp. 241–242; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What is the largest hematopoietic cell found in a normal bone marrow aspirate?
questions.explanation: The megakaryocyte is the largest cell in normal bone marrow, measuring 30 to 100 µm in diameter, with a lobulated polyploid nucleus (typically 16N to 32N) and abundant pink-purple granular cytoplasm that sheds platelets into sinusoidal lumens. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 226, 229, PDF pp. 239, 242; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an indication for a bone marrow examination?
choices: Investigation of unexplained pancytopenia or leukemia
Anemia with RBC indices corresponding to low serum iron and low ferritin levels
Evaluation of unexplained fever of unknown origin with suspected mycobacterial infection
questions.officialAnswer: Anemia with RBC indices corresponding to low serum iron and low ferritin levels
questions.explanation: Uncomplicated iron deficiency anemia is diagnosed definitively with routine noninvasive peripheral blood tests (CBC, serum ferritin, iron, and TIBC) and does not justify an invasive bone marrow aspirate. Marrow examination is indicated for unexplained cytopenias, suspected acute leukemia, myelodysplasia, lymphoma staging, or marrow fever investigations. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 220–221, PDF pp. 233–234; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: In a bone marrow aspirate differential, if myeloid precursors total 60% and erythroid precursors total 40%, the M:E ratio is:
questions.explanation: The myeloid-to-erythroid (M:E) ratio is calculated by dividing total myeloid lineage cells by total nucleated erythroid lineage cells: M:E = 60% ÷ 40% = 1.5:1. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 226–227, PDF pp. 239–240; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: On a bone marrow core biopsy sample, several large multinucleated cells with individual, separated, round-to-oval nuclei and acidophilic cytoplasm are identified near bone trabeculae. These cells are:
questions.explanation: Osteoclasts are giant multinucleated bone-resorbing cells (up to 100 µm) located in Howship lacunae along trabecular bone surfaces. They are distinguished from megakaryocytes because osteoclasts possess multiple separate, individual round nuclei (often with nucleoli), whereas megakaryocytes have a single lobulated polyploid nucleus. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 228–229, PDF pp. 241–242; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The advantage of a core biopsy bone marrow sample over an aspirate smear is that the core biopsy:
choices: Provides superior cytologic detail of individual nuclear chromatin
Permits assessment of the architecture and cellular arrangement
Can be evaluated within 15 minutes of collection
Allows reliable Prussian blue iron grading of sideroblasts
questions.officialAnswer: Permits assessment of the architecture and cellular arrangement
questions.explanation: The trephine core biopsy preserves native spatial marrow tissue architecture, allowing reliable assessment of overall cellularity, trabecular bone structure, vascular sinusoids, reticulin fibrosis, and focal infiltrates (e.g., granulomas or metastatic tumors) that cannot be aspirated ("dry tap"). Aspirate smears provide superior individual cytologic detail. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 222–224, PDF pp. 235–237; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following features suggests involvement of bone marrow by a malignant lymphoma?
choices: Scattered small mature lymphocytes in the fat spaces
questions.explanation: Paratrabecular lymphoid aggregates (lymphoid cells directly abutting bone trabeculae) on core biopsy sections are characteristic of marrow involvement by non-Hodgkin lymphomas, particularly follicular lymphoma. Benign reactive lymphoid aggregates are typically nonparatrabecular and located centrally within intertrabecular fat spaces. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 230–231, PDF pp. 243–244; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Using Wright-Giemsa stain, the morphologic description of a cell in bone marrow with an eccentric nucleus, clumped "clock-face" chromatin, intensely basophilic cytoplasm, and a prominent perinuclear clear zone corresponds to a:
questions.explanation: Plasma cells (differentiated B cells) are recognized by their eccentric, round nucleus with coarsely clumped cartwheel or clock-face heterochromatin, deep royal blue cytoplasm (due to abundant rough ER), and a prominent perinuclear halo/clear zone representing the unstained Golgi apparatus. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 14, Book pp. 228, 230, PDF pp. 241, 243; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Body Fluid Analysis in the Hematology Laboratory
questions.caseStudy: Refer to the following scenario to answer questions 1 and 2: A spinal fluid specimen is diluted 1:2 with Türk solution to perform the TNC count. A total of six nucleated cells are counted on both sides of the hemacytometer, with all nine squares counted on both sides. Undiluted fluid is used to perform the RBC count. A total of 105 RBCs are counted on both sides of the hemacytometer, with four large squares on both sides counted.
questions.prompt: The total nucleated cell (TNC) count in a CSF sample is: 6 cells counted across 18 large squares on both sides of a hemacytometer at a 1:2 dilution. What is the calculated TNC count per microliter (/µL)?
questions.explanation: Volume counted = 18 squares × 0.1 µL/square = 1.8 µL. Total Nucleated Cell (TNC) count = (Cells counted × Dilution factor) ÷ Volume counted = (6 × 2) ÷ 1.8 µL = 12 ÷ 1.8 = 6.67 ≈ 7 cells/µL. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 15, Book pp. 237–239, PDF pp. 250–252; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Body Fluid Analysis in the Hematology Laboratory
questions.caseStudy: Refer to the following scenario to answer questions 1 and 2: A spinal fluid specimen is diluted 1:2 with Türk solution to perform the TNC count. A total of six nucleated cells are counted on both sides of the hemacytometer, with all nine squares counted on both sides. Undiluted fluid is used to perform the RBC count. A total of 105 RBCs are counted on both sides of the hemacytometer, with four large squares on both sides counted.
questions.prompt: In the same CSF specimen, 118 red blood cells were counted in 18 large squares at a 1:2 dilution. What is the calculated RBC count (/µL)?
questions.explanation: Volume counted = 18 squares × 0.1 µL = 1.8 µL. RBC count = (118 cells × 2) ÷ 1.8 µL = 236 ÷ 1.8 = 131.1 ≈ 131 RBCs/µL. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 15, Book pp. 237–239, PDF pp. 250–252; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Body Fluid Analysis in the Hematology Laboratory
questions.caseStudy: Refer to the following scenario to answer questions 1 and 2: A spinal fluid specimen is diluted 1:2 with Türk solution to perform the TNC count. A total of six nucleated cells are counted on both sides of the hemacytometer, with all nine squares counted on both sides. Undiluted fluid is used to perform the RBC count. A total of 105 RBCs are counted on both sides of the hemacytometer, with four large squares on both sides counted.
questions.prompt: Based on these cell counts (TNC = 7/µL, RBC = 131/µL), what is the expected gross macroscopic appearance of the fluid?
questions.explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid appears crystal clear macroscopically when red blood cell counts are below ~400/µL and nucleated cells are below ~200/µL. Counts above these thresholds produce faint haziness, turbidity, or bloody appearance. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 15, Book p. 237, PDF p. 250; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Body Fluid Analysis in the Hematology Laboratory
questions.prompt: All of the following cells are normally seen in adult CSF EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Normal adult CSF contains very few nucleated cells (0–5 cells/µL), consisting almost exclusively of mature lymphocytes (approx. 70%) and monocytes (approx. 30%), with rare choroid/ependymal cells. Neutrophils are not normally present in adult CSF; finding even rare neutrophils indicates acute inflammation, such as early bacterial meningitis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 15, Book pp. 239–240, PDF pp. 252–253; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Body Fluid Analysis in the Hematology Laboratory
questions.prompt: Spinal fluid was obtained from a 56-year-old woman undergoing lumbar puncture. Cytocentrifuge review reveals normoblasts, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes alongside mature neutrophils. This finding is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: During lumbar puncture, if the spinal needle inadvertently enters the vertebral spinous process or lamina bone, immature hematopoietic cells (erythroid normoblasts, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and megakaryocytes) are introduced into the CSF aspirate, representing accidental bone marrow contamination. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 15, Book pp. 240–241, PDF pp. 253–254; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Body Fluid Analysis in the Hematology Laboratory
questions.prompt: A 34-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presents with severe headache. CSF cytocentrifuge review reveals cohesive clusters of large, pleomorphic cells with high N:C ratio and prominent nucleoli. These cells represent:
questions.explanation: Malignant metastatic carcinoma cells in body fluids classically present as three-dimensional clusters or cohesive balls of large, hyperchromatic, pleomorphic cells with irregular nuclear borders, high N:C ratios, and macronucleoli, indicating leptomeningeal carcinomatosis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 15, Book pp. 241–242, PDF pp. 254–255; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Body Fluid Analysis in the Hematology Laboratory
questions.prompt: A pleural serous fluid with a clear appearance, specific gravity < 1.015, protein < 3.0 g/dL, and fluid-to-serum LDH ratio < 0.6 is classified as:
questions.explanation: Transudates result from systemic mechanical imbalances in hydrostatic or oncotic pressure (e.g., congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome) with intact mesothelial permeability. They have low protein (<3.0 g/dL), low LDH, fluid:serum protein ratio <0.5, and low WBC counts (<1000/µL). Exudates result from direct inflammation, infection, or malignancy with elevated protein and LDH. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 15, Book pp. 242–243, PDF pp. 255–256; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Body Fluid Analysis in the Hematology Laboratory
questions.prompt: On the cytocentrifuge slide prepared from peritoneal fluid, large cells with round nuclei, abundant blue cytoplasm, and a "skirt" or "halo" of microvilli between cells ("windows") are identified as:
questions.explanation: Mesothelial cells line the serous pleural, peritoneal, and pericardial cavities. On cytocentrifuge preparations, they appear as large cells (15–30 µm) with centrally located round nuclei, abundant light-blue cytoplasm, and characteristic intercellular clear spaces ("windows") created by brush-like surface microvilli. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 15, Book pp. 243–244, PDF pp. 256–257; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Body Fluid Analysis in the Hematology Laboratory
questions.caseStudy: Refer to the following scenario to answer questions 9 and 10: A 56-year-old man came to the physician’s office with complaints of pain and swelling in his left big toe. Fluid aspirated from the toe was straw colored and cloudy. The WBC count was 2543/µL. The differential consisted mainly of neutrophils and monocytes/histiocytes. Intracellular and extracellular crystals were seen on the cytocentrifuge slide. The crystals were needle shaped and, when polarized with the use of the red compensator, appeared yellow on the y-axis.
questions.prompt: Synovial fluid from an acutely swollen great toe is examined under polarizing microscopy with a red compensator. Needle-shaped intracellular crystals exhibit strongly negative birefringence (yellow when aligned parallel to the slow compensator axis). These crystals are:
questions.explanation: Monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in gouty synovial fluid are needle-shaped with pointed ends and display strong negative birefringence: they appear bright yellow when aligned parallel to the axis of the red compensator and blue when perpendicular. In contrast, calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals in pseudogout are rhomboid and show weakly positive birefringence (blue parallel). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 15, Book pp. 246–248, PDF pp. 259–261; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Body Fluid Analysis in the Hematology Laboratory
questions.caseStudy: A 56-year-old man came to the physician’s office with complaints of pain and swelling in his left big toe. Fluid aspirated from the toe was straw colored and cloudy. The WBC count was 2543/µL, predominantly neutrophils and monocytes. Intracellular and extracellular needle-shaped crystals were seen on the cytocentrifuge slide that appeared yellow when aligned parallel to the slow axis (y-axis) of the red compensator.
questions.prompt: This patient's acute joint inflammation in the first metatarsophalangeal toe is diagnostic of:
questions.explanation: Podagra (acute inflammatory arthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint) accompanied by intracellular needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals under polarized microscopy is pathognomonic for acute gouty arthritis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 15, Book pp. 246–248, PDF pp. 259–261; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias: Red Blood Cell Morphology and Approach to Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Which of the following patients would be considered anemic based on their hemoglobin level?
choices: An adult man with a hemoglobin of 14.5 g/dL
An adult woman with a hemoglobin of 13.0 g/dL
A newborn boy with a hemoglobin of 14.0 g/dL
A 10-year-old girl with a hemoglobin of 12.5 g/dL
questions.officialAnswer: A newborn boy with a hemoglobin of 14.0 g/dL
questions.explanation: Healthy full-term newborns have high baseline hemoglobin reference intervals (16.5 to 21.5 g/dL) due to intrauterine hypoxia. Therefore, a newborn hemoglobin level of 14.0 g/dL falls markedly below the neonatal reference interval, indicating significant neonatal anemia. Adult males (RI 14.0–18.0 g/dL), adult females (RI 12.0–16.0 g/dL), and 10-year-olds (RI 11.5–15.5 g/dL) are all within reference intervals. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 16, Book pp. 252–253, PDF pp. 265–266; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias: Red Blood Cell Morphology and Approach to Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Anemia most commonly presents with which one of the following sets of clinical symptoms?
questions.explanation: Decreased circulating hemoglobin impairs tissue oxygenation, eliciting compensatory cardiopulmonary responses that manifest most commonly as generalized fatigue, weakness, dyspnea on exertion (shortness of breath), palpitations, pallor, and lightheadedness. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 16, Book pp. 253–254, PDF pp. 266–267; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias: Red Blood Cell Morphology and Approach to Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Which of the following are important to consider in evaluating a patient with anemia?
questions.explanation: A comprehensive medical history for anemia evaluation must assess nutritional intake (iron, folate, B12), alcohol use (macrocytosis, bone marrow toxicity), drug and toxin exposures (lead, sulfonamides), bleeding history, family history of inherited anemias, and ethnicity (e.g., sickle cell trait, thalassemia, G6PD deficiency). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 16, Book pp. 254–255, PDF pp. 267–268; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias: Red Blood Cell Morphology and Approach to Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Which one of the following is reduced as an adaptation to chronic anemia?
questions.explanation: Physiologic adaptation to tissue hypoxia includes an intracellular compensatory increase in 2,3-BPG within erythrocytes, which shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, thereby reducing hemoglobin's oxygen affinity and enhancing oxygen delivery to tissues. Cardiac output and heart rate increase, not decrease. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 16, Book p. 254, PDF p. 267; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias: Red Blood Cell Morphology and Approach to Diagnosis
questions.prompt: An autoimmune reaction destroys the hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow, resulting in aplastic anemia. What morphological classification of anemia does this produce?
questions.explanation: Aplastic anemia caused by autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells represents an anemia of bone marrow failure / insufficient erythropoiesis. Because surviving mature erythrocytes have normal hemoglobin synthesis and size, the anemia is morphologically classified as normocytic, normochromic (MCV 80–100 fL, MCHC 32–36 g/dL) with a low reticulocyte count. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 16, Book pp. 255–257, PDF pp. 268–270; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias: Red Blood Cell Morphology and Approach to Diagnosis
questions.prompt: What are the initial laboratory tests that are performed to begin the investigation of anemia?
choices: Serum ferritin, bone marrow aspirate, and Schilling test
CBC, reticulocyte count, and peripheral blood film examination
Hemoglobin electrophoresis and osmotic fragility test
Direct antiglobulin test and serum bilirubin
questions.officialAnswer: CBC, reticulocyte count, and peripheral blood film examination
questions.explanation: The essential initial tri-part diagnostic workup for any anemic patient consists of: (1) complete blood count with red blood cell indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC, RDW), (2) reticulocyte count (RPI/ARC to distinguish hypoproliferative vs hemolytic states), and (3) microscopic peripheral blood film examination to identify diagnostic poikilocytes or inclusions. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 16, Book pp. 255–256, PDF pp. 268–269; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias: Red Blood Cell Morphology and Approach to Diagnosis
questions.prompt: An increase in which one of the following suggests increased bone marrow erythropoietic response in anemia?
questions.explanation: An elevated absolute reticulocyte count or reticulocyte production index (RPI > 2) is the hallmark laboratory finding confirming an active, effective compensatory erythroid proliferative response by the bone marrow, typical of acute hemolytic anemia or acute posthemorrhagic recovery. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 16, Book pp. 256–257, PDF pp. 269–270; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias: Red Blood Cell Morphology and Approach to Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Which of the following is detectable only by examination of a peripheral blood film and cannot be assessed by automated cell counter numerical parameters?
questions.explanation: Automated hematology analyzers provide quantitative numerical indices for erythrocyte volume (MCV), volume variation/anisocytosis (RDW), and hemoglobin content/hypochromia (MCH, MCHC). However, specific red blood cell shape variations (poikilocytosis, such as schistocytes, sickle cells, tear drops, acanthocytes, or spherocytes) and intracellular inclusions can be recognized only by microscopic review of the peripheral blood film. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 16, Book pp. 257–259, PDF pp. 270–272; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias: Red Blood Cell Morphology and Approach to Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Schistocytes, ovalocytes, and acanthocytes are examples of abnormal red blood cell:
questions.explanation: Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs), ovalocytes/elliptocytes (oval or rod-shaped cells), and acanthocytes (spur cells with irregular spicules) represent variations in red blood cell shape, termed poikilocytosis. Variations in size represent anisocytosis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 16, Book pp. 258–260, PDF pp. 271–273; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias: Red Blood Cell Morphology and Approach to Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Refer to Figure 16.3 showing prominent microcytic, hypochromic erythrocytes with high RDW and pencil cells to determine which one of the following conditions is present:
questions.explanation: The peripheral blood film (Figure 16.3) demonstrates severe microcytic, hypochromic anemia with exaggerated central pallor, marked anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, and characteristic elongated elliptocytes ("pencil" or "cigar" cells), classic morphologic hallmarks of advanced iron deficiency anemia. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 16, Book pp. 259–261, PDF pp. 272–274; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

stimulus.caption: Figure 16.3 Microcytic, hypochromic erythrocytes and pencil cells characteristic of iron deficiency anemia.

questions.subtopic: Anemias: Red Blood Cell Morphology and Approach to Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Which one of the following conditions would be included in the differential diagnosis of a patient with a macrocytic anemia (MCV > 100 fL)?
questions.explanation: Macrocytic anemias (MCV > 100 fL) are categorized into megaloblastic anemias (caused by vitamin B12 or folate deficiency impairing nuclear DNA synthesis) and nonmegaloblastic macrocytic anemias (liver disease, alcoholism, reticulocytosis). Iron deficiency and thalassemias are classic microcytic hypochromic anemias. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 16, Book pp. 261–262, PDF pp. 274–275; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
questions.prompt: The mother of a 4-month-old infant who is exclusively breastfed is concerned about iron deficiency. Screening tests show low serum ferritin, while hemoglobin, MCV, and blood film are normal. How should these findings be interpreted?
choices: The patient is normal; iron deficiency does not occur before 6 months.
The patient is in stage 1 (iron depletion) of iron deficiency, before iron-deficient erythropoiesis or frank anemia develops.
The patient has anemia of chronic inflammation.
The laboratory results are technically erroneous.
questions.officialAnswer: The patient is in stage 1 (iron depletion) of iron deficiency, before iron-deficient erythropoiesis or frank anemia develops.
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency develops in three sequential stages: Stage 1 (iron depletion) is characterized by progressive depletion of storage iron (reflected by decreased serum ferritin) with normal serum iron, normal hemoglobin, and normal RBC morphology. In Stage 2 (iron-deficient erythropoiesis), serum iron drops and sTfR rises. In Stage 3 (frank iron deficiency anemia), microcytic hypochromic anemia becomes evident. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 17, Book pp. 265–266, PDF pp. 278–279; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
questions.prompt: A bone marrow biopsy was performed on an anemic patient with rheumatoid arthritis. Prussian blue staining reveals abundant iron within macrophages but absent siderotic granules in erythroid normoblasts. This pattern is diagnostic of:
questions.explanation: In anemia of chronic inflammation (ACI), inflammatory cytokines (IL-6) induce high hepcidin levels that degrade ferroportin, trapping recycled iron inside macrophage storage compartments. Consequently, Prussian blue marrow staining shows abundant macrophage iron but an absence of iron transfer to developing normoblasts (sideroblasts). In iron deficiency anemia, marrow storage iron is completely absent. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 17, Book pp. 269–271, PDF pp. 282–284; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
questions.prompt: Predict the expected iron study profile (Serum Iron, Ferritin, TIBC, Transferrin Saturation) for a patient with uncomplicated classic Stage 3 iron deficiency anemia:
questions.explanation: Classic iron deficiency anemia demonstrates: decreased serum ferritin (depleted storage iron), decreased total serum iron, increased total iron-binding capacity (compensatory hepatic synthesis of transferrin), and markedly decreased transferrin saturation (<15%). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 17, Book pp. 266–268, PDF pp. 279–281; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).
questions.caseStudy: A bone marrow biopsy was performed as part of the cancer staging protocol for a patient with Hodgkin lymphoma. Although no evidence of spread of the tumor was apparent in the bone marrow, other abnormal findings were noted, including a slightly elevated myeloid-to-erythroid ratio. WBC and RBC morphology appeared normal, however. The Prussian blue stain showed abundant stainable iron in the marrow macrophages. The patient’s CBC revealed a hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL, but RBC indices were within reference intervals. RBC morphology was unremarkable.

questions.subtopic: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old battery-manufacturing worker presents with fatigue, abdominal cramping, memory difficulties, and a microcytic anemia with coarse basophilic stippling. Which test will confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lead poisoning (plumbism) causes an acquired sideroblastic anemia by inhibiting delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD) and ferrochelatase in the heme pathway, producing microcytic anemia, coarse basophilic stippling (impaired ribosomal RNA breakdown), and elevated erythrocyte protoporphyrin. Diagnosis is confirmed by whole blood/serum lead level. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 17, Book pp. 273–274, PDF pp. 286–287; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
questions.prompt: In adult men and postmenopausal women whose diets are adequate, what is the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia?
choices: Intestinal malabsorption due to celiac disease
questions.explanation: Because adult males and postmenopausal women lose minimal physiological iron (~1 mg/day), dietary iron deficiency is rare. In this demographic, iron deficiency anemia must be presumed to stem from occult, chronic gastrointestinal bleeding (e.g., peptic ulcers, diverticula, angiodysplasia, or colon adenocarcinoma) until proven otherwise. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 17, Book pp. 264–265, PDF pp. 277–278; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
questions.prompt: Which one of the following individuals is at greatest risk for developing dietary iron deficiency?
choices: A 15-year-old adolescent boy undergoing a rapid growth spurt who eats mainly junk food
A 40-year-old multiparous woman with a history of hysterectomy
questions.officialAnswer: A 15-year-old adolescent boy undergoing a rapid growth spurt who eats mainly junk food
questions.explanation: Adolescents experience accelerated skeletal growth, muscle expansion, and blood volume expansion that dramatically increase iron requirements. An adolescent male on a poor diet lacking bioavailable heme iron is at high risk for dietary iron deficiency. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 17, Book pp. 264–265, PDF pp. 277–278; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
questions.prompt: Which of the following individuals is at the greatest risk for developing anemia of chronic inflammation (ACI)?
choices: An adult male blood donor who donates twice a year
A 30-year-old man with severe active rheumatoid arthritis
questions.officialAnswer: A 30-year-old man with severe active rheumatoid arthritis
questions.explanation: Anemia of chronic inflammation (ACI) is driven by persistent immune activation and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ) found in chronic autoimmune conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, SLE), systemic infections, and malignancies, which stimulate hepatic hepcidin production. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 17, Book pp. 269–270, PDF pp. 282–283; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
questions.prompt: In what situation will increased levels of free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP) or zinc protoporphyrin (ZPP) be found?
choices: Any condition that prevents iron incorporation into protoporphyrin IX
questions.officialAnswer: Any condition that prevents iron incorporation into protoporphyrin IX
questions.explanation: When iron is unavailable (iron deficiency) or its insertion into protoporphyrin IX is enzymatically blocked by ferrochelatase inhibition (lead poisoning), protoporphyrin IX accumulates. Zinc is enzymatically inserted instead, forming zinc protoporphyrin (ZPP/FEP). In contrast, globin synthesis defects like thalassemia minor do not impair iron insertion and typically have normal ZPP. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 17, Book pp. 268, 273, PDF pp. 281, 286; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
questions.prompt: In the pathogenesis of the anemia of chronic inflammation, elevated circulating hepcidin levels:
choices: Increase during inflammation and reduce iron absorption from enterocytes while trapping iron in macrophages
Enhance ferroportin channel activity on cell membranes
questions.officialAnswer: Increase during inflammation and reduce iron absorption from enterocytes while trapping iron in macrophages
questions.explanation: Inflammatory cytokines (primarily IL-6) induce hepatocytes to overproduce hepcidin. Hepcidin binds to the iron exporter ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages, triggering its internalization and degradation. This blocks dietary iron absorption and sequesters recycled iron within macrophages, causing hypoferremia and iron-restricted erythropoiesis despite abundant storage iron. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 17, Book pp. 269–271, PDF pp. 282–284; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
questions.prompt: Sideroblastic anemias result from:
choices: Excessive loss of iron in the urine
Failure of transferrin to bind iron
Increased destruction of mature erythrocytes in the spleen
Failure to incorporate iron into protoporphyrin IX
questions.officialAnswer: Failure to incorporate iron into protoporphyrin IX
questions.explanation: Sideroblastic anemias are a group of disorders caused by inherited or acquired defects in mitochondrial heme biosynthesis enzymes (e.g., ALAS2 mutations, lead poisoning, MDS-RS). Iron enters the erythroblast mitochondria but cannot be incorporated into protoporphyrin IX, accumulating as non-heme iron within mitochondria circling the nucleus (ring sideroblasts). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 17, Book pp. 271–273, PDF pp. 284–286; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
questions.prompt: In general, most instances of hereditary hemochromatosis (e.g., HFE mutations C282Y) result from defects in:
questions.explanation: Classical hereditary hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by homozygous mutations in the HFE gene (C282Y), impairing iron sensing and resulting in inappropriately low hepcidin synthesis. Unchecked ferroportin activity causes unregulated continuous intestinal iron absorption, leading to progressive systemic iron overload, tissue deposition, and organ damage. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 17, Book pp. 274–276, PDF pp. 287–289; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Disorders of Iron Kinetics and Heme Metabolism
questions.prompt: In the erythropoietic porphyrias, a characteristic clinical hallmark caused by porphyrin deposition in the skin is:
choices: Heightened propensity for sunburn and severe cutaneous photosensitivity
questions.officialAnswer: Heightened propensity for sunburn and severe cutaneous photosensitivity
questions.explanation: Porphyrias arise from enzyme deficiencies in the heme pathway. In erythropoietic porphyrias (such as congenital erythropoietic porphyria and erythropoietic protoporphyria), excess porphyrins accumulate and deposit in tissues. Absorption of long-wave ultraviolet light (Soret band ~400 nm) produces reactive oxygen radicals, resulting in extreme cutaneous photosensitivity, burning, erythema, and scarring on sun exposure. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 17, Book pp. 276–278, PDF pp. 289–291; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias Caused by Defects of DNA Metabolism
questions.prompt: Which of the following complete blood count findings is most consistent with megaloblastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic anemia is classically characterized by marked macrocytosis, with MCV typically ranging from 100 to 140 fL, accompanied by oval macrocytes on the blood film, elevated RDW, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia with an inappropriately low reticulocyte count. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 18, Book pp. 283–285, PDF pp. 296–298; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias Caused by Defects of DNA Metabolism
questions.prompt: A patient has a clinical picture of megaloblastic anemia. What is the expected MCHC value?
questions.explanation: Although red cell volume is markedly increased (elevated MCV), hemoglobin synthesis and cytoplasmic maturation proceed normally in megaloblastic anemia. Therefore, the concentration of hemoglobin per unit volume of erythrocyte remains normal, keeping the MCHC within the normal reference interval (32 to 36 g/dL; normochromic). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 18, Book pp. 284–285, PDF pp. 297–298; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias Caused by Defects of DNA Metabolism
questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements characterizes the relationship between macrocytic anemia and megaloblastic anemia?
choices: Macrocytic anemia and megaloblastic anemia are synonymous terms.
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic anemia is a specific subset of macrocytic anemias characterized by impaired nuclear DNA synthesis (megaloblastic marrow maturation). All megaloblastic anemias are macrocytic, but not all macrocytic anemias are megaloblastic (nonmegaloblastic macrocytic anemias include liver disease, alcoholism, and reticulocytosis). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 18, Book pp. 282–284, PDF pp. 295–297; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias Caused by Defects of DNA Metabolism
questions.prompt: Which of the following peripheral blood film findings is most suggestive and sensitive for megaloblastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Hypersegmented neutrophils (neutrophils with 5 or more distinct nuclear lobes, or a single neutrophil with 6 or more lobes) are one of the earliest, most sensitive, and specific morphologic hallmarks of megaloblastic anemia, often appearing in peripheral blood before macrocytosis fully develops. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 18, Book pp. 285–286, PDF pp. 298–299; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias Caused by Defects of DNA Metabolism
questions.prompt: In the description of a bone marrow smear in megaloblastic anemia, which feature is characteristic?
choices: Nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony with immature-appearing chromatin alongside mature hemoglobinized cytoplasm
Erythroid nuclei that are more mature than cytoplasm
questions.officialAnswer: Nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony with immature-appearing chromatin alongside mature hemoglobinized cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony is the morphological hallmark of megaloblastosis: impaired DNA replication delays nuclear chromatin condensation (nuclei appear open, delicate, and immature), while RNA synthesis and cytoplasmic hemoglobinization progress unhindered (mature-appearing cytoplasm). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 18, Book pp. 286–288, PDF pp. 299–301; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias Caused by Defects of DNA Metabolism
questions.prompt: Which one of the following findings would be INCONSISTENT with a diagnosis of vitamin B12 deficiency?
choices: Oval macrocytes on peripheral blood film
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. In vitamin B12 deficiency, methylmalonyl-CoA cannot be converted to succinyl-CoA, causing marked accumulation and elevation of methylmalonic acid (MMA) in both serum and urine. Therefore, a low or normal MMA level is inconsistent with true vitamin B12 deficiency. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 18, Book pp. 289–291, PDF pp. 302–304; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias Caused by Defects of DNA Metabolism
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most metabolically active transport protein that delivers vitamin B12 to cells throughout the body?
questions.explanation: Transcobalamin (TC II) binds newly absorbed vitamin B12 in the ileum to form holotranscobalamin (holoTC), which accounts for 10% to 30% of circulating B12 but represents the sole metabolically active form capable of binding specific receptors to deliver B12 to dividing tissues. Haptocorrin carries the inert storage fraction. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 18, Book pp. 288–289, PDF pp. 301–302; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias Caused by Defects of DNA Metabolism
questions.prompt: Folate and vitamin B12 work together in the critical biochemical production of:
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 and folate biochemically interact in the methionine synthase reaction. Vitamin B12 deficiency traps folate as 5-methyl-THF ("methylfolate trap"), preventing its conversion into 5,10-methylene-THF, which is required to convert dUMP to dTMP for DNA thymidine synthesis, arresting cellular DNA replication. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 18, Book pp. 288–290, PDF pp. 301–303; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias Caused by Defects of DNA Metabolism
questions.prompt: The macrocytosis associated with megaloblastic anemia is caused by:
choices: Reduced numbers of cell divisions with normal cytoplasmic development
Accelerated cell division in marrow cords
questions.officialAnswer: Reduced numbers of cell divisions with normal cytoplasmic development
