questions.explanation: Because DNA synthesis is severely slowed, precursor cell cycle transit times are prolonged and one or more mitotic divisions are skipped during normoblast development. However, RNA and protein synthesis continue at a normal pace, producing abnormally large, oval erythrocytes (macro-ovalocytes). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 18, Book pp. 283–285, PDF pp. 296–298; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Anemias Caused by Defects of DNA Metabolism
questions.prompt: Which one of the following demographic groups has the highest prevalence of pernicious anemia?
choices: Infants younger than 1 year of age
Persons older than 60 years of age
questions.officialAnswer: Persons older than 60 years of age
questions.explanation: Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune disorder characterized by atrophic gastritis and autoantibodies against gastric parietal cells or intrinsic factor, most commonly diagnosed in individuals older than 60 years of age (prevalence increases progressively with advancing age). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 18, Book pp. 291–292, PDF pp. 304–305; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The clinical consequences of pancytopenia include:
questions.explanation: Pancytopenia is the simultaneous reduction in all three peripheral blood cell lines: anemia causes fatigue and pallor; neutropenia leads to recurrent bacterial/fungal infections; and thrombocytopenia causes mucocutaneous hemorrhage, petechiae, and bruising. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 19, Book pp. 300–301, PDF pp. 313–314; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia is due to a(n):
questions.explanation: In idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia (accounting for 70% to 80% of acquired aplastic anemia cases), no clear external inciting environmental toxin, drug, or viral trigger can be identified; bone marrow failure is mediated by autoimmune cytotoxic T-cell destruction of stem cells. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 19, Book p. 301, PDF p. 314; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The pathophysiologic mechanism in acquired idiosyncratic aplastic anemia is:
choices: Direct dose-dependent destruction of stem cells by chemical agents
Destruction of stem cells by autoimmune T cells
Accelerated apoptosis due to lack of growth factor receptors
Infiltration of bone marrow by malignant plasma cells
questions.officialAnswer: Destruction of stem cells by autoimmune T cells
questions.explanation: Acquired aplastic anemia is predominantly an immune-mediated disorder wherein activated oligoclonal cytotoxic T cells (CD8⁺) infiltrate the bone marrow and secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF-α) that upregulate Fas receptor expression on CD34⁺ hematopoietic stem cells, triggering extensive apoptotic stem cell depletion. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 19, Book pp. 301–303, PDF pp. 314–316; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Based on the criteria in Table 19.1, what is the aplastic anemia classification for a patient with bone marrow cellularity < 25%, absolute neutrophil count (ANC) 0.15 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 15 × 10⁹/L, and reticulocyte count 10 × 10⁹/L?
questions.explanation: According to Camitta criteria (Table 19.1), severe aplastic anemia (SAA) requires marrow cellularity <25% plus at least two of: ANC <0.5 × 10⁹/L, platelets <20 × 10⁹/L, or reticulocytes <20 × 10⁹/L. When the ANC is less than 0.2 × 10⁹/L (here 0.15 × 10⁹/L), the disease is classified as very severe aplastic anemia (VSAA). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 19, Book p. 303, PDF p. 316; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

stimulus.caption: Table 19.1 Diagnostic Criteria for Aplastic Anemia
rows: Hypocellular bone marrow plus at least two cytopenias

stimulus.alt: Rodak Table 19.1: Aplastic anemia diagnostic criteria
stimulus.caption: Table 19.1

questions.prompt: The most consistent peripheral blood findings in severe aplastic anemia are:
choices: Target cells, teardrop cells, and leukoerythroblastosis
questions.explanation: Aplastic anemia typically presents with pancytopenia accompanied by a mildly elevated MCV (normocytic to mildly macrocytic RBCs, 95–110 fL), severe neutropenia, severe thrombocytopenia, and a markedly reduced reticulocyte count without abnormal circulating blasts. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 19, Book pp. 303–304, PDF pp. 316–317; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The treatment that has shown the best long-term success and cure rate for severe aplastic anemia in patients younger than 40 years of age is:
choices: Immunosuppressive therapy with antithymocyte globulin (ATG) and cyclosporine
Bone marrow transplant with an HLA-identical sibling
questions.officialAnswer: Bone marrow transplant with an HLA-identical sibling
questions.explanation: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) from an HLA-matched sibling donor is the first-line curative therapy of choice for young patients (<40 years old) with severe aplastic anemia, yielding cure rates >80% to 90%. Immunosuppression (ATG + cyclosporine) is reserved for older patients or those lacking an HLA-matched sibling. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 19, Book pp. 304–305, PDF pp. 317–318; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The diagnostic laboratory test that is most useful in differentiating Fanconi anemia from other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes is:
choices: Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59
questions.explanation: Fanconi anemia (FA) is caused by mutations in DNA interstrand cross-link repair genes. The definitive diagnostic gold standard is measuring increased chromosomal breakage, radial figures, and gaps in peripheral blood lymphocytes exposed in vitro to DNA cross-linking agents such as diepoxybutane (DEB) or mitomycin C (MMC). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 19, Book pp. 305–307, PDF pp. 318–320; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Mutations in genes that code for the telomerase complex (e.g., TERT, TERC, DKC1) lead to bone marrow failure primarily by causing:
choices: Uncontrolled proliferation of cytotoxic T cells
Premature death and exhaustion of hematopoietic stem cells
questions.officialAnswer: Premature death and exhaustion of hematopoietic stem cells
questions.explanation: Telomerase complex mutations (dyskeratosis congenita and familial aplastic anemia) impair the maintenance of telomere length during cell division. Unusually rapid telomere shortening triggers premature cellular senescence, DNA damage responses, and apoptotic exhaustion of the hematopoietic stem cell pool. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 19, Book pp. 307–308, PDF pp. 320–321; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Diamond-Blackfan anemia differs from Fanconi anemia in that:
questions.explanation: Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) is a congenital pure red cell aplasia (ribosomopathy) in which only the erythroid lineage is severely deficient (normoblasts absent in marrow with normal WBCs and platelets). In contrast, Fanconi anemia leads to progressive aplastic pancytopenia affecting all three cell lines. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 19, Book pp. 308–309, PDF pp. 321–322; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which anemia should be suspected in a patient with refractory macrocytic or normocytic anemia, prominent multinucleated erythroblasts with nuclear bridging in the bone marrow, and secondary hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation: Congenital dyserythropoietic anemias (CDAs) are rare hereditary anemias characterized by ineffective erythropoiesis, secondary iron overload, and striking dysplastic erythroblast morphology in the bone marrow (multinucleated erythroblasts, nuclear lobulation, internuclear chromatin bridging, and "Swiss cheese" heterochromatin in CDA II). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 19, Book pp. 309–310, PDF pp. 322–323; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The primary pathophysiologic mechanism of anemia associated with chronic renal disease is:
choices: Severe iron malabsorption in the jejunum
Folate deficiency due to dialysis loss
questions.explanation: The primary cause of normocytic, normochromic anemia in chronic kidney disease is decreased synthesis of erythropoietin (EPO) by damaged peritubular interstitial cells in the failing renal parenchyma. Recombinant human EPO therapy successfully restores hemoglobin levels. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 19, Book pp. 310–311, PDF pp. 323–324; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following findings is NOT consistent with pure red cell aplasia (PRCA)?
choices: Normal white blood cell count and differential
questions.explanation: Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is characterized by near-complete absence of erythroid precursors (<0.5% normoblasts) in an otherwise cellular bone marrow, producing severe anemia with a profound reticulocytopenia (<1%). Reticulocytosis is entirely inconsistent with PRCA and indicates an intact proliferative erythroid response. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 19, Book pp. 308–309, PDF pp. 321–322; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Introduction to Increased Destruction of Erythrocytes
questions.prompt: The term hemolytic disorder in general refers to a disorder in which there is:
choices: Increased destruction of RBCs in the blood, bone marrow, or spleen
Excessive loss of RBCs from the body through acute hemorrhage
Inadequate RBC production by the bone marrow
Increased plasma volume with unchanged red cell mass
questions.officialAnswer: Increased destruction of RBCs in the blood, bone marrow, or spleen
questions.explanation: A hemolytic disorder is defined by a shortened red blood cell circulating lifespan (<120 days) resulting from premature erythrocyte destruction within the peripheral circulation (intravascular hemolysis) or in reticuloendothelial tissues such as the spleen, liver, and marrow (extravascular hemolysis). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 20, Book pp. 317–318, PDF pp. 330–331; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Introduction to Increased Destruction of Erythrocytes
questions.prompt: RBC destruction that occurs when macrophages ingest senescent or antibody-coated red blood cells in the spleen and liver is termed:
questions.explanation: Extravascular hemolysis (macrophage-mediated hemolysis) occurs when erythrocytes are phagocytosed and catabolized by reticuloendothelial macrophages in the splenic red pulp cords and liver Kupffer cells, accounting for ~90% of normal senescence and most immune-mediated hemolytic anemias. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 20, Book pp. 318–320, PDF pp. 331–333; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Introduction to Increased Destruction of Erythrocytes
questions.prompt: A sign of hemolysis that is typically associated with increased extravascular catabolism of heme is:
choices: Markedly decreased serum haptoglobin with hemoglobinemia
questions.explanation: In extravascular hemolysis, excess protoporphyrin is converted by macrophages to unconjugated bilirubin, conjugated in the liver, excreted in bile, and converted by intestinal flora to urobilinogen. Increased enterohepatic reabsorption produces elevated urobilinogen levels in urine and stool. Hemoglobinuria and hemosiderinuria occur in intravascular hemolysis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 20, Book pp. 320–322, PDF pp. 333–335; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Introduction to Increased Destruction of Erythrocytes
questions.prompt: An elderly woman is evaluated for worsening anemia. Physical examination reveals scleral icterus and mild splenomegaly. What physical finding corresponds to elevated unconjugated bilirubin?
questions.explanation: Accelerated red cell destruction overwhelms hepatic glucuronide-conjugating capacity, causing indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin to accumulate in plasma. Lipid-soluble bilirubin binds elastin in tissues, producing yellow discoloration of sclerae (icterus) and skin (jaundice). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 20, Book pp. 320–322, PDF pp. 333–335; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Introduction to Increased Destruction of Erythrocytes
questions.prompt: Which of the following routine laboratory tests provides the best initial indication of compensatory bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia in response to hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow compensation for shortened RBC survival manifests as erythroid hyperplasia and accelerated output of young erythrocytes into the bloodstream, detected directly by an elevated reticulocyte count (elevated absolute reticulocyte count, reticulocyte percentage, and RPI > 2). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 20, Book pp. 322–323, PDF pp. 335–336; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Introduction to Increased Destruction of Erythrocytes
questions.prompt: A 5-year-old girl developed bloody diarrhea after eating an undercooked hamburger and presented several days later with acute pallor, oliguria, and schistocytes on the blood film. This hemolytic anemia is classified as:
questions.explanation: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), triggered by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC), is a classic microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) categorized as an acquired fragmentation (intravascular mechanical) hemolysis, wherein erythrocytes shear upon encountering microvascular platelet-fibrin thrombi. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 20, Book pp. 323–325, PDF pp. 336–338; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Introduction to Increased Destruction of Erythrocytes
questions.prompt: A patient has a personal and family history of mild chronic jaundice and gallstones. Which peripheral blood film finding would indicate an intrinsic inherited membrane disorder?
choices: Spherocytes on the peripheral blood film
questions.officialAnswer: Spherocytes on the peripheral blood film
questions.explanation: Spherocytes (densely stained erythrocytes lacking central pallor) on peripheral blood in a patient with a family history of anemia, splenomegaly, and bilirubin cholelithiasis (gallstones) are indicative of hereditary spherocytosis, an intrinsic red cell membrane defect. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 20, Book pp. 325–327, PDF pp. 338–340; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Introduction to Increased Destruction of Erythrocytes
questions.prompt: Under normal circumstances, the major fraction of bilirubin transported in plasma to the liver is:
choices: Macrophage-secreted indirect bilirubin bound to albumin
questions.officialAnswer: Macrophage-secreted indirect bilirubin bound to albumin
questions.explanation: Heme oxygenase in reticuloendothelial macrophages degrades heme protoporphyrin into biliverdin, which biliverdin reductase reduces to unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin. Because indirect bilirubin is hydrophobic and water-insoluble, it is released into plasma bound tightly to albumin for transport to hepatocytes. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 20, Book pp. 319–321, PDF pp. 332–334; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Introduction to Increased Destruction of Erythrocytes
questions.prompt: A patient has an unexplained normocytic anemia that has been worsening over several months. To determine whether the anemia is due to hemolysis, which of the following observations would exclude a significant hemolytic process?
choices: Normal white blood cell count and platelet count
Evidence of increased protoporphyrin catabolism is lacking (normal bilirubin, LDH, and haptoglobin)
questions.officialAnswer: Evidence of increased protoporphyrin catabolism is lacking (normal bilirubin, LDH, and haptoglobin)
questions.explanation: Ongoing hemolysis is characterized by biochemical markers of accelerated erythrocyte breakdown: elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), elevated unconjugated bilirubin, and depleted serum haptoglobin. The absence of these hallmarks effectively rules out a significant ongoing hemolytic process. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 20, Book pp. 327–328, PDF pp. 340–341; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Introduction to Increased Destruction of Erythrocytes
questions.prompt: Which of the following sets of laboratory test results is typical of acute severe intravascular hemolysis (Serum Haptoglobin, Urine Free Hemoglobin, Urine Hemosiderin)?
questions.explanation: In acute intravascular hemolysis, free hemoglobin released directly into plasma rapidly saturates and depletes serum haptoglobin (decreased). Excess free alpha-beta dimers pass through the renal glomerulus into urine, causing hemoglobinuria (positive). Renal tubular epithelial cells absorb and catabolize hemoglobin, sloughing days later as urine hemosiderin (positive). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 20, Book pp. 321–323, PDF pp. 334–336; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
questions.prompt: A patient with hereditary spherocytosis (HS) presents with jaundice and splenomegaly. The primary molecular defect in HS involves:
choices: G6PD enzyme deficiency in the hexose monophosphate shunt
Abnormal beta-globin chain amino acid substitution
Defects in vertical cytoskeletal protein interactions (ankyrin, band 3, spectrin, or protein 4.2)
GPI anchor deficiency on the stem cell membrane
questions.officialAnswer: Defects in vertical cytoskeletal protein interactions (ankyrin, band 3, spectrin, or protein 4.2)
questions.explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is caused by inherited defects in vertical membrane structural linkages (ankyrin, band 3, α- or β-spectrin, and protein 4.2) that connect the lipid bilayer to the underlying spectrin cytoskeleton. Uncoupling causes membrane lipid vesicle shedding, loss of surface area, and spherical transformation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 21, Book pp. 337–340, PDF pp. 350–353; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
questions.prompt: In hereditary spherocytosis, the osmotic fragility test typically demonstrates:
choices: Decreased osmotic fragility (shifts to the left)
Increased osmotic fragility (shifts to the right)
Normal osmotic fragility after 24 hours of incubation
questions.officialAnswer: Increased osmotic fragility (shifts to the right)
questions.explanation: Because spherocytes have a reduced surface-area-to-volume ratio, they have limited capacity to expand in hypotonic saline solutions and lyse at higher concentrations of NaCl than normal discocytes, producing an osmotic fragility curve shifted to the right (increased osmotic fragility). Incubation at 37° C for 24 hours further accentuates the defect. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 21, Book pp. 341–343, PDF pp. 354–356; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
questions.prompt: The eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding test by flow cytometry is diagnostic for hereditary spherocytosis because EMA binds specifically to:
choices: Band 3 protein in the erythrocyte membrane
questions.officialAnswer: Band 3 protein in the erythrocyte membrane
questions.explanation: The flow cytometric eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding test measures mean fluorescence intensity of EMA, a fluorescent dye that binds covalently to lysine-430 on Band 3 (anion exchanger 1) and associated complexes. In hereditary spherocytosis, membrane surface area loss and Band 3 deficiency produce a characteristic decrease in EMA fluorescence (>90% sensitivity and specificity). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 21, Book pp. 342–344, PDF pp. 355–357; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
questions.prompt: The underlying molecular abnormality in hereditary elliptocytosis (HE) is characterized by defective:
choices: Horizontal cytoskeletal protein interactions (spectrin dimer-dimer self-association or spectrin-actin-protein 4.1 complex)
Vertical interactions between the bilayer and ankyrin
questions.officialAnswer: Horizontal cytoskeletal protein interactions (spectrin dimer-dimer self-association or spectrin-actin-protein 4.1 complex)
questions.explanation: Hereditary elliptocytosis (HE) results from mutations that disrupt horizontal cytoskeletal interactions within the submembranous lattice: most commonly mutations in α- or β-spectrin impairing spectrin dimer self-association into tetramers, or mutations in protein 4.1R. Repetitive microvascular shear stress causes progressive, permanent plastic deformation of discocytes into elliptocytes. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 21, Book pp. 344–346, PDF pp. 357–359; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
questions.prompt: Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis (HPP) is a severe subtype of hereditary elliptocytosis characterized by:
choices: Thermal instability of erythrocytes with fragmentation occurring at 45° C to 46° C (normally 49° C)
Resistance to heat-induced fragmentation up to 55° C
Severe microcytosis (MCV 50–65 fL) with extreme poikilocytosis and thermal sensitivity at 45° C
Biallelic mutations in Band 3 with normal spectrin
questions.officialAnswer: Resistance to heat-induced fragmentation up to 55° C
questions.explanation: Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis (HPP) is a severe compound heterozygous or homozygous form of hereditary elliptocytosis presenting in infancy with severe hemolytic anemia, extreme poikilocytosis (elliptocytes, budding red cells, microspherocytes), marked microcytosis (MCV 50–65 fL), and marked thermal sensitivity, with in vitro red cell fragmentation occurring at 45° C (normal control red cells fragment at 49° C). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 21, Book pp. 346–348, PDF pp. 359–361; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
questions.prompt: Overhydrated hereditary stomatocytosis (OHS) is characterized by:
choices: Markedly increased intracellular sodium and water with decreased MCHC and stomatocytes on the blood film
Dehydrated cells with increased MCHC and xerocytes
Intracellular potassium accumulation with elevated MCHC
questions.officialAnswer: Markedly increased intracellular sodium and water with decreased MCHC and stomatocytes on the blood film
questions.explanation: In overhydrated hereditary stomatocytosis (OHS), red cell membrane cation permeability is defective, resulting in massive passive influx of sodium and water that overwhelms the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump. Erythrocytes become overhydrated, swollen (MCV 110–150 fL), and hypochromic (low MCHC), displaying slit-like or mouth-shaped central pallor (stomatocytes). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 21, Book pp. 348–350, PDF pp. 361–363; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
questions.prompt: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is caused by an acquired somatic mutation in which gene?
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the X-linked PIGA gene in a hematopoietic stem cell. PIGA is required for the biosynthesis of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchors. Lack of GPI anchors leaves cell membranes deficient in complement regulatory proteins CD55 (DAF) and CD59 (MIRL), causing complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 21, Book pp. 350–353, PDF pp. 363–366; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
questions.prompt: The current gold standard diagnostic test for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is:
choices: Flow cytometric analysis of CD55, CD59, and FLAER on granulocytes and monocytes
questions.officialAnswer: Flow cytometric analysis of CD55, CD59, and FLAER on granulocytes and monocytes
questions.explanation: High-sensitivity multicolor flow cytometry using monoclonal antibodies against CD55 and CD59 alongside fluorescently labeled aerolysin (FLAER, which binds directly to the GPI anchor) on granulocytes and monocytes is the gold standard diagnostic method for detecting and quantifying PNH clones, replacing the historic Ham test. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 21, Book pp. 353–355, PDF pp. 366–368; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
questions.prompt: The most common human erythrocyte enzyme deficiency, which causes acute episodic hemolytic anemia following oxidant exposure, is:
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency is an X-linked recessive enzymopathy affecting over 400 million people worldwide. G6PD catalyzes the first step of the hexose monophosphate shunt, generating NADPH to maintain reduced glutathione. Without GSH, oxidant stress (fava beans, primaquine, dapsone, infections) causes hemoglobin oxidation, Heinz body precipitation, and acute intravascular/extravascular hemolysis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 21, Book pp. 355–358, PDF pp. 368–371; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
questions.prompt: During an acute hemolytic episode in a patient with G6PD deficiency, classic morphologic erythrocytes seen on the blood film after splenic macrophage "pitting" of Heinz bodies are:
questions.explanation: In G6PD deficiency under oxidant stress, denatured hemoglobin precipitates as rigid Heinz bodies against the inner erythrocyte membrane. As these cells transit the splenic cords, macrophages pit out the rigid precipitates, creating characteristic "bite cells" (degmacytes) and "blister cells" with eccentric cytoplasmic vacuolation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 21, Book pp. 357–359, PDF pp. 370–372; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
questions.prompt: The second most common red cell enzymopathy, and the most frequent defect of the Embden-Meyerhof glycolytic pathway, is:
questions.explanation: Pyruvate kinase (PK) deficiency is an autosomal recessive enzymopathy of the Embden-Meyerhof pathway that impairs conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate, severely reducing ATP production. ATP depletion causes cation pump failure, potassium loss, cell dehydration, and chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 21, Book pp. 359–361, PDF pp. 372–374; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Intrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction
questions.prompt: An important compensatory physiological mechanism that helps patients with pyruvate kinase deficiency tolerate chronic anemia with minimal symptoms is:
choices: Compensatory shift to the left in the oxygen dissociation curve
Marked accumulation of upstream 2,3-BPG, shifting the oxygen dissociation curve to the right
Increased affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen
questions.officialAnswer: Marked accumulation of upstream 2,3-BPG, shifting the oxygen dissociation curve to the right
questions.explanation: In pyruvate kinase deficiency, the metabolic block at the terminal step of glycolysis causes accumulation of upstream intermediates, specifically 1,3-BPG, which is shunted into the Rapoport-Luebering pathway to produce high intracellular concentrations of 2,3-BPG (up to twice normal). High 2,3-BPG shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, enhancing tissue oxygen unloading and minimizing anemic symptoms. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 21, Book pp. 360–361, PDF pp. 373–374; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Nonimmune Causes
questions.prompt: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) is characterized by which peripheral blood film finding?
questions.explanation: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) is caused by mechanical fragmentation of red blood cells as they circulate through damaged microvascular beds containing fibrin strands or platelet thrombi. The hallmark morphologic finding on the peripheral blood film is schistocytes (triangular, helmet-shaped, or fragmented red cells) typically accompanied by thrombocytopenia. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 22, Book pp. 364–366, PDF pp. 377–379; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Nonimmune Causes
questions.prompt: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is caused by a severe deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is caused by severe deficiency (<10%) of the plasma metalloprotease ADAMTS13 (congenital Upshaw-Schulman syndrome or acquired autoantibodies). In the absence of ADAMTS13, ultra-large VWF multimers accumulate, spontaneously binding platelets and inducing microvascular platelet thrombosis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 22, Book pp. 366–368, PDF pp. 379–381; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Nonimmune Causes
questions.prompt: The classic clinical pentad of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) includes microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, neurologic symptoms, fever, and:
questions.explanation: The classic historical clinical pentad of TTP comprises: (1) microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, (2) thrombocytopenia, (3) neurologic abnormalities (headache, confusion, seizures), (4) renal dysfunction (elevated BUN/creatinine, hematuria, proteinuria), and (5) fever. However, the presence of the dyad of unexplained MAHA and thrombocytopenia alone is sufficient to initiate emergent plasma exchange. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 22, Book pp. 366–367, PDF pp. 379–380; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Nonimmune Causes
questions.prompt: Typical hemolytic uremic syndrome (STEC-HUS) in young children is most commonly associated with infection by:
questions.explanation: Typical (diarrhea-associated) HUS classically follows acute gastroenteritis with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC, notably serotype O157:H7) or Shigella dysenteriae. Shiga toxins bind Gb3 receptors on glomerular capillary endothelial cells, causing microvascular endothelial damage, localized platelet thrombosis, and acute renal failure. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 22, Book pp. 368–370, PDF pp. 381–383; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Nonimmune Causes
questions.prompt: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) is characterized by dysregulation of:
questions.explanation: Atypical HUS (aHUS) is a non-Shiga toxin-mediated disorder caused by uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway, resulting from inherited mutations in complement regulatory genes (complement factor H [CFH], factor I, MCP/CD46) or autoantibodies against CFH, treated effectively with the terminal complement C5 inhibitor eculizumab. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 22, Book pp. 370–371, PDF pp. 383–384; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Nonimmune Causes
questions.prompt: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) differs from TTP and HUS in that coagulation screening tests in DIC show:
choices: Normal PT, normal PTT, and normal fibrinogen
Normal PT, prolonged PTT, and elevated D-dimer
Prolonged PT, prolonged PTT, decreased fibrinogen, and markedly elevated D-dimer
Shortened PT and PTT with normal platelet counts
questions.officialAnswer: Prolonged PT, prolonged PTT, decreased fibrinogen, and markedly elevated D-dimer
questions.explanation: In DIC, widespread systemic activation of both platelets and the secondary coagulation cascade leads to consumption of clotting factors and platelets: PT and PTT are prolonged, fibrinogen is consumed/decreased, and D-dimer/FDPs are markedly elevated. In TTP and HUS, secondary coagulation tests (PT and PTT) are typically normal. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 22, Book pp. 371–372, PDF pp. 384–385; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Nonimmune Causes
questions.prompt: March hemoglobinuria is a nonimmune hemolytic condition caused by:
choices: Direct physical mechanical trauma to erythrocytes in the feet during prolonged strenuous running or marching on hard surfaces
A bacterial toxin from Clostridium perfringens
questions.officialAnswer: Direct physical mechanical trauma to erythrocytes in the feet during prolonged strenuous running or marching on hard surfaces
questions.explanation: March hemoglobinuria is an exercise-induced traumatic intravascular hemolysis that occurs when erythrocytes in dermal capillaries of the soles are mechanically crushed during repetitive impact from prolonged running or marching on hard surfaces without cushioned footwear. Blood film shows minimal to absent schistocytes, but transient hemoglobinemia and hemoglobinuria occur after exertion. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 22, Book p. 373, PDF p. 386; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Nonimmune Causes
questions.prompt: What RBC morphology is characteristically found in peripheral blood smears of patients suffering extensive, severe third-degree thermal burns?
questions.explanation: Direct exposure of circulating erythrocytes to temperatures >47° C to 49° C during severe thermal burns damages spectrin, causing membrane loss, budding, fragmentation, and marked cellular rounding. The peripheral smear shows striking poikilocytosis with abundant microspherocytes, schistocytes, and budding red cells alongside marked microcytosis (MCV 50–70 fL). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 22, Book pp. 373–374, PDF pp. 386–387; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Nonimmune Causes
questions.prompt: A 36-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department with acute confusion, fever, purpura, severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count 12 × 10⁹/L), microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with prominent schistocytes, normal PT and PTT, and elevated indirect bilirubin. The most likely diagnosis requiring immediate plasma exchange is:
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of acute MAHA, severe thrombocytopenia, neurologic dysfunction, fever, and normal coagulation times (PT/PTT) is diagnostic of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Immediate initiation of therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) with fresh frozen plasma is lifesaving, reducing mortality from >90% to <15%. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 22, Book pp. 366–368, PDF pp. 379–381; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Nonimmune Causes
questions.prompt: Which of the following laboratory test results is part of the classic HELLP syndrome profile in pregnant patients with severe preeclampsia?
choices: Elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
questions.officialAnswer: Elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
questions.explanation: HELLP syndrome is a microangiopathic complication of severe preeclampsia defined by: Hemolysis (schistocytes on blood smear, elevated LDH, indirect bilirubin), Elevated Liver enzymes (AST/ALT ≥ 70 U/L), and Low Platelets (<100 × 10⁹/L). Prompt delivery of the fetus and placenta is the definitive management. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 22, Book pp. 372–373, PDF pp. 385–386; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Immune Causes
questions.prompt: Immune hemolytic anemia is due to a(n):
choices: Inherited structural defect in spectrin or ankyrin
Allo- or autoantibody against an RBC antigen
Mechanical trauma from prosthetic heart valves
questions.officialAnswer: Allo- or autoantibody against an RBC antigen
questions.explanation: Immune hemolytic anemias (IHAs) are caused by premature red blood cell destruction mediated by immune mechanisms, specifically the binding of antibodies (autoantibodies directed against self-antigens, alloantibodies directed against foreign transfused or fetal red cell antigens, or drug-dependent antibodies) with or without complement activation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 23, Book pp. 379–380, PDF pp. 392–393; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Immune Causes
questions.prompt: The pathophysiology of immune hemolysis with IgM antibodies involves activation of:
questions.explanation: IgM is a pentameric immunoglobulin with multiple binding sites that efficiently binds and activates the C1q classical complement cascade upon binding red cell antigens. Intravascular hemolysis occurs if the full membrane attack complex (C5b-9) is assembled; extravascular hemolysis occurs if C3b-opsonized cells are recognized by macrophage CR1 receptors in the liver. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 23, Book pp. 380–382, PDF pp. 393–395; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Immune Causes
questions.prompt: In hemolysis mediated by warm-reacting IgG antibodies, which abnormal red cell morphology is characteristically seen on the peripheral blood film?
questions.explanation: In warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA), IgG-sensitized erythrocytes transit the splenic cords where macrophages bind the Fc portion of IgG. Macrophages phagocytose part of the red cell membrane without completely engulfing the cell ("partial phagocytosis"). The remaining membrane reseals around the unaltered volume, forming rigid microspherocytes. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 23, Book pp. 381–383, PDF pp. 394–396; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Immune Causes
questions.prompt: The most important laboratory finding in the diagnostic confirmation of an immune hemolytic anemia is:
choices: Demonstration of IgG and/or C3d on the RBC surface via a positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT)
questions.officialAnswer: Demonstration of IgG and/or C3d on the RBC surface via a positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT)
questions.explanation: The direct antiglobulin test (DAT, direct Coombs test) is the definitive diagnostic assay that differentiates immune hemolytic anemias from nonimmune hemolytic anemias by demonstrating in vivo sensitization of circulating patient erythrocytes with IgG autoantibodies and/or complement fragments (C3d). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 23, Book pp. 380–381, PDF pp. 393–394; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Immune Causes
questions.prompt: In warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA), a positive DAT typically indicates that:
choices: Complement alone is activated at 4° C
Alloantibodies against donor cells are circulating
IgG antibody is sensitizing the patient’s red blood cells (often accompanied by C3d)
questions.officialAnswer: IgG antibody is sensitizing the patient’s red blood cells (often accompanied by C3d)
questions.explanation: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (accounting for 70% to 80% of AIHA cases) is mediated by polyclonal warm-reacting IgG autoantibodies that bind optimally at 37° C. The DAT is positive for IgG alone (approx. 20% to 40% of cases) or both IgG and C3d (approx. 50% to 60% of cases). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 23, Book pp. 382–384, PDF pp. 395–397; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Immune Causes
questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the recognized mechanisms of drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia (DIIHA)?
choices: Drug adsorption (hapten mechanism, e.g., high-dose penicillin)
Immune complex (innocent bystander mechanism, e.g., quinidine)
Induction of true autoantibodies (e.g., fludarabine, methyldopa)
IgM autoantibody sensitization of RBCs after exposure to cold temperatures
questions.officialAnswer: IgM autoantibody sensitization of RBCs after exposure to cold temperatures
questions.explanation: Recognized mechanisms of drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia include: drug adsorption/hapten (penicillin), nonimmunologic protein adsorption (cephalosporins), neoantigen/immune complex (quinidine), and true autoantibody induction (methyldopa). Cold-reacting IgM agglutination is the mechanism of cold agglutinin disease, not a drug-induced hemolytic mechanism. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 23, Book pp. 388–390, PDF pp. 401–403; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Immune Causes
questions.prompt: Which of the following describes the penicillin-type drug adsorption mechanism of immune hemolysis?
choices: Extravascular hemolysis, positive DAT with IgG, gradual anemia occurring only with massive intravenous doses
Acute intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria after a single oral dose
Positive DAT with C3d only, with high titer cold agglutinins
Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction occurring 14 days post-infusion
questions.officialAnswer: Extravascular hemolysis, positive DAT with IgG, gradual anemia occurring only with massive intravenous doses
questions.explanation: In the drug adsorption (hapten) mechanism, high-dose intravenous penicillin binds covalently to red blood cell membrane proteins. Antipenicillin IgG antibodies bind to the drug-membrane complex. Coated RBCs undergo extravascular clearance by splenic macrophages, yielding a strongly positive DAT with anti-IgG and gradual extravascular hemolysis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 23, Book pp. 388–389, PDF pp. 401–402; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Immune Causes
questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements is true regarding a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR)?
choices: It is mediated primarily by preformed anti-A or anti-B IgM antibodies.
It produces immediate hyperacute hypotension and shock within minutes of transfusion.
It is due to an anamnestic response after repeat exposure to a blood group antigen (e.g., Kidd or Duffy) in a previously sensitized patient.
The DAT is negative at all times.
questions.officialAnswer: It is due to an anamnestic response after repeat exposure to a blood group antigen (e.g., Kidd or Duffy) in a previously sensitized patient.
questions.explanation: Delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions occur 3 to 14 days following transfusion in patients previously alloimmunized by prior pregnancy or transfusion whose antibody titers had dropped below detectable screening limits. Re-exposure elicits an anamnestic secondary IgG response (classically anti-Jkᵃ or anti-Fyᵃ), resulting in gradual extravascular clearance of transfused red cells and a newly positive DAT. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 23, Book pp. 387–388, PDF pp. 400–401; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Immune Causes
questions.prompt: Chronic secondary cold agglutinin disease (CAD) is most often associated with which underlying condition?
choices: B cell malignancies (such as lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma / Waldenström macroglobulinemia)
questions.officialAnswer: B cell malignancies (such as lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma / Waldenström macroglobulinemia)
questions.explanation: Chronic cold agglutinin disease (CAD) is typically a monoclonal lymphoproliferative B-cell disorder (producing monoclonal IgM-kappa autoantibodies, usually with anti-I specificity), frequently associated with low-grade B-cell lymphomas or clonal cold agglutinin disease. Acute transient CAD is seen after M. pneumoniae (anti-I) or EBV (anti-i). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 23, Book pp. 384–386, PDF pp. 397–399; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Immune Causes
questions.prompt: A 63-year-old man treated with fludarabine for chronic lymphocytic leukemia develops sudden severe jaundice, fatigue, spherocytes on blood smear, and a strongly positive DAT with anti-IgG. This drug-induced hemolytic anemia is caused by:
choices: RBC autoantibody induction via immune dysregulation
questions.officialAnswer: RBC autoantibody induction via immune dysregulation
questions.explanation: Purine analogues such as fludarabine disrupt regulatory T-cell suppression, inducing the production of warm-reacting IgG autoantibodies that recognize native red blood cell antigens (autoantibody induction mechanism). The resulting clinical syndrome is indistinguishable from idiopathic WAIHA and persists even after drug withdrawal. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 23, Book pp. 389–390, PDF pp. 402–403; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Extrinsic Defects Leading to Increased Erythrocyte Destruction—Immune Causes
questions.prompt: A group A, Rh-negative mother gave birth to a group A, Rh-positive infant who presented with jaundice and severe anemia at birth with a strongly positive DAT (4+ IgG). The most likely explanation is:
choices: ABO incompatibility hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN)
Severe hereditary spherocytosis in the infant
The mother was previously immunized to the D antigen, producing maternal anti-D IgG that crossed the placenta
Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria in the neonate
questions.officialAnswer: The mother was previously immunized to the D antigen, producing maternal anti-D IgG that crossed the placenta
questions.explanation: Rh (anti-D) hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN) occurs when an Rh-negative mother previously sensitized to the D antigen (by prior Rh-positive pregnancy or transfusion) produces maternal IgG anti-D antibodies. These cross the placenta via FcRn receptors and bind to fetal Rh-positive red cells, leading to severe extravascular hemolysis, hydrops fetalis, and a strongly positive infant DAT. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 23, Book pp. 386–387, PDF pp. 399–400; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: A qualitative abnormality in hemoglobin involves:
choices: Decreased production of structurally normal globin chains
Complete absence of alpha globin gene loci
A defective iron-incorporation step in mitochondria
Structural alterations in the amino acid sequence of a globin chain
questions.officialAnswer: Structural alterations in the amino acid sequence of a globin chain
questions.explanation: Hemoglobinopathies are qualitative hemoglobin disorders resulting from genetic mutations that alter the primary amino acid sequence of a globin chain (e.g., Hb S, Hb C, Hb E). In contrast, thalassemias are quantitative disorders characterized by reduced or absent synthesis of structurally normal globin chains. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 395–396, PDF pp. 408–409; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The substitution of valine for glutamic acid at the sixth position of the beta globin chain (β6(A3)Glu→Val) produces sickle hemoglobin (Hb S), which under deoxygenated conditions:
choices: Precipitates as Heinz bodies with oxidant injury
Polymerizes to form tactoid crystals, deforming the erythrocyte into a sickle shape
Forms hexagonal intracellular bars of crystallized hemoglobin
Permanently locks hemoglobin in the high-affinity relaxed state
questions.officialAnswer: Polymerizes to form tactoid crystals, deforming the erythrocyte into a sickle shape
questions.explanation: In Hb S (β6 Glu→Val), replacement of a hydrophilic, negatively charged glutamic acid residue with a hydrophobic valine creates an adhesive hydrophobic contact zone on the beta chain surface. Upon deoxygenation, Hb S tetramers polymerize into 14-strand helical fibers and tactoid crystals that distort the cell into a rigid, nondeformable sickle shape. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 396–399, PDF pp. 409–412; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Patients with sickle cell disease (Hb SS) usually do NOT exhibit clinical symptoms during the first 6 months of life because:
choices: The spleen is not yet functional
High maternal iron levels protect the infant
Higher levels of Hb F are present, which inhibits Hb S polymerization
The infant blood vessels have larger diameters
questions.officialAnswer: Higher levels of Hb F are present, which inhibits Hb S polymerization
questions.explanation: Fetal hemoglobin (Hb F, α₂γ₂) contains gamma chains that lack the mutated beta residue and possess glutamine at position 87, which disrupts Hb S polymer contacts. High levels of Hb F (>20% to 80%) in neonates strongly inhibit deoxy-Hb S polymerization, delaying onset of sickle symptoms until Hb F declines after 6 months of age. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 399–400, PDF pp. 412–413; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Megaloblastic episodes in sickle cell disease resulting from bone marrow hyperplasia can be prevented by daily dietary supplementation with:
questions.explanation: Patients with chronic hemolytic anemias like sickle cell disease experience continuous marrow erythroid hyperplasia with high erythrocyte turnover, depleting endogenous folate stores. Daily oral folic acid (1 mg/day) supplementation is routinely prescribed to prevent folate-deficient megaloblastic marrow crises. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 402–403, PDF pp. 415–416; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most definitive electrophoretic method for separating Hb S from Hb D and Hb G, and separating Hb C from Hb A₂, Hb E, and Hb O?
choices: Hemoglobin electrophoresis at acid pH (citrate agar at pH 6.0 to 6.2)
questions.officialAnswer: Hemoglobin electrophoresis at acid pH (citrate agar at pH 6.0 to 6.2)
questions.explanation: On alkaline cellulose acetate (pH 8.4), Hb S comigrates with Hb D and Hb G, while Hb C comigrates with Hb A₂, Hb E, and Hb O. Citrate agar electrophoresis at acid pH (6.0 to 6.2) exploits differences in agar-binding properties to definitively separate Hb S (migrates toward cathode) from Hb D/G, and Hb C from Hb A₂/E. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 406–408, PDF pp. 419–421; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: A patient presents with mild normochromic, normocytic anemia. Peripheral blood smear demonstrates numerous target cells and intracellular hexagonal crystals of dense hemoglobin. What is the specific genetic mutation responsible?
choices: Substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the β chain
Substitution of lysine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the β chain
Substitution of lysine for glutamic acid at position 26 of the β chain
questions.officialAnswer: Substitution of lysine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the β chain
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin C (Hb C) results from substitution of lysine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta globin chain (β6(A3)Glu→Lys). Lysine decreases hemoglobin solubility, causing Hb C to precipitate into characteristic intracellular oblong, hexagonal, or "bar-of-gold" crystals alongside prominent target cells. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 409–411, PDF pp. 422–424; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: A well-mixed blood specimen obtained for a CBC from a cyanotic patient has a brown, chocolate-colored appearance that fails to turn red upon vigorous aeration. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin M variants are autosomal dominant hemoglobinopathies caused by amino acid substitutions in the heme pocket (e.g., proximal or distal histidine replaced by tyrosine), stabilizing heme iron in the oxidized ferric (Fe³⁺, methemoglobin) state. Blood containing methemoglobin has a distinct dark chocolate-brown color that does not oxygenate to red upon aeration. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 415–416, PDF pp. 428–429; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Through routine genetic screening, prospective parents are found to both have sickle cell trait (heterozygous Hb AS). What is the probability that their biological child will have sickle cell disease (homozygous Hb SS)?
questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive disorder. When two carrier parents with sickle cell trait (genotypes AS × AS) conceive, Mendelian inheritance predicts: 25% homozygous normal (AA), 50% sickle cell trait (AS), and 25% homozygous sickle cell disease (SS). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 396–397, PDF pp. 409–410; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Painful crises in patients with sickle cell disease occur as a direct result of:
choices: Aplastic marrow arrest from parvovirus B19
Vasoocclusion of microvascular beds by sickled erythrocytes producing tissue ischemia and infarction
questions.officialAnswer: Vasoocclusion of microvascular beds by sickled erythrocytes producing tissue ischemia and infarction
questions.explanation: Vasoocclusive crises (pain crises) are the hallmark clinical complication of sickle cell anemia, caused by rigid sickled erythrocytes, activated neutrophils, and sticky platelets adhering to vascular endothelium and occluding microcirculatory flow, resulting in localized hypoxia, tissue ischemia, infarction, and intense bone pain. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 401–402, PDF pp. 414–415; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The screening solubility test for Hb S (e.g., Sickledex) utilizes a reducing agent (sodium dithionite) because deoxygenated Hb S molecules:
choices: Are insoluble in reduced, deoxygenated form and form a turbid solution
questions.officialAnswer: Are insoluble in reduced, deoxygenated form and form a turbid solution
questions.explanation: The hemoglobin solubility test exposes whole blood to saponin (which lyses red cells) and sodium hydrosulfite/dithionite (which deoxygenates hemoglobin). Whereas normal Hb A is soluble and produces a clear red solution, deoxy-Hb S is insoluble in high-molarity phosphate buffer, polymerizing into crystalline tactoids that scatter light and render the solution turbid. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 405–406, PDF pp. 418–419; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: DNA analysis documents that a patient has inherited the mutated β^S allele from both parents (β^S/β^S). This genetic state is termed:
questions.explanation: Inheriting identical mutant alleles at the beta-globin locus from both parents (β^S/β^S) represents the homozygous state, manifesting clinically as sickle cell disease (sickle cell anemia). Inheriting one normal β allele and one β^S allele (β^A/β^S) represents the heterozygous state (sickle cell trait). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 396–397, PDF pp. 409–410; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: In which of the following geographic areas is the prevalence of the Hb S gene mutation highest?
questions.explanation: The Hb S mutation originated in equatorial tropical regions with high endemicity of Plasmodium falciparum malaria, with trait frequencies reaching 20% to 40% in equatorial Sub-Saharan Africa due to positive natural selection (balanced polymorphism / malaria hypothesis). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 395–396, PDF pp. 408–409; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which hemoglobinopathy is the third most common hemoglobin variant worldwide and is particularly prevalent in Southeast Asia?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin E (β26(B8)Glu→Lys) is the second most prevalent hemoglobinopathy worldwide and the most common variant in Southeast Asia (Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, where carrier frequencies reach 30% to 50%). Hb E produces a mild microcytic hypochromic blood picture. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 411–412, PDF pp. 424–425; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following Hb S compound heterozygotes exhibits the mildest symptoms?
questions.explanation: Hb SG (compound heterozygosity for Hb S and Hb G-Philadelphia) produces an extraordinarily mild clinical picture because the α-chain mutation in Hb G does not promote deoxy-Hb S polymerization, presenting with minimal to no clinical sickling crises compared to Hb SC, Hb S-β-thalassemia, or Hb SC-Harlem. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 413–415, PDF pp. 426–428; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: A 1-year-old Indian patient presents with anemia. Both parents claim to have an "inherited anemia." Peripheral blood shows target cells; hemoglobin solubility is negative. Alkaline electrophoresis shows a band in the Hb C position and an Hb F band. Acid electrophoresis shows two distinct bands. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: On alkaline electrophoresis (pH 8.4), Hb O-Arab comigrates with Hb C (and Hb A₂ and Hb E). However, on acid citrate agar electrophoresis (pH 6.0–6.2), Hb O-Arab separates cleanly from Hb C, migrating between Hb A and Hb S. Finding an alkaline "Hb C" position band with negative solubility and two distinct bands on acid electrophoresis in an Indian patient is diagnostic of compound heterozygous Hb C/O-Arab. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 412–414, PDF pp. 425–427; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Unstable hemoglobins (such as Hb Köln) exhibit all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Precipitation of Heinz bodies within erythrocytes
Positive isopropanol and heat denaturation tests
Resistance to heat denaturation up to 60° C
questions.officialAnswer: Resistance to heat denaturation up to 60° C
questions.explanation: Unstable hemoglobins have amino acid mutations that weaken heme-globin contacts or subunit interfaces, causing premature spontaneous denaturation into Heinz bodies in circulation. They precipitate readily in heat stability tests at 50° C (they are definitely not heat-resistant up to 60° C) and precipitate rapidly in 17% isopropanol buffer. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 24, Book pp. 414–415, PDF pp. 427–428; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Thalassemia is caused by:
choices: Structurally abnormal hemoglobins with single amino acid substitutions
Absent or reduced synthesis of a polypeptide chain of hemoglobin
questions.officialAnswer: Absent or reduced synthesis of a polypeptide chain of hemoglobin
questions.explanation: Thalassemias are hereditary quantitative hemoglobin disorders characterized by mutations that cause decreased or absent synthesis of one or more structurally normal globin peptide chains (e.g., α or β globin), resulting in globin chain imbalance, ineffective erythropoiesis, and microcytic hypochromic anemia. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 425–426, PDF pp. 438–439; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Thalassemia is more prevalent in individuals of Mediterranean, African, Middle Eastern, and Southeast Asian ancestry because of:
choices: Dietary zinc deficiencies in tropical latitudes
Resistance to severe malaria in heterozygotes with a thalassemia mutation
High rates of spontaneous mutation in hot climates
questions.officialAnswer: Resistance to severe malaria in heterozygotes with a thalassemia mutation
questions.explanation: Heterozygous carriers of alpha and beta thalassemia mutations enjoy a selective survival advantage against lethal complications of Plasmodium falciparum malaria infection (balanced polymorphism), explaining the high gene frequencies historically maintained across the Mediterranean malaria belt, Middle East, Africa, and Southeast Asia. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book p. 425, PDF p. 438; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The hemolytic anemia and ineffective erythropoiesis associated with β-thalassemia major is primarily caused by:
choices: Direct toxicity of elevated free serum iron
Lack of ATP in mature erythrocytes
Precipitation of excess beta chains forming Hb H tetramers
Precipitation of excess unpaired α chains in erythroid precursors and mature RBCs
questions.officialAnswer: Precipitation of excess unpaired α chains in erythroid precursors and mature RBCs
questions.explanation: In severe β-thalassemia, severe deficiency of β-globin leaves an excess of unpaired α-globin chains. Unpaired α-chains cannot form stable tetramers and precipitate as insoluble hemichromes within erythroid precursors, damaging cell membranes, generating reactive oxygen species, and triggering massive apoptosis in the bone marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) and extravascular splenic hemolysis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 426–428, PDF pp. 439–441; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: β-Thalassemia minor (heterozygous β/β⁺ or β/β⁰) characteristically exhibits which diagnostic hemoglobin electrophoresis finding?
questions.explanation: The hallmark diagnostic laboratory finding in heterozygous β-thalassemia minor is an elevated hemoglobin A₂ level (typically 3.5% to 7.0%, normal <3.5%) caused by compensatory delta-chain synthesis, often accompanied by slightly elevated Hb F (1%–3%) and mild microcytic, hypochromic anemia (MCV 60–75 fL) with an RBC count > 5.0 × 10¹²/L. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 431–432, PDF pp. 444–445; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: RBC morphologic features in untreated β-thalassemia major (Cooley anemia) include:
choices: Microcytes, hypochromia, target cells, RBC inclusions, and circulating NRBCs
Normocytic RBCs with Heinz bodies exclusively
questions.officialAnswer: Microcytes, hypochromia, target cells, RBC inclusions, and circulating NRBCs
questions.explanation: Peripheral blood in β-thalassemia major demonstrates severe microcytic, hypochromic anemia with extreme anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, numerous target cells (codocytes), teardrop cells, basophilic stippling, Howell-Jolly bodies, and abundant nucleated red blood cells (NRBCs) reflecting massive erythroid stress. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 428–430, PDF pp. 441–443; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: β-Thalassemia major of the genotype β⁰/β⁰ produces NO detectable:
questions.explanation: In homozygous β⁰-thalassemia (β⁰/β⁰), mutations completely abolish the synthesis of normal beta globin chains. Because beta chains are completely absent, no normal adult hemoglobin A (α₂β₂) can be assembled; total circulating hemoglobin consists of 95% to 98% Hb F (α₂γ₂) and 2% to 5% Hb A₂ (α₂δ₂). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 428–429, PDF pp. 441–442; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Homozygotes for deletional-type hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin (HPFH) are characterized by:
choices: 100% Hb F with slightly hypochromic, microcytic RBCs and no clinical anemia
Elevated Hb A₂ (>8%) with normal Hb F
questions.officialAnswer: 100% Hb F with slightly hypochromic, microcytic RBCs and no clinical anemia
questions.explanation: Hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin (HPFH) results from large deletions in the beta-cluster that prevent the developmental gamma-to-beta switch. Homozygotes produce 100% Hb F (pancellular distribution) with mild microcytosis, normal total hemoglobin levels, and zero clinical symptoms because gamma chains completely compensate for absent beta chains. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 433–434, PDF pp. 446–447; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What abnormal fast-migrating hemoglobin is present in adult patients with three-gene deletion alpha-thalassemia (– –/–α)?
questions.explanation: In three-gene deletion alpha-thalassemia (– –/–α, Hemoglobin H disease), profound alpha-chain deficiency leaves an excess of beta chains that assemble into unstable, nonfunctional homotetramers of four beta chains (β₄), termed Hemoglobin H (Hb H). Hb H migrates rapidly toward the anode on alkaline electrophoresis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 435–437, PDF pp. 448–450; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Hemoglobin Bart is composed of:
choices: Two alpha and two delta chains (α₂δ₂)
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin Bart is a nonfunctional fast-migrating homotetramer composed of four gamma globin chains (γ₄). It forms in fetuses and neonates with alpha-thalassemia due to excess unpaired gamma chains; it accounts for 80% to 100% of hemoglobin in hydrops fetalis (four-gene deletion, – –/– –). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 435–438, PDF pp. 448–451; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: When one alpha gene is deleted (–α/αα, silent carrier), what clinical and hematologic picture is present?
choices: Normal hemoglobin levels and normal RBC indices (silent carrier)
questions.officialAnswer: Normal hemoglobin levels and normal RBC indices (silent carrier)
questions.explanation: The deletion of a single alpha globin gene (–α/αα, silent carrier / α-thalassemia-2 trait) leaves three functional alpha genes that synthesize sufficient alpha chains. Patients are completely asymptomatic with normal hemoglobin, normal or borderline-low MCV (78–82 fL), and normal adult electrophoresis patterns. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 435–436, PDF pp. 448–449; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: In which part of the world is the two-gene cis alpha-deletion (– –/αα, α-thalassemia-1) most common?
questions.explanation: The cis-deletion mutation of two alpha genes on the same chromosome (– –/αα) is highly prevalent in Southeast Asia and parts of the Mediterranean, explaining why homozygous inheritance resulting in fatal Hb Bart hydrops fetalis (– –/– –) occurs predominantly in Southeast Asian populations. In Africa, the trans deletion (–α/–α) predominates. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 435–437, PDF pp. 448–450; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: A patient with microcytic hypochromic anemia (MCV 68 fL) has a hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrating 65% Hb S, 25% Hb A, 6% Hb A₂, and 4% Hb F. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In classic sickle cell trait (Hb AS), Hb A exceeds Hb S (approx. 60% A vs 40% S), MCV is normal, and Hb A₂ is normal. In compound heterozygous Hb S-β⁺-thalassemia, reduced synthesis of normal beta chains from the β⁺ allele results in Hb S predominating over Hb A (typically 60%–80% S, 10%–30% A), microcytosis (MCV < 75 fL), and elevated Hb A₂ (>3.5%). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 438–440, PDF pp. 451–453; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Hemoglobin H inclusions in an incubated supravital stain preparation (brilliant cresyl blue) appear as:
choices: A single large purple inclusion adjacent to the inner membrane
Small, evenly distributed, greenish-blue granules giving the RBC a "golf-ball" appearance
questions.officialAnswer: Small, evenly distributed, greenish-blue granules giving the RBC a "golf-ball" appearance
questions.explanation: When whole blood from a patient with Hemoglobin H disease is incubated with a supravital stain (such as brilliant cresyl blue or new methylene blue), the unstable β₄ tetramers precipitate into hundreds of fine, evenly distributed, greenish-blue inclusions throughout the erythrocyte, classically described as a "golf-ball" or "raspberry" appearance. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 436–437, PDF pp. 449–450; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following laboratory findings is inconsistent with β-thalassemia minor?
choices: A slightly elevated RBC count and marked microcytosis
Target cells and basophilic stippling on the peripheral blood film
questions.explanation: β-Thalassemia minor characteristically features microcytic, hypochromic erythrocytes (decreased MCV, decreased or low-normal MCH/MCHC), high RBC count disproportionate to anemia (erythrocytosis), target cells, and basophilic stippling. Spherocytes and an elevated MCHC (>36 g/dL) are characteristic of hereditary spherocytosis, not thalassemia minor. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 431–433, PDF pp. 444–446; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: A 9-month-old infant of Asian heritage presents with failure to thrive, pallor, marked hepatosplenomegaly, severe anemia (hemoglobin 4.5 g/dL), and microcytosis (MCV 56 fL). Electrophoresis shows 95% Hb F, 5% Hb A₂, and 0% Hb A. This infant has:
questions.explanation: The presentation of severe infantile transfusion-dependent microcytic anemia, massive hepatosplenomegaly, complete absence of Hb A, and near 100% Hb F is diagnostic of homozygous β⁰-thalassemia major (β⁰/β⁰, Cooley anemia). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 25, Book pp. 428–430, PDF pp. 441–443; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following inherited leukocyte disorders is characterized by hyposegmentation of granulocyte nuclei into bilobed (pince-nez spectacles) or round unsegmented shapes with normal cellular function?
questions.explanation: Pelger-Huët anomaly is an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations in the lamin B receptor (LBR) gene, resulting in failure of normal granulocyte nuclear segmentation. Neutrophils possess bilobed nuclei connected by a thin chromatin filament ("pince-nez" spectacles) or unsegmented round/peanut shapes with coarse chromatin. Neutrophil function and patient health are entirely normal. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 26, Book pp. 446–447, PDF pp. 459–460; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following inherited leukocyte disorders is characterized by large, pale blue cytoplasmic inclusions in granulocytes and monocytes that resemble Döhle bodies, accompanied by giant platelets and thrombocytopenia?
questions.explanation: May-Hegglin anomaly is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the MYH9 gene (non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA). It is characterized by the triad of: (1) large spindle-shaped, pale blue Döhle-like cytoplasmic inclusion bodies composed of precipitated myosin filaments in leukocytes, (2) giant hypogranular platelets, and (3) mild to moderate thrombocytopenia. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 26, Book pp. 448–449, PDF pp. 461–462; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following inherited leukocyte disorders is characterized by prominent, dark azurophilic granules resembling toxic granulation in all types of leukocytes, caused by incomplete degradation of mucopolysaccharides?
questions.explanation: Alder-Reilly anomaly is an autosomal recessive condition associated with mucopolysaccharidoses (such as Hurler and Hunter syndromes). Deficiencies in lysosomal enzymes lead to accumulation of partially degraded glycosaminoglycans that form dense, dark purple/azurophilic granules in the cytoplasm of neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes (unlike toxic granulation, which is limited to neutrophils). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 26, Book pp. 447–448, PDF pp. 460–461; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following lysosomal storage diseases is characterized by a deficiency of glucocerebrosidase, leading to large lipid-laden histiocytes with eccentric nuclei and cytoplasm described as "wrinkled tissue paper"?
questions.explanation: Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase (acid beta-glucosidase). Glucosylceramide accumulates within reticuloendothelial macrophages, transforming them into diagnostic Gaucher cells: large macrophages (20–100 µm) with small eccentric nuclei and characteristic fibrillar, striate cytoplasm resembling crumpled or wrinkled tissue paper. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 26, Book pp. 450–452, PDF pp. 463–465; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The neutrophils in chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) are characterized by which of the following?
choices: Normal morphology, normal phagocytosis and degranulation, but failure to generate the respiratory burst (superoxide radicals)
questions.explanation: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is an inherited immunodeficiency (most commonly X-linked) caused by mutations in NADPH oxidase subunits (such as gp91phox). Neutrophils have normal morphology and ingest bacteria normally, but cannot generate the respiratory burst (superoxide, hydrogen peroxide), failing to kill catalase-positive bacteria (confirmed by negative nitroblue tetrazolium or dihydrorhodamine 123 assay). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 26, Book pp. 449–450, PDF pp. 462–463; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Individuals with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (X-SCID) have a mutation in the gene encoding:
choices: Common gamma chain (γc) shared by the IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21 receptors
questions.officialAnswer: Common gamma chain (γc) shared by the IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21 receptors
questions.explanation: X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (X-SCID) accounts for ~50% of SCID cases and is caused by mutations in IL2RG, which encodes the common gamma chain (γc) shared by interleukin receptors IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21, crippling T-cell and NK-cell signaling and causing absent cellular and humoral immunity. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 26, Book pp. 453–455, PDF pp. 466–468; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: An absolute lymphocytosis with reactive (Downey) lymphocytes exhibiting flared basophilic cytoplasmic borders scalloping around neighboring erythrocytes is typical of:
choices: Viral infection (such as Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis)
questions.officialAnswer: Viral infection (such as Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis)
questions.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis (caused by Epstein-Barr virus) and other viral infections (CMV, acute hepatitis) classically trigger polyclonal stimulation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8⁺), which appear as reactive (Downey type II) lymphocytes with abundant pale cytoplasm that flairs into royal-blue edges and indents or scallops around adjacent erythrocytes. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 26, Book pp. 455–458, PDF pp. 468–471; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: What leukocyte cytoplasmic inclusion is composed of lamellar aggregates of rough endoplasmic reticulum and appears as a light gray-blue oval structure in neutrophils during severe infection or burns?
questions.explanation: Döhle bodies are single or multiple light blue-gray, oval or round peripheral cytoplasmic inclusions in neutrophils and bands composed of parallel aggregates of rough endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomal RNA, classically found alongside toxic granulation and vacuolization in severe bacterial infections, burns, trauma, or cytokine administration. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 26, Book pp. 445–446, PDF pp. 458–459; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: The expected complete blood cell count (CBC) in an acute severe bacterial infection typically shows:
choices: High total WBC count with a shift to the left in neutrophils and toxic changes
questions.officialAnswer: High total WBC count with a shift to the left in neutrophils and toxic changes
questions.explanation: In acute bacterial infections, systemic inflammatory cytokines mobilize the post-mitotic bone marrow reserve pool and accelerate granulopoiesis, producing leukocytosis (WBC > 11.0 × 10⁹/L), neutrophilia, a "shift to the left" (increased bands, metamyelocytes), and toxic reactive changes (toxic granulation, cytoplasmic vacuolation, Döhle bodies). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 26, Book pp. 445–446, PDF pp. 458–459; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true of reactive lymphocytes seen in infectious mononucleosis?
choices: They are clonal malignant B cells.
They are unreactive Epstein-Barr virus-infected B cells.
The reactive lymphocytes have increased cytoplasm with variable basophilia and represent polyclonal activated T cells responding to infected B cells.
They are always CD4-positive helper T cells.
questions.officialAnswer: The reactive lymphocytes have increased cytoplasm with variable basophilia and represent polyclonal activated T cells responding to infected B cells.
questions.explanation: Although Epstein-Barr virus infects B lymphocytes via CD21, the atypical/reactive lymphocytes seen in peripheral blood are non-malignant, polyclonal activated CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes responding immunologically to the infected B cells, displaying abundant, pleomorphic cytoplasm with variable basophilia and indented nuclear contours. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 26, Book pp. 455–458, PDF pp. 468–471; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Lymphomas differ from leukemias in that they initially present as:
choices: Solid tumors primarily localized in lymph nodes and secondary lymphoid tissues
Marrow-based blasts exceeding 20% in the blood
Disorders limited to the myeloid lineage
questions.officialAnswer: Solid tumors primarily localized in lymph nodes and secondary lymphoid tissues
questions.explanation: Leukemias primarily originate in the bone marrow and disseminate into the peripheral blood, whereas lymphomas originate as solid malignant tumors within secondary lymphoid tissues (lymph nodes, spleen, MALT) before potentially spreading secondarily to the bone marrow or blood. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 27, Book pp. 467–468, PDF pp. 480–481; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following viruses is known to cause adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL)?
questions.explanation: Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) is an oncogenic retrovirus endemic in southwestern Japan, the Caribbean basin, and central Africa that directly infects CD4⁺ T cells, causing adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) characterized by malignant "flower cells" with cloverleaf nuclei. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 27, Book p. 469, PDF p. 482; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Loss-of-function mutations in tumor suppressor genes in hematologic neoplasms promote malignancy primarily by:
choices: Allowing cells with damaged DNA to progress through the cell cycle without undergoing repair or apoptosis
questions.officialAnswer: Allowing cells with damaged DNA to progress through the cell cycle without undergoing repair or apoptosis
questions.explanation: Tumor suppressor genes (such as TP53, RB1, and CDKN2A) encode proteins that normally enforce cell-cycle checkpoints, facilitate DNA damage repair, or trigger apoptosis. Loss-of-function mutations eliminate these critical brakes, permitting cells harboring oncogenic mutations to survive and divide unchecked. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 27, Book pp. 469–471, PDF pp. 482–484; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Proto-oncogenes converted to oncogenes act in a dominant fashion because:
choices: Both alleles must be inactivated to produce a phenotype
They are located on the X chromosome exclusively
A gain-of-function mutation in only one allele is sufficient to promote a malignant phenotype
questions.officialAnswer: A gain-of-function mutation in only one allele is sufficient to promote a malignant phenotype
questions.explanation: Oncogenes represent dominant gain-of-function genetic alterations: activating mutations, amplifications, or chromosomal translocations involving only a single allele (e.g., BCR-ABL1, MYC) generate constitutively active proteins that promote cell proliferation and survival, overcoming normal regulatory signals. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 27, Book pp. 469–471, PDF pp. 482–484; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is NOT one of the classic hallmarks of cancer?
choices: Evading growth suppressors and resisting cell death
Acceleration of DNA catabolism and rapid cellular shrinkage
Inducing angiogenesis and enabling replicative immortality
