questions.officialAnswer: Acceleration of DNA catabolism and rapid cellular shrinkage
questions.explanation: The classic hallmarks of cancer (Hanahan & Weinberg) include: sustaining proliferative signaling, evading growth suppressors, resisting cell death, enabling replicative immortality, inducing angiogenesis, activating invasion and metastasis, avoiding immune destruction, and reprogramming energy metabolism. DNA catabolism and shrinkage represent apoptosis, which cancer cells specifically evade. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 27, Book pp. 470–472, PDF pp. 483–485; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is a classic example of a tumor suppressor gene frequently mutated across diverse hematologic malignancies?
questions.explanation: TP53, located on chromosome 17p, encodes the p53 tumor suppressor protein ("guardian of the genome"), which halts the cell cycle at G1/S upon DNA damage or induces apoptosis. TP53 deletion/mutation is associated with poor prognosis and chemotherapy resistance in MDS, AML, and CLL. BCR-ABL1, MYC, and JAK2 are oncogenes. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 27, Book pp. 470–471, PDF pp. 483–484; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) is provided as supportive treatment during leukemia chemotherapy to:
choices: Reduce the duration of severe neutropenia and reduce the risk of life-threatening infection
questions.officialAnswer: Reduce the duration of severe neutropenia and reduce the risk of life-threatening infection
questions.explanation: Intensive myelosuppressive chemotherapy eradicates bone marrow hematopoietic precursors, causing prolonged severe neutropenia (ANC < 0.5 × 10⁹/L). Recombinant G-CSF (filgrastim) is administered as supportive therapy to stimulate neutrophil proliferation and maturation, shortening neutropenia duration and reducing infection-related mortality. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 27, Book pp. 473–474, PDF pp. 486–487; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Imatinib mesylate is an example of what type of antineoplastic therapy in hematologic malignancies?
questions.explanation: Imatinib (Gleevec) is a revolutionary targeted small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that binds specifically to the ATP-binding pocket of the constitutively active BCR-ABL1 fusion tyrosine kinase in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), blocking oncogenic downstream phosphorylation and inducing apoptosis in leukemic cells. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 27, Book pp. 473–475, PDF pp. 486–488; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements is FALSE regarding epigenetic modifications in hematologic neoplasms?
choices: Epigenetic modifications alter gene expression without altering the primary DNA sequence.
DNA methylation occurs predominantly on cytosine residues in CpG islands.
Hypermethylation of CpG islands in gene promoters results in their overactivation and increased transcription.
Histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi) and hypomethylating agents are approved therapies for hematologic malignancies.
questions.officialAnswer: Hypermethylation of CpG islands in gene promoters results in their overactivation and increased transcription.
questions.explanation: DNA methylation of CpG islands in gene promoter regions is a repressive epigenetic mark that recruits chromatin-condensing complexes and silences gene transcription (it does NOT overactivate transcription). Tumor suppressor genes (e.g., p15, p16) are frequently silenced by promoter hypermethylation in MDS and acute leukemias. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 27, Book pp. 471–473, PDF pp. 484–486; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is NOT an established source of hematopoietic stem cells used for therapeutic allogeneic stem cell transplantation?
questions.explanation: Standard clinical graft sources of hematopoietic stem cells for therapeutic transplantation include: (1) bone marrow aspirates collected from posterior iliac crests, (2) peripheral blood progenitor cells mobilized with G-CSF (and collected via apheresis), and (3) umbilical cord blood. The spleen is not a clinical stem cell graft harvest source. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 27, Book pp. 474–475, PDF pp. 487–488; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Flow Cytometric Analysis in Hematologic Disorders
questions.prompt: What is the most common clinical diagnostic application of multicolor flow cytometry in the hematology laboratory?
choices: Measurement of red blood cell folate
Immunophenotyping for the diagnosis and classification of leukemias and lymphomas
questions.officialAnswer: Immunophenotyping for the diagnosis and classification of leukemias and lymphomas
questions.explanation: Multicolor flow cytometric immunophenotyping is essential in diagnostic hematopathology for: establishing cell lineage (B, T, or myeloid), identifying aberrant antigen co-expression or loss, determining cell maturity/blast populations, establishing monoclonality (light-chain restriction), and detecting minimal residual disease (MRD) in acute leukemias, lymphoproliferative disorders, and plasma cell neoplasms. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 28, Book pp. 478–480, PDF pp. 491–493; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Flow Cytometric Analysis in Hematologic Disorders
questions.prompt: Which of the following is true of the CD45 leukocyte common antigen in flow cytometric gating?
choices: It is expressed only on mature B lymphocytes.
It is expressed on all hematopoietic cells, with the exception of mature erythrocytes, megakaryocytes, and late erythroid precursors.
It is absent on mature neutrophils.
It is an intracellular cytoplasmic marker.
questions.officialAnswer: It is expressed on all hematopoietic cells, with the exception of mature erythrocytes, megakaryocytes, and late erythroid precursors.
questions.explanation: CD45 (leukocyte common antigen) is a transmembrane tyrosine phosphatase expressed on all white blood cell lineages. Its expression density increases with hematopoietic maturation: blasts have low/dim CD45, monocytes have moderate CD45, and lymphocytes have the highest/bright CD45. Mature red cells, platelet-shedding megakaryocytes, and late normoblasts lack CD45. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 28, Book pp. 480–482, PDF pp. 493–495; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Flow Cytometric Analysis in Hematologic Disorders
questions.prompt: Erythroid precursors in the bone marrow are characterized flow cytometrically by the prominent expression of which surface marker alongside CD117 and glycophorin A?
questions.explanation: Erythroid lineage precursors exhibit high expression of CD71 (transferrin receptor 1, required for iron uptake during hemoglobin synthesis) and CD235a (glycophorin A), while lacking leukocyte markers like CD45 (dim/negative) and myeloid markers like CD13 and CD33. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 28, Book pp. 482–483, PDF pp. 495–496; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Flow Cytometric Analysis in Hematologic Disorders
questions.prompt: In CD45 versus side scatter (SS) flow cytometric gating (Figure 28.2A), the cell population with the bright/highest CD45 expression and low side scatter corresponds to:
questions.explanation: On a CD45 vs side scatter (SSC) dot plot (Figure 28.2A), white blood cell subsets segregate characteristically: mature lymphocytes have low side scatter (few internal granules) and bright/strong CD45; monocytes have intermediate side scatter and moderate CD45; mature granulocytes have very high side scatter and moderate CD45; and blasts cluster with low side scatter and dim CD45. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 28, Book pp. 481–482, PDF pp. 494–495; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Flow Cytometric Analysis in Hematologic Disorders
questions.prompt: Antigens characteristically co-expressed by B lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL) cells include:
questions.explanation: B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL / precursor B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia) is immunophenotypically defined by B-lineage surface markers CD19, CD22, and CD79a, combined with immature/progenitor markers CD34, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), and CD10 (common ALL antigen / CALLA). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 28, Book pp. 484–486, PDF pp. 497–499; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Flow Cytometric Analysis in Hematologic Disorders
questions.prompt: Which of the following is true of flow cytometric gating?
choices: It is best defined as the software-based selection of a specific target cell population for detailed phenotypic analysis based on physical scatter and fluorescence parameters.
It physically discards unwanted cells from the specimen suspension prior to analysis.
It requires destruction of white cell membranes.
It cannot be performed using multiple antibodies.
questions.officialAnswer: It is best defined as the software-based selection of a specific target cell population for detailed phenotypic analysis based on physical scatter and fluorescence parameters.
questions.explanation: Gating in flow cytometry is a software analysis technique whereby an electronic boundary (gate) is drawn around a distinct cluster of events on a bivariate dot plot (e.g., CD45 vs SSC, or forward vs side scatter) to isolate that specific cell subpopulation (such as blasts or lymphocytes) for selective multidimensional immunophenotyping. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 28, Book pp. 480–482, PDF pp. 493–495; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Flow Cytometric Analysis in Hematologic Disorders
questions.prompt: Collection of ungated list-mode events in clinical flow cytometry:
choices: Facilitates comprehensive retrospective analysis of all cellular events and prevents inadvertent exclusion of unexpected abnormal populations
Limits the storage size of electronic data files
Is prohibited by clinical laboratory regulatory guidelines
questions.officialAnswer: Facilitates comprehensive retrospective analysis of all cellular events and prevents inadvertent exclusion of unexpected abnormal populations
questions.explanation: Acquiring ungated list-mode data stores raw multidimensional parameter data for every single intercepted event without preset hardware filters. This allows pathologists to perform comprehensive retrospective analysis, re-examine backgating, and identify unexpected malignant or rare populations (such as hemodiluted blasts) that might otherwise be discarded by rigid live acquisition gating. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 28, Book pp. 480–481, PDF pp. 493–494; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Flow Cytometric Analysis in Hematologic Disorders
questions.prompt: Mycosis fungoides / Sézary syndrome (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma) is immunophenotypically characterized by:
choices: Loss of pan-T-cell antigens (such as CD7 and/or CD26) compared with normal mature helper T-cell populations
Expression of myeloid peroxidase and CD33
questions.officialAnswer: Loss of pan-T-cell antigens (such as CD7 and/or CD26) compared with normal mature helper T-cell populations
questions.explanation: Malignant T cells in mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome are CD4⁺ helper T cells that characteristically exhibit aberrant immunophenotypic antigen loss—most notably the loss of pan-T-cell markers CD7 and/or CD26, and occasionally CD2, CD3, or CD5—distinguishing them from benign reactive T-cell infiltrates. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 28, Book pp. 487–488, PDF pp. 500–501; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Flow Cytometric Analysis in Hematologic Disorders
questions.prompt: Mature neutrophilic granulocytes in bone marrow and peripheral blood show strong surface expression of:
choices: CD15, CD33, and CD13 (with CD16 on mature segmented neutrophils)
questions.officialAnswer: CD15, CD33, and CD13 (with CD16 on mature segmented neutrophils)
questions.explanation: Myeloid granulocytic maturation is characterized by sequential expression of pan-myeloid markers: CD13, CD33, and CD15, with mature segmented neutrophils acquiring high-density CD16 (FcγRIIIb) and CD11b alongside intense orthogonal light scatter from specific granules. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 28, Book pp. 482–484, PDF pp. 495–497; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Flow Cytometric Analysis in Hematologic Disorders
questions.prompt: During the initial flow cytometric evaluation of cellular complexity and granularity, which optical parameter provides information on internal cytoplasmic structure and nuclear lobularity?
questions.explanation: Side scatter (SSC, measured at 90° orthogonal to the incident laser beam) results from light refraction and internal reflection by cytoplasmic granules, organelle membranes, and nuclear contours, quantifying internal structural complexity. Forward scatter (FSC) measures light diffraction proportional to cell cross-sectional area and volume. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 28, Book pp. 478–480, PDF pp. 491–493; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.subtopic: Flow Cytometric Analysis in Hematologic Disorders
questions.prompt: The most important immunophenotypic criterion for confirming that a mature B-cell lymphoproliferative population is neoplastic rather than reactive is the demonstration of:
choices: Clonal surface immunoglobulin light chain restriction (an exclusively kappa- or lambda-positive population)
questions.officialAnswer: Clonal surface immunoglobulin light chain restriction (an exclusively kappa- or lambda-positive population)
questions.explanation: A normal/reactive polyclonal B-cell population displays an admixed ratio of kappa (κ) and lambda (λ) light-chain-expressing cells (normal κ:λ ratio approx. 1.2:1 to 2.0:1). The demonstration of extreme light-chain restriction (κ:λ ratio > 3:1 or < 0.3:1, or >95% single light-chain expression) is the hallmark flow cytometric proof of monoclonality diagnostic of B-cell lymphoma or leukemia. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 28, Book pp. 486–488, PDF pp. 499–501; Appendix C, PDF p. 862).

questions.prompt: If the DNA template nucleotide sequence is 5'-ATTAGC-3', then the mRNA sequence transcribed from this template is:
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase synthesizes mRNA in the 5' to 3' direction antiparallel and complementary to the DNA template strand. The complementary sequence to 5'-ATTAGC-3' read in the antiparallel direction (3' to 5') is 3'-UAAUCG-5', which corresponds to 5'-GCUAAU-3'. Uracil (U) substitutes for thymine (T) in RNA. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 29, Book pp. 499–501, PDF pp. 512–514; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: Cells with damaged DNA and mutated or nonfunctioning cell cycle regulatory proteins:
choices: Are arrested in G1 and the DNA is repaired
Continue to divide, which leads to tumor progression
Divide normally, producing identical daughter cells
questions.officialAnswer: Continue to divide, which leads to tumor progression
questions.explanation: Normal cell cycle checkpoints (G1/S and G2/M) arrest the cell cycle when DNA damage is sensed, allowing DNA repair or initiating apoptosis (programmed cell death) if damage is irreparable. Mutated or inactivated checkpoint proteins (e.g., TP53, Rb) permit cells with damaged DNA to bypass checkpoints and continue dividing, acquiring additional mutations and driving tumor progression. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 29, Book pp. 501–504, PDF pp. 514–517; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: To initiate DNA replication, DNA polymerase requires an available 3' hydroxyl group found on the:
questions.explanation: DNA polymerases can only add deoxynucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs) to a pre-existing 3'-hydroxyl (-OH) terminus. During DNA replication in vivo or in vitro (such as PCR), RNA primase or synthesized oligonucleotide primers provide the requisite free 3'-OH group to initiate nucleotide polymerization. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 29, Book pp. 504–506, PDF pp. 517–519; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: Ligase joins Okazaki fragments of the:
questions.explanation: Because DNA synthesis proceeds exclusively in the 5' to 3' direction, the lagging strand is replicated discontinuously as short Okazaki fragments away from the replication fork. DNA ligase seals the phosphodiester nicks between adjacent Okazaki fragments after RNA primer removal, yielding a continuous lagging strand. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 29, Book pp. 505–507, PDF pp. 518–520; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: A 40-year-old patient enters the hospital with a rare form of cancer caused by faulty cell division regulation. This cancer localized in the patient's spleen. An ambitious laboratory developed a molecular test to verify the type of cancer present. This molecular test would require patient specimens taken from which two tissues?
choices: Abnormal growths found on the skin and in the bone marrow
Normal splenic tissue and cancerous tissue
Cancerous tissue in spleen and bone marrow
Peripheral blood and cancerous tissue in the spleen
questions.officialAnswer: Normal splenic tissue and cancerous tissue
questions.explanation: To verify somatic tumor-specific genetic mutations or altered expression patterns, molecular analysis requires comparing the abnormal neoplastic tissue against unaffected constitutional/normal tissue from the same organ or individual to control for germline polymorphisms. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 29, Book pp. 507–510, PDF pp. 520–523; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: One main difference between standard PCR and reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) is that:
choices: PCR uses reverse transcriptase to elongate the primers
Reverse transcriptase PCR uses cDNA as a template
Reverse transcriptase PCR requires ligase to amplify the target DNA
questions.officialAnswer: Reverse transcriptase PCR uses cDNA as a template
questions.explanation: Standard PCR amplifies double-stranded genomic DNA directly. In reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR), RNA transcripts are first converted into complementary DNA (cDNA) by the enzyme reverse transcriptase, and the resulting cDNA is then amplified by DNA polymerase. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 29, Book pp. 511–513, PDF pp. 524–526; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements about gel electrophoresis is FALSE?
choices: The gel is oriented in the chamber with the wells at the positive terminal
A buffer solution is required to maintain the electrical current
The matrix of a polyacrylamide gel is tighter than that of an agarose gel
The larger DNA fragments will be closest to the wells of the gel
questions.officialAnswer: The gel is oriented in the chamber with the wells at the positive terminal
questions.explanation: DNA has a net negative charge due to its sugar-phosphate backbone and therefore migrates toward the positive terminal (anode). The wells must be placed at the negative terminal (cathode) so that fragments migrate through the gel matrix toward the positive terminal. Placing wells at the positive terminal causes DNA to run off into the buffer. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 29, Book pp. 514–516, PDF pp. 527–529; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: In which of the following applications would it be most appropriate to use next-generation sequencing (NGS) technology?
choices: Testing for a point mutation in the FV gene
Testing for the BCR-ABL1 translocation in CML
questions.explanation: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) offers massive parallel sequencing capacity suitable for whole-genome, whole-exome, or multi-gene cancer panel sequencing across thousands of bases simultaneously. Single point mutations (e.g., Factor V Leiden) are readily tested by targeted PCR-RFLP or allele-specific PCR, and BCR-ABL1 is monitored by RT-qPCR. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 29, Book pp. 517–520, PDF pp. 530–533; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: One major difference between end-point PCR and real-time PCR (qPCR) is that:
choices: End-point PCR requires thermostable DNA polymerase, deoxynucleotides, and primers
End-point PCR requires a separate step to detect the amplicons formed in the reaction
Real-time PCR uses capillary gel electrophoresis to detect amplicons during PCR cycling
Real-time PCR detects and quantifies amplicons using cleavage-based signal amplification
questions.officialAnswer: End-point PCR requires a separate step to detect the amplicons formed in the reaction
questions.explanation: In end-point PCR, amplicons are analyzed only after all thermal cycles are completed (typically by agarose or capillary gel electrophoresis). Real-time PCR (qPCR) monitors fluorescent signal accumulation cycle-by-cycle as amplification occurs, allowing quantitative analysis without post-amplification manipulation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 29, Book pp. 512–514, PDF pp. 525–527; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about minimal residual disease (MRD) is TRUE?
choices: Clinical remission of hematologic cancers is determined by molecular techniques such as PCR and flow cytometry
Real-time quantitative PCR-determined copy number of BCR-ABL1 transcripts will always be lower in molecular remission than in clinical remission
Qualitative PCR that uses a known copy number of a target sequence is of use in determining minimal residual disease levels
Minimal residual disease assessment can aid physicians in making treatment decisions but does not yet offer insights into prognosis
questions.officialAnswer: Real-time quantitative PCR-determined copy number of BCR-ABL1 transcripts will always be lower in molecular remission than in clinical remission
questions.explanation: Clinical remission is defined by morphological disappearance of leukemic blasts (<5% in marrow, normal peripheral counts), which can still harbor up to 10^9 to 10^10 leukemic cells. Molecular remission corresponds to deep undetectable or negligible transcript copy numbers on RT-qPCR (e.g., Major Molecular Response with ≥3-log reduction, MR4.5 with ≥4.5-log reduction), which is orders of magnitude lower than clinical remission levels. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 29, Book pp. 520–522, PDF pp. 533–535; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: G-banding refers to the technique of staining chromosomes:
choices: To isolate those in the G group (i.e., chromosomes 21 and 22)
In the G0 or resting stage
To emphasize areas high in guanine residues
questions.explanation: G-banding (Giemsa banding) involves brief enzymatic treatment of metaphase chromosome spreads with trypsin followed by staining with Giemsa stain. This produces characteristic alternating dark (AT-rich, gene-poor) and light (GC-rich, gene-rich) bands unique to each chromosome pair. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 30, Book pp. 528–530, PDF pp. 541–543; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: Which of the following compounds is used to halt mitosis in metaphase for chromosome analyses?
questions.explanation: Colchicine (or its synthetic derivative Colcemid) disrupts mitotic spindle apparatus microtubules, arresting dividing cells at metaphase when chromosomes are maximally condensed and suitable for karyotypic banding analysis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 30, Book pp. 528–530, PDF pp. 541–543; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: One arm of a chromosome has 30 bands. Which band would be nearest the centromere?
questions.explanation: In cytogenetic nomenclature (ISCN), chromosome band numbering on each arm (p or q) proceeds sequentially outward from the centromere toward the telomere. Band 1 is closest to the centromere, while the highest numbered band is at the distal telomeric end. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 30, Book pp. 529–531, PDF pp. 542–544; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of the use of fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)?
choices: It can be used on nondividing cells
It can be used on paraffin-embedded tissue
It can detect mutations that do not result in abnormal banding patterns
It must be performed on dividing cells
questions.officialAnswer: It must be performed on dividing cells
questions.explanation: Unlike conventional metaphase cytogenetics which requires live, proliferating cells in cell culture, interphase FISH does not require dividing cells and can be performed directly on non-mitotic interphase nuclei, blood smears, and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 30, Book pp. 531–533, PDF pp. 544–546; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: Which of the following types of mutations would likely NOT be detectable with cytogenetic banding techniques?
choices: Point mutation resulting in a single amino acid substitution
Transfer of genetic material from one chromosome to another
Loss of genetic material from a chromosome that does not appear on any other chromosome
Duplication of a chromosome resulting in 3n of that genetic material
questions.officialAnswer: Point mutation resulting in a single amino acid substitution
questions.explanation: Standard cytogenetic G-banding has a optical resolution limit of approximately 3 to 5 megabases (Mb). Point mutations involving single nucleotide changes (e.g., JAK2 V617F or sickle beta-globin) cannot alter microscopic chromosome banding and require molecular sequencing or PCR. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 30, Book pp. 530–532, PDF pp. 543–545; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a chromosomal deletion?
choices: Point mutation resulting in a single amino acid substitution
Transfer of genetic material from one chromosome to another
Loss of genetic material from a chromosome that does not appear on any other chromosome
Duplication of a chromosome resulting in 3n of that genetic material
questions.officialAnswer: Loss of genetic material from a chromosome that does not appear on any other chromosome
questions.explanation: A deletion (del) is a structural chromosomal aberration involving the physical loss of a segment of genetic material from a chromosome arm without translocation to another recipient chromosome. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 30, Book pp. 532–534, PDF pp. 545–547; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.caseStudy: The chromosome analysis performed on a patient’s leukemic cells is reported as 47, XY,+4,del(5)(q31)[20]. Answer questions 7 to 9 based on this description.
questions.prompt: A chromosome analysis performed on a patient's leukemic cells is reported as 47,XY,+4,del(5)(q31)[20]. This patient's cells have which of the following mutations?
choices: Loss of the entire number 31 chromosome
Loss of the entire number 5 chromosome
Loss of a portion of the short arm of chromosome 4
Loss of a portion of the long arm of chromosome 5
questions.officialAnswer: Loss of a portion of the long arm of chromosome 5
questions.explanation: In cytogenetic nomenclature, "del(5)(q31)" denotes an interstitial or terminal deletion of chromosome 5 on the long arm ("q") involving band 31. The short arm is designated "p". (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 30, Book pp. 533–535, PDF pp. 546–548; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.caseStudy: The chromosome analysis performed on a patient’s leukemic cells is reported as 47, XY,+4,del(5)(q31)[20]. Answer questions 7 to 9 based on this description.
questions.prompt: Based on the karyotype 47,XY,+4,del(5)(q31)[20], what other mutation is present in this patient's cells?
questions.explanation: The designation "+4" indicates trisomy 4 (the gain of an entire additional copy of chromosome 4), bringing the modal total chromosome count to 47 instead of the diploid 46. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 30, Book pp. 533–535, PDF pp. 546–548; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.caseStudy: The chromosome analysis performed on a patient’s leukemic cells is reported as 47, XY,+4,del(5)(q31)[20]. Answer questions 7 to 9 based on this description.
questions.prompt: Based on the karyotype 47,XY,+4,del(5)(q31)[20], this patient's leukemic cells demonstrate:
choices: Both structural and numeric chromosomal defects
questions.officialAnswer: Both structural and numeric chromosomal defects
questions.explanation: The karyotype exhibits a numeric abnormality (+4, gain of a chromosome yielding 47 chromosomes, an aneuploidy) and a structural abnormality (del(5)(q31), deletion of genetic material on 5q), representing both structural and numerical defects. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 30, Book pp. 533–535, PDF pp. 546–548; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: Aneuploidy describes a total chromosome number:
choices: That is a multiple of the haploid number
That reflects a loss or gain of a single chromosome
That is diploid but has a balanced deletion and duplication of whole chromosomes
In gametes; diploid is the number in somatic cells
questions.officialAnswer: That reflects a loss or gain of a single chromosome
questions.explanation: Aneuploidy refers to an abnormal chromosome number that is not an exact multiple of the haploid number (n = 23), resulting from the loss (monosomy, 2n - 1) or gain (trisomy, 2n + 1) of one or more individual chromosomes. Multiples of the haploid number (3n, 4n) are termed polyploidy. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 30, Book pp. 534–536, PDF pp. 547–549; Appendix C, PDF p. 863).

questions.prompt: According to the WHO classification, except in leukemias with specific recurring genetic abnormalities, the minimal percentage of blasts in the peripheral blood or bone marrow necessary for a diagnosis of acute leukemia is:
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization (WHO) classification defines acute leukemia by the presence of ≥20% blasts in the peripheral blood or bone marrow, lowering the historic FAB threshold of 30%. In cases with recurring cytogenetic abnormalities [e.g., t(8;21), inv(16), or t(15;17)], a diagnosis of AML is established regardless of blast count. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 31, Book pp. 542–544, PDF pp. 555–557; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A 20-year-old patient has an elevated WBC count with 70% blasts, 4% neutrophils, 5% lymphocytes, and 21% monocytes in the peripheral blood. Eosinophils with dysplastic basophilic granules are seen in the bone marrow. AML with which of the following karyotypes would be most likely?
questions.explanation: AML with inv(16)(p13.1q22) or t(16;16)(p13.1;q22) disrupts CBFB-MYH11 and is characteristically associated with myelomonocytic proliferation and abnormal bone marrow eosinophils containing large, dysplastic basophilic purple-violet granules (acute myelomonocytic leukemia with eosinophilia, AML M4eo). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 31, Book pp. 543–545, PDF pp. 556–558; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following would be considered a sign of potentially favorable prognosis in children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)?
questions.explanation: In pediatric B-ALL, hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes) and the cryptic translocation t(12;21)(p13;q22) [ETV6-RUNX1] are strongly associated with favorable treatment response and high cure rates (>90%). Conversely, hypodiploidy and t(9;22) [BCR-ABL1] carry adverse prognoses. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 31, Book pp. 549–551, PDF pp. 562–564; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Signs and symptoms of cerebral infiltration with blasts (central nervous system involvement) are more commonly seen in:
questions.explanation: Central nervous system (CNS) blast infiltration, manifesting as headache, nausea, papilledema, and cranial nerve palsies, occurs substantially more often in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) than in AML. Consequently, CNS prophylaxis (intrathecal chemotherapy) is standard in ALL treatment protocols. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 31, Book pp. 548–550, PDF pp. 561–563; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: An oncology patient exhibiting signs of renal failure with seizures shortly after beginning induction chemotherapy is most likely developing:
questions.explanation: Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) occurs when massive, rapid lysis of leukemic blasts following induction chemotherapy releases intracellular contents into systemic circulation, leading to severe hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia. Hypocalcemia provokes neuromuscular irritability and seizures, while uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals cause acute renal failure. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 31, Book pp. 547–549, PDF pp. 560–562; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is most characteristically seen in association with acute leukemia harboring which of the following mutations?
questions.explanation: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) with t(15;17)(q22;q12) [PML-RARA] is notorious for presenting with severe, life-threatening consumptive coagulopathy (DIC) and primary hyperfibrinolysis driven by the release of procoagulant tissue-factor-like substances and annexin II from abnormal promyelocyte granules. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 31, Book pp. 544–546, PDF pp. 557–559; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following acute leukemias affects primarily children, is characterized by an increase in monoblasts and monocytes, and is frequently associated with extramedullary tissue infiltration such as gingival hyperplasia and cutaneous chloromas?
questions.explanation: AML with t(9;11)(p22;q23) involves KMT2A (MLL)-MLLT3 fusion and characteristically exhibits monocytic or monoblastic morphology, commonly presenting in infants and young children with extramedullary infiltration into gingiva (gum swelling), skin (leukemia cutis), and meninges. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 31, Book pp. 545–547, PDF pp. 558–560; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A 20-year-old patient presents with fatigue, pallor, easy bruising, and swollen gums. Bone marrow examination reveals 82% blasts with delicate chromatin and prominent nucleoli that are CD14+, CD4+, CD11b+, and CD36+. Which of the following acute leukemias is most likely?
questions.explanation: The immunophenotypic profile expressing CD14, CD4, CD11b, CD36, and CD64, alongside clinical features of gingival hypertrophy, is diagnostic of acute monoblastic/monocytic leukemia (AML with monocytic differentiation). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 31, Book pp. 545–548, PDF pp. 558–561; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Pure erythroid leukemia is a rare neoplasm defined by the presence of:
choices: All forms of developing RBC precursors
Equal numbers of pronormoblasts and myeloblasts
questions.explanation: Pure erythroid leukemia (PEL) is a high-grade myeloid neoplasm defined by WHO criteria as a proliferation of ≥80% immature erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, with ≥30% being early, primitive pronormoblasts and basophilic normoblasts without a significant myeloblastic component. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 31, Book pp. 546–548, PDF pp. 559–561; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A patient with normal chromosomes has a WBC count of 3.0 × 10^9/L and multilineage dysplasia. There are 60% blasts of varying sizes. The blasts stain positive for CD61. The most likely type of leukemia is:
questions.explanation: CD61 (platelet glycoprotein IIIa) and CD41 (glycoprotein IIb) are specific platelet/megakaryocytic surface glycoproteins. Blasts staining positive for CD41, CD61, or CD42 are diagnostic of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AML-M7). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 31, Book pp. 546–548, PDF pp. 559–561; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Sudan Black B (SBB) stains which of the following cellular components?
questions.explanation: Sudan Black B is a lipophilic cytochemical dye that partitions into cellular lipids, sterols, and phospholipids present in the primary and secondary granules of granulocytic myeloid precursors and to a lesser extent monocytes, distinguishing AML from ALL (which is SBB negative). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 31, Book pp. 550–552, PDF pp. 563–565; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: The cytochemical stain α-naphthyl butyrate is a nonspecific esterase stain that shows diffuse positivity in cells of which lineage?
questions.explanation: Non-specific esterase (NSE) stains, including α-naphthyl butyrate and α-naphthyl acetate, show intense diffuse cytoplasmic positivity in monocytic cells that is inhibited by sodium fluoride (NaF). Granulocytic precursors are negative or weakly positive, whereas myeloblasts stain positive with specific esterase (naphthol AS-D chloroacetate esterase). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 31, Book pp. 551–553, PDF pp. 564–566; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A peripheral blood film that shows increased neutrophils, basophils, eosinophils, and platelets across all stages of myeloid maturation is highly suggestive of:
questions.explanation: Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is characterized by massive pan-myelosis with leukocytosis, absolute basophilia, absolute eosinophilia, thrombocytosis, and the entire spectrum of maturing granulocytic precursors from myeloblasts to segmented neutrophils ("the spectrum of granulopoiesis") visible in the peripheral blood. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 32, Book pp. 559–563, PDF pp. 572–576; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following chromosome abnormalities is associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML)?
questions.explanation: CML is defined cytogenetically by the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2), which fuses the BCR gene on chromosome 22 with the ABL1 proto-oncogene on chromosome 9, producing a constitutively active p210 BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 32, Book pp. 558–561, PDF pp. 571–574; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A patient has a WBC count of 30 × 10^9/L and the following differential: Segmented neutrophils 38%, Bands 17%, Metamyelocytes 7%, Myelocytes 20%, Promyelocytes 10%, Eosinophils 3%, Basophils 5%. Which of the following test results would be most helpful in confirming a diagnosis of CML?
questions.explanation: Demonstration of the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) or RT-qPCR confirms the Philadelphia translocation and provides definitive diagnostic distinction between CML and a leukemoid reaction. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 32, Book pp. 562–565, PDF pp. 575–578; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A patient in whom CML has previously been diagnosed has circulating blasts and promyelocytes that total 30% of leukocytes. The disease is considered to be in what phase?
questions.explanation: Blast phase (blast crisis or acute leukemia transformation) of CML is defined by the presence of ≥20% blasts in the peripheral blood or bone marrow, or extramedullary blast proliferation, behaving biologically as an aggressive acute leukemia (two-thirds myeloid, one-third lymphoid). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 32, Book pp. 564–566, PDF pp. 577–579; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: The most common mutation found in patients with primary polycythemia vera (PV) is:
questions.explanation: More than 95% of patients with polycythemia vera harbor the somatic activating point mutation JAK2 V617F in exon 14 (valine substituted by phenylalanine at codon 617), with nearly all remaining patients possessing JAK2 exon 12 mutations. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 32, Book pp. 568–572, PDF pp. 581–585; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: The peripheral blood in polycythemia vera typically manifests:
questions.explanation: Although absolute erythrocytosis (elevated RBC count, hemoglobin, and hematocrit) dominates, PV is a trilineage pan-myelosis; concurrent neutrophilic leukocytosis and thrombocytosis (>450 × 10^9/L) are present in the majority of patients. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 32, Book pp. 569–573, PDF pp. 582–586; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A patient has a platelet count of 700 × 10^9/L with abnormalities in the size, shape, and granularity of platelets, a WBC count of 12 × 10^9/L, and hemoglobin of 11 g/dL. The Philadelphia chromosome is absent. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Essential thrombocythemia (ET) is a BCR-ABL1-negative myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by sustained thrombocytosis (≥450 × 10^9/L), abnormal platelet morphology, megakaryocytic marrow hyperplasia, and absence of significant polycythemia or primary myelofibrosis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 32, Book pp. 574–578, PDF pp. 587–591; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Complications of essential thrombocythemia (ET) include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The clinical consequences of ET stem primarily from vascular circulatory disturbances caused by dysfunctional, hyperaggregable platelets (thrombosis and microvascular occlusion leading to strokes, seizures, digital ischemia) or acquired von Willebrand syndrome at extremely high platelet counts (hemorrhage). Severe infections are not a direct complication of ET. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 32, Book pp. 575–578, PDF pp. 588–591; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following morphological patterns is characteristic of the peripheral blood in patients with primary myelofibrosis (PMF)?
choices: Teardrop-shaped erythrocytes, nucleated RBCs, immature granulocytes
Hypochromic erythrocytes, immature granulocytes, and normal platelets
Spherocytes, immature granulocytes, and increased numbers of platelets
questions.officialAnswer: Teardrop-shaped erythrocytes, nucleated RBCs, immature granulocytes
questions.explanation: Primary myelofibrosis produces a classic leukoerythroblastic peripheral blood picture characterized by dacryocytes (teardrop-shaped RBCs), circulating nucleated red blood cells, immature granulocytic precursors (myelocytes, metamyelocytes), and giant bizarre platelets due to extramedullary hematopoiesis in the spleen and liver. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 32, Book pp. 578–582, PDF pp. 591–595; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: The progressive bone marrow myelofibrosis associated with PMF is a result of:
choices: Apoptosis resistance in the fibroblasts of the bone marrow
Impaired production of normal collagenase by the mutated cells
Enhanced activity of fibroblasts as a result of increased stimulatory cytokines
Increased numbers of fibroblasts as a result of cytokine stimulation of the pluripotential stem cells
questions.officialAnswer: Enhanced activity of fibroblasts as a result of increased stimulatory cytokines
questions.explanation: Fibroblasts in PMF are polyclonal and non-neoplastic. Fibrous tissue deposition (collagen types I and III) is a secondary reactive process provoked by excessive release of fibrogenic and angiogenic cytokines [transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), PDGF, bFGF] from clonal, dysplastic megakaryocytes and monocytes undergoing intramedullary death. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 32, Book pp. 579–583, PDF pp. 592–596; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are most common in which age group?
questions.explanation: MDS is predominantly a disease of older adults, with the median age at diagnosis between 70 and 75 years and incidence rising sharply in individuals older than 50 years. It is rare in children and young adults. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 33, Book pp. 591–593, PDF pp. 604–606; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is a major hallmark indication of MDS in the peripheral blood and bone marrow?
choices: Normal bone marrow with abnormal peripheral blood features
questions.explanation: The defining diagnostic hallmark of MDS is dyspoiesis (morphologic dysplasia affecting erythroid, myeloid, and/or megakaryocytic lineages) accompanied by peripheral cytopenias resulting from ineffective hematopoiesis in a hypercellular bone marrow. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 33, Book pp. 592–595, PDF pp. 605–608; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: An alert hematologist should recognize all of the following peripheral blood abnormalities as diagnostic clues in MDS EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Dysplastic morphological signs characteristic of MDS include oval macrocytes, pseudo-Pelger-Huët hyposegmented/agranular neutrophils, circulating micromegakaryocytes, and giant platelets. Target cells are non-specific findings typically associated with hemoglobinopathies, thalassemias, liver disease, or splenectomy. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 33, Book pp. 593–596, PDF pp. 606–609; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: For an erythroid precursor to be classified as a ring sideroblast, the iron-laden mitochondria must encircle how much of the nucleus?
questions.explanation: By International Working Group and WHO criteria, a ring sideroblast is defined as an erythroblast with five or more Prussian-blue-positive iron granules encircling at least one-third of the nucleus, reflecting pathological non-ferritin iron accumulation in perinuclear mitochondria. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 33, Book pp. 594–596, PDF pp. 607–609; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: According to the WHO classification of MDS, what percentage of blasts would constitute transformation to acute myeloid leukemia?
questions.explanation: A blast count of ≥20% in the peripheral blood or bone marrow fulfills WHO criteria for transformation of MDS into acute myeloid leukemia (AML with myelodysplasia-related changes). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 33, Book pp. 595–598, PDF pp. 608–611; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A patient has anemia, oval macrocytes, and hypersegmented neutrophils. Which of the following tests would be most efficient in differential diagnosis of this disorder from megaloblastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Both MDS and megaloblastic anemia feature oval macrocytic anemia and dysplastic/hypersegmented granulocytes. Measuring serum vitamin B12 and folate levels is the most rapid, noninvasive initial step to rule out a correctable nutritional vitamin deficiency before performing invasive bone marrow biopsies and cytogenetics for MDS. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 33, Book pp. 596–598, PDF pp. 609–611; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A 60-year-old woman comes to the physician with fatigue and malaise. Her hemoglobin is 8 g/dL, hematocrit is 25%, RBC count is 2.00 × 10^12/L, platelet count is 550 × 10^9/L, and WBC count is 3.8 × 10^9/L. Bone marrow shows erythroid hypoplasia and hypolobulated megakaryocytes; granulopoiesis appears normal. Ring sideroblasts are rare. Chromosome analysis reveals an isolated deletion of 5q [del(5q)]. Based on the classification of this disorder, what therapy would be most appropriate?
choices: Supportive therapy; lenalidomide if the disease progresses
Low-dose cytosine arabinoside, accompanied by cis-retinoic acid
questions.officialAnswer: Supportive therapy; lenalidomide if the disease progresses
questions.explanation: MDS with isolated del(5q) (5q- syndrome) carries a favorable prognosis and typically responds dramatically to the immunomodulatory agent lenalidomide, which induces transfusion independence and cytogenetic remissions. Aggressive chemotherapy or transplantation is unwarranted in this low-risk subtype. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 33, Book pp. 597–600, PDF pp. 610–613; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is LEAST likely to contribute to death in patients with myelodysplastic syndromes?
questions.explanation: The primary causes of mortality in MDS are severe cytopenias resulting in overwhelming infection/sepsis (from profound neutropenia), fatal hemorrhage (from thrombocytopenia), iron overload organ failure (hemochromatosis from chronic transfusions), or leukemic transformation. Peripheral neuropathy is not a direct life-threatening feature of MDS. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 33, Book pp. 598–600, PDF pp. 611–613; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Into what other hematologic disease does myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) most frequently convert?
questions.explanation: Approximately 30% of patients with MDS experience disease progression and transformation into acute myeloid leukemia (secondary AML / AML with myelodysplasia-related changes), which is often refractory to standard chemotherapy regimens. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 33, Book pp. 597–600, PDF pp. 610–613; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) is classified in the WHO system as:
questions.explanation: CMML displays overlapping features of both effective proliferation (persistent absolute monocytosis >1 × 10^9/L, leukocytosis, splenomegaly) and dysplastic cytopenias, leading the WHO to classify it within the hybrid category of Myelodysplastic/Myeloproliferative Neoplasms (MDS/MPN). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 33, Book pp. 599–601, PDF pp. 612–614; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can be best differentiated from reactive lymphoid hyperplasia by:
choices: Demonstration of immunophenotypic clonality or clonal gene rearrangement
questions.officialAnswer: Demonstration of immunophenotypic clonality or clonal gene rearrangement
questions.explanation: Reactive lymphoid hyperplasias are polyclonal, demonstrating a balanced mixture of kappa- and lambda-positive B cells and diverse T-cell subsets. Mature lymphoid neoplasms are clonal expansions exhibiting light chain restriction (exclusively kappa or lambda) or clonal immunoglobulin / T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangements. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 34, Book pp. 606–609, PDF pp. 619–622; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which laboratory test result is most suggestive of autoimmune hemolytic anemia in a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)?
questions.explanation: Up to 10% to 20% of CLL patients develop secondary autoimmune complications, most frequently warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) or immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) provoked by immune dysregulation. A positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT) confirms warm IgG autoantibodies directed against erythrocytes. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 34, Book pp. 609–612, PDF pp. 622–625; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the best test or method for determining whether a clonal population of mature T cells is present in a lymph node or peripheral blood specimen?
choices: T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement analysis by PCR
questions.officialAnswer: T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement analysis by PCR
questions.explanation: Because T cells lack a surrogate clonal surface marker equivalent to light chain restriction in B cells, molecular detection of clonal TCR-gamma (TRG) or TCR-beta (TRB) gene rearrangements by PCR is the definitive method for demonstrating T-cell clonality. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 34, Book pp. 612–615, PDF pp. 625–628; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A rise in the absolute lymphocyte count from 4.1 × 10^9/L to 5.5 × 10^9/L in an asymptomatic 68-year-old patient who has an established monoclonal B-cell population (CD19+, CD5+, CD23+, dim surface Ig) indicates:
choices: Transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Spurious elevation due to cold agglutinins
Progression from monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL) to chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)
questions.officialAnswer: Progression from monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL) to chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)
questions.explanation: Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL) is defined as a clonal B-cell population with CLL immunophenotype in the peripheral blood but with an absolute B-cell lymphocyte count <5.0 × 10^9/L and no lymphadenopathy. When the clonal B-cell count reaches ≥5.0 × 10^9/L, the diagnostic criteria for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) are fulfilled. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 34, Book pp. 609–612, PDF pp. 622–625; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which immunophenotypic or cytogenetic test is most reliable for differentiating chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) from mantle cell lymphoma (MCL)?
questions.explanation: Both CLL and MCL express the mature B-cell marker CD19 and the aberrant T-cell marker CD5. However, CLL is characteristically CD23-positive and CD200-positive with dim surface Ig, whereas mantle cell lymphoma is CD23-negative, CD200-negative, strongly bright surface Ig-positive, and defined by t(11;14)(q13;q32) producing cyclin D1 overexpression. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 34, Book pp. 611–614, PDF pp. 624–627; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: If not treated, which of the following mature lymphoid neoplasms would generally be associated with the most rapid clinical progression and shortest patient survival?
questions.explanation: Burkitt lymphoma is one of the fastest-growing human malignancies, with a proliferation fraction (Ki-67) approaching 100% and a doubling time under 24 to 48 hours driven by MYC translocation [t(8;14)]. Without emergent intensive therapy, it is rapidly fatal within weeks. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 34, Book pp. 614–617, PDF pp. 627–630; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What fundamental immunologic feature do chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and multiple myeloma have in common?
questions.explanation: Both CLL and plasma cell myeloma represent clonal neoplasms of the B-cell lineage. As neoplastic clonal B-cell proliferations, both demonstrate light chain restriction—CLL on the surface membrane of leukemic lymphocytes and myeloma as secreted monoclonal kappa or lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins/paraproteins). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 34, Book pp. 610–612, 620–622, PDF pp. 623–625, 633–635; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: In classical Hodgkin lymphoma, the Reed-Sternberg cell is the diagnostic malignant cell, whereas in nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL), the diagnostic malignant cell is the:
questions.explanation: In NLPHL, the characteristic neoplastic cells are "popcorn cells" (also termed lymphocytic and histiocytic [L&H] or LP cells), which have folded, multi-lobulated nuclei resembling popped corn kernels and express B-cell markers (CD20, CD79a, BCL6), unlike classic Reed-Sternberg cells. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 34, Book pp. 618–621, PDF pp. 631–634; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: In most routine diagnostic clinical settings, the initial diagnosis of non-Hodgkin lymphoma relies on all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Histopathologic examination of affected lymph nodes
Immunophenotyping by flow cytometry or immunohistochemistry
Peripheral blood examination and complete blood count
questions.explanation: Primary diagnosis and subclassification of non-Hodgkin lymphomas are reliably established using architectural histopathology on tissue biopsy combined with immunophenotyping (IHC/flow cytometry). Extensive molecular sequencing is not universally required for every standard routine lymphoma diagnosis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 34, Book pp. 607–610, PDF pp. 620–623; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following clinical features is typically ABSENT in monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) but present in multiple myeloma?
choices: Clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow
questions.explanation: MGUS is defined by a serum M-protein <3.0 g/dL, <10% bone marrow clonal plasma cells, and the strict absence of CRAB end-organ damage (no Hypercalcemia, no Renal insufficiency, no Anemia, and no Bone lesions). Hypercalcemia indicates active, symptomatic plasma cell myeloma requiring therapy. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 34, Book pp. 621–624, PDF pp. 634–637; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What vascular intimal cell synthesizes and stores von Willebrand factor (VWF)?
questions.explanation: Vascular endothelial cells line the vessel lumen and actively synthesize VWF, storing it within intracellular storage granules termed Weibel-Palade bodies for regulated or constitutive release. Megakaryocytes also synthesize VWF and package it into platelet alpha-granules. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 628–631, PDF pp. 641–644; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What subendothelial structural transmembrane protein triggers in vivo coagulation through high-affinity binding and activation of factor VII?
questions.explanation: Tissue factor (TF, thromboplastin, CD142) is a subendothelial transmembrane glycoprotein exposed upon vascular wall injury. It forms an enzymatic complex with circulating factor VII/VIIa, activating factors IX and X to initiate in vivo extrinsic/tissue factor pathway coagulation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 633–636, PDF pp. 646–649; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What key coagulation plasma protein should be assayed when platelets fail to aggregate in response to standard agonists in platelet aggregation studies?
questions.explanation: Fibrinogen (factor I) is essential for primary hemostatic platelet plug formation, serving as the divalent bridge that cross-links activated platelet GP IIb/IIIa (αIIbβ3) receptors during platelet aggregation. In afibrinogenemia, platelet aggregation curves are profoundly abnormal with all agonists except ristocetin. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 631–634, PDF pp. 644–647; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the primary biochemical role of vitamin K for the prothrombin group coagulation factors (factors II, VII, IX, and X)?
choices: Provides a surface on which the proteolytic reactions of the factors occur
Protects them from inappropriate activation by compounds such as thrombin
Accelerates the binding of the serine proteases and their cofactors
Carboxylates the factors to allow calcium binding
questions.officialAnswer: Carboxylates the factors to allow calcium binding
questions.explanation: Vitamin K functions as an essential cofactor for hepatic gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which post-translationally carboxylates glutamic acid residues into gamma-carboxyglutamic acid (Gla) domains. Negative Gla domains bind divalent Ca2+ ions, enabling calcium-dependent anchoring to negatively charged platelet phospholipid surfaces. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 636–638, PDF pp. 649–651; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the biological source of prothrombin fragment 1.2 (F1.2)?
choices: Proteolysis of prothrombin by factor Xa
questions.explanation: Prothrombin fragment 1.2 is cleaved from prothrombin (factor II) by the prothrombinase complex (FXa, FVa, Ca2+, phospholipids) during the activation of prothrombin to active thrombin, serving as an in vivo molecular marker of active thrombin generation and hypercoagulability. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 637–640, PDF pp. 650–653; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What serine protease forms an active enzymatic complex with cofactor factor VIIIa, and what is the physiological substrate of this complex?
questions.explanation: Activated factor IX (FIXa) is the serine protease of the intrinsic tenase complex; in the presence of calcium and a phospholipid membrane, it binds non-enzymatic cofactor FVIIIa to proteolytically cleave and activate substrate factor X to factor Xa. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 638–641, PDF pp. 651–654; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What protein secreted by endothelial cells initiates physiological fibrinolysis by converting plasminogen into plasmin?
questions.explanation: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) is synthesized and released by vascular endothelial cells. When bound to fibrin, tPA proteolytically converts clot-bound plasminogen into active plasmin, which then digests the insoluble fibrin mesh into soluble degradation products. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 642–645, PDF pp. 655–658; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What two regulatory proteins form an anticoagulant complex that proteolytically degrades activated factors V (Va) and VIII (VIIIa)?
choices: APC (activated protein C) and protein S
questions.officialAnswer: APC (activated protein C) and protein S
questions.explanation: Thrombin bound to endothelial thrombomodulin activates protein C. Activated protein C (APC) complexes with its cofactor, protein S, on phospholipid surfaces to inactivate factors Va and VIIIa by targeted proteolysis, halting further thrombin amplification. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 641–644, PDF pp. 654–657; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What are the two primary hemostatic roles of von Willebrand factor (VWF)?
choices: Inhibit excess coagulation and activate protein C
Activate plasmin and promote lysis of fibrinogen
Mediate platelet adhesion and serve as a carrier molecule for factor VIII
Mediate platelet aggregation via the GP IIb/IIIa receptor
questions.officialAnswer: Mediate platelet adhesion and serve as a carrier molecule for factor VIII
questions.explanation: VWF performs two critical functions: (1) it acts as a molecular bridge binding exposed subendothelial collagen and platelet GP Ib/IX/V complexes to mediate platelet adhesion under high shear stress; and (2) it circulates as a non-covalent carrier complex with procoagulant factor VIII, protecting FVIII from premature proteolytic degradation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 629–633, PDF pp. 642–646; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Most plasma coagulation factors are synthesized primarily in:
questions.explanation: With the exception of VWF (produced by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes) and factor VIII (produced in endothelial cells and hepatic sinusoidal cells), all plasma procoagulant factors and natural anticoagulant serine protease inhibitors are synthesized by hepatocytes in the liver. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 633–635, PDF pp. 646–648; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: The cascade of proteolytic events involved in secondary hemostasis:
choices: Lead to the formation of a stable fibrin clot
Usually occur independently of primary hemostasis
Are the first line of defense against blood loss
questions.officialAnswer: Lead to the formation of a stable fibrin clot
questions.explanation: Primary hemostasis forms an unstable platelet plug at the site of vascular disruption. Secondary hemostasis comprises sequential enzymatic activations of coagulation zymogens that culminate in thrombin generation and conversion of soluble fibrinogen into a cross-linked, insoluble fibrin network that stabilizes the hemostatic seal. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 633–636, PDF pp. 646–649; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following coagulation factors is activated by thrombin and mediates the covalent stabilization and cross-linking of the fibrin clot?
questions.explanation: Factor XIII (fibrin stabilizing factor) is a transglutaminase activated by thrombin and calcium. Activated factor XIII (FXIIIa) forms covalent isopeptide bonds between lysine and glutamine residues of adjacent fibrin monomers, converting loose hydrogen-bonded fibrin polymers into an insoluble, mechanically resilient cross-linked clot. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 639–642, PDF pp. 652–655; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following endogenous plasma inhibitors is (are) important for the control and downregulation of excessive in vivo thrombin generation?
questions.explanation: Antithrombin (AT) is the principal circulating serine protease inhibitor (serpin) that neutralizes thrombin and factor Xa (accelerated ~1,000-fold by heparin). Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) inhibits the TF-FVIIa complex via feedback inhibition through FXa, tightly regulating extrinsic coagulation initiation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 35, Book pp. 640–643, PDF pp. 653–656; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the most common acquired bleeding disorder encountered in acute critical care and massive hemorrhage?
questions.explanation: Trauma-induced coagulopathy (TIC) is an acute acquired coagulopathy developing within minutes following major severe trauma and tissue hypoperfusion, driven by systemic endothelial activation, consumption of factors, hyperfibrinolysis, hypothermia, and acidosis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 36, Book pp. 652–655, PDF pp. 665–668; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a classic manifestation of anatomic (deep tissue) bleeding typical of coagulation factor deficiencies?
questions.explanation: Anatomic or deep bleeding (hemarthroses, deep muscle hematomas, retroperitoneal hemorrhages, and intracranial/CNS bleeds) is characteristic of secondary hemostatic coagulation factor deficiencies (e.g., hemophilia A or B). Mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae, epistaxis, menorrhagia) is typical of primary hemostatic defects (platelet disorders or VWD). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 36, Book pp. 653–656, PDF pp. 666–669; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What coagulation factor becomes deficient earliest in progressive hepatic disease, and what screening assay does its deficiency first prolong?
questions.explanation: Factor VII has the shortest plasma half-life (approx. 4 to 6 hours) of all coagulation factors. Consequently, as hepatic synthetic capacity declines in liver disease, factor VII levels drop earliest, resulting in isolated prolongation of the prothrombin time (PT) before the PTT becomes prolonged. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 36, Book pp. 656–658, PDF pp. 669–671; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions characteristically causes a prolonged thrombin time (TT)?
questions.explanation: The thrombin time (TT) measures the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin upon addition of exogenous thrombin. It is sensitive to quantitative deficiencies of fibrinogen (<100 mg/dL), qualitative fibrinogen abnormalities (dysfibrinogenemia), and inhibitors of thrombin such as heparin or elevated fibrin degradation products (FDPs). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 36, Book pp. 658–660, PDF pp. 671–673; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: In what type or subtype of von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation (RIPA) test characteristically positive (hyper-responsive) when ristocetin is used at a low concentration of less than 0.5 mg/mL?
questions.explanation: VWD subtype 2B is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the VWF A1 domain that increase its binding affinity for platelet GP Ib. Platelet aggregation occurs at subthreshold concentrations of ristocetin (≤0.5 mg/mL) that do not aggregate normal platelets, leading to in vivo clearance of high-molecular-weight multimers and mild-to-moderate thrombocytopenia. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 36, Book pp. 661–664, PDF pp. 674–677; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the immediate treatment of choice for severe vitamin K deficiency when an active life-threatening hemorrhage is present?
choices: Vitamin K and four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC)
questions.officialAnswer: Vitamin K and four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC)
questions.explanation: While intravenous vitamin K stimulates hepatic synthesis of carboxylated factors II, VII, IX, and X, newly synthesized factors require 6 to 24 hours to achieve hemostatic levels. Immediate rapid reversal of life-threatening bleeding requires prompt infusion of four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC), which immediately restores all vitamin-K-dependent factors. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 36, Book pp. 657–660, PDF pp. 670–673; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: If a patient presents with recurrent anatomic soft tissue bleeding and poor wound healing, but routine screening PT, PTT, thrombin time, platelet count, and platelet functional assay results are all completely normal, what factor deficiency should be evaluated?
questions.explanation: Routine PT and PTT assays terminate upon initial formation of hydrogen-bonded soluble fibrin monomers and do not evaluate factor XIII-mediated cross-linking. Factor XIII deficiency manifests with severe bleeding, umbilical stump bleeding, and poor wound healing despite normal PT, PTT, TT, and platelet counts, diagnosed by clot solubility in 5M urea or 1% monochloroacetic acid. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 36, Book pp. 665–667, PDF pp. 678–680; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What hemostatic therapy may be used for an actively bleeding boy with severe hemophilia A who has developed a high-titer factor VIII inhibitor (alloantibody)?
questions.explanation: When a patient with hemophilia A develops a high-titer neutralizing inhibitor against factor VIII (≥5 Bethesda units), standard FVIII concentrates are rendered ineffective. Bypassing agents—such as recombinant activated factor VII (rFVIIa) or activated prothrombin complex concentrates (FEIBA)—bypass the need for factor VIII by directly activating factor X on activated platelet surfaces to generate thrombin. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 36, Book pp. 663–666, PDF pp. 676–679; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the most prevalent form of inherited von Willebrand disease (VWD)?
questions.explanation: Type 1 VWD accounts for approximately 75% to 80% of all diagnosed cases of von Willebrand disease. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and characterized by a mild to moderate quantitative reduction in structurally and functionally normal VWF multimers and factor VIII. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 36, Book pp. 660–663, PDF pp. 673–676; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following coagulation assays is most useful for distinguishing nutritional vitamin K deficiency from severe end-stage liver disease?
questions.explanation: Both vitamin K deficiency and liver disease produce a prolonged PT due to low factors II, VII, and X. However, factor V is synthesized in the liver independent of vitamin K. Factor V activity is markedly decreased in severe hepatic disease but normal in uncomplicated vitamin K deficiency, making factor V assay the definitive differentiator. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 36, Book pp. 656–658, PDF pp. 669–671; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Mucocutaneous hemorrhage (petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, epistaxis, and mucosal bleeding) is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Mucocutaneous bleeding is the clinical hallmark of quantitative or qualitative primary hemostatic defects, including thrombocytopenia, platelet function disorders, and von Willebrand disease. In contrast, deep anatomic bleeding (hemarthroses, muscle hematomas) reflects secondary hemostatic coagulation factor deficiencies. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 36, Book pp. 652–655, PDF pp. 665–668; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: The clinical presentation of platelet-related bleeding may include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Platelet disorders (thrombocytopenia or qualitative thrombopathies) cause mucocutaneous hemorrhage characterized by petechiae, easy bruising (purpura, ecchymoses), epistaxis, and menorrhagia. In contrast, hemarthroses (joint bleeding) and deep muscular hematomas are classic hallmarks of secondary coagulation factor deficiencies such as hemophilia A or B. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 37, Book pp. 678–680, PDF pp. 691–693; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A severe congenital defect or absence of the platelet membrane glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (αIIbβ3) complex causes:
questions.explanation: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by quantitative deficiency or qualitative dysfunction of the GP IIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3) complex. Because GP IIb/IIIa is the essential fibrinogen receptor required for platelet-to-platelet bridging, platelets completely fail to aggregate with all physiological agonists (ADP, collagen, thrombin, epinephrine), whereas ristocetin agglutination remains normal. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 37, Book pp. 680–682, PDF pp. 693–695; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Patients with Bernard-Soulier syndrome have which of the following characteristic laboratory findings?
choices: Abnormal platelet aggregation in response to ADP, collagen, and epinephrine
Giant platelets and abnormal platelet agglutination with ristocetin that does not correct with normal plasma
Normal bleeding time and elevated platelet count
questions.officialAnswer: Giant platelets and abnormal platelet agglutination with ristocetin that does not correct with normal plasma
questions.explanation: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the GP Ib/IX/V complex (the platelet receptor for VWF). It is characterized by moderate thrombocytopenia, giant platelets on peripheral smear, and absent platelet agglutination with ristocetin that is not corrected by adding exogenous normal plasma or VWF (differentiating it from von Willebrand disease). Aggregation with ADP, collagen, and epinephrine is normal. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 37, Book pp. 682–684, PDF pp. 695–697; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most common of the hereditary qualitative platelet function disorders?
questions.explanation: Storage pool deficiencies, specifically delta-storage pool disease (dense granule deficiency), are the most common congenital qualitative platelet defects. A lack of dense granules (depleted ATP, ADP, serotonin, and calcium) impairs secondary platelet aggregation and granule secretion. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 37, Book pp. 684–686, PDF pp. 697–699; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A reduction in thrombin generation in patients with Scott syndrome results from:
choices: Defective platelet procoagulant activity caused by impaired exposure of phosphatidylserine on the outer membrane
questions.officialAnswer: Defective platelet procoagulant activity caused by impaired exposure of phosphatidylserine on the outer membrane
questions.explanation: Scott syndrome is an extremely rare bleeding disorder characterized by defective "scramblase" activity, preventing the normal calcium-induced translocation of negatively charged phosphatidylserine from the inner to the outer platelet membrane leaflet. Without externalized phosphatidylserine, assembly of the tenase and prothrombinase complexes is severely impaired, resulting in deficient surface thrombin generation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 37, Book pp. 686–688, PDF pp. 699–701; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: The impaired platelet function seen in myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) results from:
choices: Clonal intrinsic platelet defects involving membrane receptors and intracellular signaling pathways
questions.officialAnswer: Clonal intrinsic platelet defects involving membrane receptors and intracellular signaling pathways
questions.explanation: Platelets in myeloproliferative neoplasms (such as essential thrombocythemia and polycythemia vera) originate from an abnormal neoplastic stem cell clone. They frequently exhibit defective in vitro aggregation responses (particularly to epinephrine), decreased granule stores, loss of adrenergic and prostaglandin receptors, and abnormal signal transduction pathways. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 37, Book pp. 687–689, PDF pp. 700–702; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: The acquired platelet defect associated with high concentrations of paraproteins in monoclonal gammopathies (such as Waldenström macroglobulinemia or multiple myeloma) is:
choices: Impaired platelet adhesion and aggregation caused by paraprotein coating of platelet membranes
Direct proteolytic destruction of GP Ib/IX receptors by light chains
Immune clearance mediated by antiplatelet autoantibodies
Impaired megakaryocytic endomitosis in the bone marrow
questions.officialAnswer: Impaired platelet adhesion and aggregation caused by paraprotein coating of platelet membranes
questions.explanation: Excessive circulating monoclonal immunoglobulins (IgM, IgG, or IgA) non-specifically coat platelet membrane surfaces, physically blocking interaction with agonists, fibrinogen, and subendothelial VWF. Paraproteins also interfere with fibrin polymerization, contributing to clinical bleeding. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 37, Book pp. 688–690, PDF pp. 701–703; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: In uremia associated with chronic renal failure, platelet function is impaired primarily by higher than normal circulating levels of:
questions.explanation: Uremic bleeding is multifactorial but directly driven by retention of dialyzable toxic metabolites—notably guanidinosuccinic acid (GSA), methylguanidine, and phenolic compounds. These toxins induce excessive nitric oxide production by endothelial cells and platelets, inhibiting platelet adhesion and aggregation. Hemodialysis or DDAVP substantially improves platelet function. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 37, Book pp. 688–690, PDF pp. 701–703; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction associated with the use of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) during open-heart surgery is caused primarily by:
choices: Platelet activation, degranulation, and mechanical fragmentation upon contact with foreign circuit surfaces
Antiplatelet autoantibody formation against GP IIb/IIIa
Massive hepatic sequestration of functional platelets
Direct suppression of bone marrow megakaryocytopoiesis
questions.officialAnswer: Platelet activation, degranulation, and mechanical fragmentation upon contact with foreign circuit surfaces
questions.explanation: Passage of blood through the synthetic extracorporeal bypass tubing and oxygenator exposes platelets to extensive shear stress and foreign surfaces. Platelets become prematurely activated, shed membrane receptors (GP Ib and GP IIb/IIIa), release their alpha and dense granules, and are cleared, leaving behind "exhausted," dysfunctional circulating platelets. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 37, Book pp. 689–691, PDF pp. 702–704; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Aspirin ingestion irreversibly inhibits platelet function by blocking the synthesis of:
questions.explanation: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) permanently acetylates and inactivates cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1, prostaglandin G/H synthase 1) in platelets. This abolishes the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H2, preventing synthesis of thromboxane A2 (TXA2)—a potent platelet agonist and vasoconstrictor—for the entire 7- to 10-day lifespan of the affected platelets. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 37, Book pp. 689–692, PDF pp. 702–705; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the pharmacological mechanism of action of antiplatelet drugs such as abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban?
choices: Irreversible antagonism of P2Y12 ADP receptors
Targeted blockade of platelet GP IIb/IIIa (αIIbβ3) fibrinogen binding sites
questions.officialAnswer: Targeted blockade of platelet GP IIb/IIIa (αIIbβ3) fibrinogen binding sites
questions.explanation: Abciximab (Fab fragment chimeric antibody), eptifibatide (cyclic heptapeptide), and tirofiban (non-peptide small molecule) are GP IIb/IIIa receptor antagonists. By directly occupying the RGD binding sites on activated GP IIb/IIIa complexes, they block fibrinogen and VWF binding, completely inhibiting platelet aggregation regardless of the upstream activating stimulus.
