(Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 37, Book pp. 690–692, PDF pp. 703–705; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions is an inherited, congenital qualitative platelet disorder?
questions.explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the WAS gene encoding the WAS protein (WASP), an actin cytoskeleton regulator. It features microthrombocytopenia (very small platelets), defective platelet function and aggregation, severe immunodeficiency, and eczema. In contrast, senile purpura and Henoch-Schönlein purpura are vascular purpuras, and uremic bleeding is an acquired disorder. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 37, Book pp. 684–686, PDF pp. 697–699; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: The autosomal dominant inherited disorder associated with decreased platelet production, giant platelets, and pale blue cytoplasmic leukocyte inclusions resembling Döhle bodies is:
questions.explanation: May-Hegglin anomaly is an autosomal dominant macrothrombocytopenia caused by mutations in the MYH9 gene encoding nonmuscle myosin heavy chain IIA. Patients present with giant platelets, thrombocytopenia, and spindle-shaped blue leukocyte inclusions (MYH9 aggregates) in granulocytes and monocytes. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 38, Book pp. 699–701, PDF pp. 712–714; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following findings is NOT a characteristic hallmark of immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)?
questions.explanation: ITP is defined by isolated immune-mediated thrombocytopenia resulting from autoantibody opsonization and macrophage phagocytosis in the spleen and liver. Significant splenomegaly is characteristically ABSENT in uncomplicated ITP; its presence should prompt evaluation for alternative diagnoses such as lymphoma, portal hypertension, or systemic lupus erythematosus. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 38, Book pp. 703–706, PDF pp. 716–719; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: The specific platelet membrane antigen most commonly responsible for maternal alloimmunization in fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (FNAIT) is:
questions.explanation: In FNAIT, an HPA-1a-negative mother becomes alloimmunized to the HPA-1a (PlA1) antigen carried on fetal platelet GP IIIa inherited from the father. Maternal IgG anti-HPA-1a antibodies cross the placenta, causing profound fetal thrombocytopenia and intracranial hemorrhage in up to 80% to 85% of FNAIT cases. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 38, Book pp. 707–709, PDF pp. 720–722; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A 2-year-old child presents with an abrupt onset of petechiae and an unexpected platelet count of 15 × 10^9/L following a routine upper respiratory viral illness 2 weeks earlier. The physical examination is unremarkable aside from bruising, and the peripheral blood film shows large platelets with normal red and white cell lineages. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Acute ITP is primarily a disease of young children (aged 2 to 5 years), occurring abruptly 1 to 3 weeks following a common viral infection (e.g., respiratory or gastrointestinal illness). It features isolated profound thrombocytopenia with normal hemoglobin and WBC counts. Over 80% of pediatric cases resolve spontaneously within weeks to months without progressing to chronic disease. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 38, Book pp. 704–706, PDF pp. 717–719; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which pharmacological agent causes a reduction in platelet count by selectively inhibiting megakaryocyte differentiation and maturation in the bone marrow?
questions.explanation: Anagrelide (Agrylin) is an oral imidazoquinazoline agent used clinically to lower elevated platelet counts in essential thrombocythemia. It selectively inhibits megakaryocyte endoreduplication, maturation, and polyploidization without suppressing erythroid or myeloid stem cell proliferation at therapeutic dosages. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 38, Book pp. 715–717, PDF pp. 728–730; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A defect in primary hemostasis (platelet plug formation in response to vascular endothelial injury) typically manifests clinically as:
choices: Joint hemarthroses and deep intramuscular bleeding
Delayed bleeding occurring 24 to 48 hours post-injury
questions.explanation: Primary hemostasis involves platelets and the microvasculature. Impairment results in immediate superficial mucocutaneous hemorrhage characterized by tiny pinpoint capillary petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, and gastrointestinal/menstrual bleeding. Deep anatomic bleeding indicates secondary coagulation cascade defects. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 38, Book pp. 698–700, PDF pp. 711–713; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: When a medication acts as a hapten to induce immune thrombocytopenia, the pathogenic drug-dependent antibody binds to:
choices: The drug circulating freely in plasma only
A neoantigen formed by the drug covalently bound to a platelet membrane glycoprotein
questions.officialAnswer: A neoantigen formed by the drug covalently bound to a platelet membrane glycoprotein
questions.explanation: Under the classic hapten (or drug-dependent) mechanism (such as with penicillin or quinine-type reactions), the drug binds non-covalently or covalently to a platelet surface glycoprotein (e.g., GP Ib/IX or GP IIb/IIIa), creating a novel compound epitope recognized by high-affinity IgG or IgM antibodies, leading to complement activation or macrophage clearance. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 38, Book pp. 706–708, PDF pp. 719–721; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: The acronym TAR syndrome refers to:
choices: Abnormal platelet morphology in which radial striations are observed
Transient aplastic red cell marrow failure
questions.explanation: TAR syndrome (Thrombocytopenia with Absent Radii) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by 1q21.1 microdeletions and RBM8A mutations. Infants present with bilateral absence of the radial bones in the forearms (with conserved thumbs, distinguishing it from Fanconi anemia) and severe hypomegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia at birth. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 38, Book pp. 700–702, PDF pp. 713–715; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Neonatal autoimmune thrombocytopenia occurs in infants born to mothers who have:
choices: An alloantibody directed against fetal HPA-1a antigens
Active or history of maternal ITP, where maternal IgG autoantibodies cross the placenta
questions.officialAnswer: Active or history of maternal ITP, where maternal IgG autoantibodies cross the placenta
questions.explanation: Neonatal autoimmune thrombocytopenia arises when a mother with active or past immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) or systemic lupus erythematosus passes IgG autoantibodies across the placenta into the fetal circulation, targeting both maternal and fetal platelets. In contrast, neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (FNAIT) occurs when an antigen-negative mother forms alloantibodies against a paternal platelet antigen absent on her own platelets. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 38, Book pp. 707–709, PDF pp. 720–722; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Typical hemolytic uremic syndrome (D+ HUS) in children is most frequently triggered by:
choices: Diarrhea caused by Shiga toxin-producing bacteria (e.g., E. coli O157:H7)
Inherited deficiency of complement factor H
questions.officialAnswer: Diarrhea caused by Shiga toxin-producing bacteria (e.g., E. coli O157:H7)
questions.explanation: Over 90% of pediatric HUS cases follow a prodromal diarrheal illness caused by Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC, notably serotype O157:H7) or Shigella dysenteriae. Shiga toxin enters renal microvascular endothelial cells via the Gb3 receptor, triggering apoptosis, microvascular thrombosis, acute renal failure, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), and consumptive thrombocytopenia. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 38, Book pp. 710–712, PDF pp. 723–725; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Treatment with a monoclonal anticomplement C5 inhibitor such as eculizumab is first-line targeted therapy for which microangiopathic disorder?
questions.explanation: Atypical HUS (aHUS) is driven by uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway due to inherited mutations in complement regulatory genes (CFH, CFI, MCP, CD46) or autoantibodies against factor H. Eculizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody that blocks cleavage of complement C5 into C5a and C5b-9 (MAC), halts complement-mediated endothelial damage and is the first-line targeted treatment. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 38, Book pp. 711–714, PDF pp. 724–727; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements regarding thrombocytosis is NOT true?
choices: Reactive thrombocytosis occurs secondary to inflammation, tissue injury, iron deficiency, or splenectomy
Platelet counts in reactive thrombocytosis rarely exceed 1,000 × 10^9/L
Reactive thrombocytosis is commonly accompanied by spontaneous arterial and venous thrombosis
Autonomous thrombocytosis is driven by clonal myeloproliferative disorders such as essential thrombocythemia
questions.officialAnswer: Reactive thrombocytosis is commonly accompanied by spontaneous arterial and venous thrombosis
questions.explanation: In reactive (secondary) thrombocytosis, elevated platelets are functionally normal and stimulated by reactive cytokines (such as IL-6); thrombotic or hemorrhagic complications are extraordinarily rare even when platelet counts exceed 1,000 × 10^9/L. In contrast, clonal autonomous thrombocytosis in essential thrombocythemia frequently causes microvascular thrombosis, stroke, myocardial infarction, or bleeding. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 38, Book pp. 714–717, PDF pp. 727–730; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the approximate annual incidence and prevalence of venous thromboembolism (VTE) in the general population of the United States?
questions.explanation: Venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism) occurs at an overall annual incidence of approximately 1 in 1,000 individuals (0.1% per year) in Caucasian populations, rising exponentially with age from less than 1 in 10,000 in children to nearly 1% per year in the elderly. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 722–724, PDF pp. 735–737; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the definition of thrombophilia?
choices: Predisposition to thrombosis secondary to a congenital or acquired defect in the hemostatic mechanism
Bleeding tendency caused by defective primary hemostasis
Congenital absence of venous valves in the lower extremities
Platelet hyperaggregability caused by elevated von Willebrand factor
questions.officialAnswer: Predisposition to thrombosis secondary to a congenital or acquired defect in the hemostatic mechanism
questions.explanation: Thrombophilia is defined as any inherited or acquired disorder of the coagulation cascade, natural anticoagulant pathways, or fibrinolytic mechanisms that significantly predisposes an individual to the development of venous or arterial thrombosis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 723–725, PDF pp. 736–738; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What major acquired thrombosis risk factor is assessed directly in the specialized hemostasis laboratory?
questions.explanation: While age, immobilization, surgery, and estrogen therapy are clinical thrombosis risk factors, antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant [LAC], anticardiolipin [aCL], and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I [aβ2GPI]) represent the primary acquired prothrombotic risk factors evaluated through laboratory coagulation and immunoassay testing. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 725–728, PDF pp. 738–741; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Trousseau syndrome, a low-grade chronic migratory thrombophlebitis and DIC, is classically associated with:
choices: Adenocarcinomas of the pancreas, gastrointestinal tract, or lung
questions.officialAnswer: Adenocarcinomas of the pancreas, gastrointestinal tract, or lung
questions.explanation: Trousseau syndrome is a cancer-associated hypercoagulable state manifesting as migratory superficial thrombophlebitis and arterial/venous thromboembolism. It is classically associated with visceral mucin-secreting adenocarcinomas (especially of the pancreas, stomach, and lung) that release procoagulant mucins and tissue factor into the circulation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 726–729, PDF pp. 739–742; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the most prevalent heritable genetic thrombophilia risk factor in Caucasian populations?
choices: Activated protein C resistance (Factor V Leiden mutation)
questions.officialAnswer: Activated protein C resistance (Factor V Leiden mutation)
questions.explanation: Activated protein C resistance (APCR), caused in >90% of cases by the Factor V Leiden mutation (FV R506Q point mutation), is present in 3% to 8% of European Caucasians, making it by far the most common heritable thrombophilia defect. Prothrombin G20210A is second (approx. 2% to 3%), while AT, PC, and PS deficiencies are rare (<0.5%). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 727–730, PDF pp. 740–743; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: In most laboratory lupus anticoagulant (LAC) testing profiles, what screening assay is recommended as primary because it is sensitive and robust against factor VIII deficiencies?
questions.explanation: The dilute Russell viper venom time (dRVVT) directly activates factor X to Xa in the presence of rate-limiting phospholipids, bypassing contact factors and factors VIII and IX. This makes it highly sensitive to phospholipid-dependent lupus anticoagulants without interference from intrinsic pathway factor deficiencies or FVIII inhibitors. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 731–734, PDF pp. 744–747; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A patient with acute venous thrombosis is tested for protein S deficiency. Total protein S is normal, but free protein S is markedly decreased. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Type III (or type IIb) protein S deficiency
questions.explanation: Protein S circulates in two forms: free (approx. 40%, biologically active as an APC cofactor) and bound to C4b-binding protein (approx. 60%, inactive). In Type II (qualitative/dysfunctional) protein S deficiency, total and free PS antigen levels may appear normal while anticoagulant functional activity is reduced; in Type III, total PS is normal but free PS antigen is specifically reduced. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 734–737, PDF pp. 747–750; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: An elevated plasma level of what regulatory fibrinolytic system protein is recognized as an independent risk factor for both arterial and venous thrombosis?
questions.explanation: Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) is the primary physiological inhibitor of tPA and uPA. Pathologically elevated levels of PAI-1 suppress fibrinolysis by preventing plasmin formation, impairing clot dissolution and predisposing to thrombosis in metabolic syndrome and coronary artery disease. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 736–738, PDF pp. 749–751; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: How does elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] promote thrombosis and premature cardiovascular disease?
choices: It causes elevated factor VIII synthesis in endothelial cells
It binds to antithrombin and destroys its heparin-binding domain
Its apolipoprotein(a) moiety shares structural homology with plasminogen, competing with plasminogen for fibrin binding and inhibiting fibrinolysis
questions.officialAnswer: Its apolipoprotein(a) moiety shares structural homology with plasminogen, competing with plasminogen for fibrin binding and inhibiting fibrinolysis
questions.explanation: Apolipoprotein(a) in Lp(a) possesses extensive structural homology with plasminogen kringle domains. By competitively binding to fibrin lysine-binding sites without possessing proteolytic activity, Lp(a) prevents plasminogen binding and tPA activation, directly suppressing physiological fibrinolysis while promoting atherogenesis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 737–739, PDF pp. 750–752; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What testing step is required by International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) guidelines to confirm the presence of a lupus anticoagulant (LAC)?
choices: A confirmatory phospholipid-neutralization test demonstrating shortening of clotting time upon addition of excess phospholipids
questions.officialAnswer: A confirmatory phospholipid-neutralization test demonstrating shortening of clotting time upon addition of excess phospholipids
questions.explanation: ISTH diagnostic criteria for lupus anticoagulants require: (1) prolongation of at least one phospholipid-dependent screening test (e.g., dRVVT or LAC-sensitive PTT); (2) failure to correct with 1:1 normal plasma mixing (demonstrating an inhibitor); and (3) confirmatory demonstration that addition of excess bilayer or hexagonal-phase phospholipids bypasses the inhibitor and significantly shortens the clotting time. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 732–735, PDF pp. 745–748; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What definitive molecular genetic test is used to confirm the diagnosis of hereditary activated protein C (APC) resistance?
choices: Factor V Leiden (FV 1691G>A / R506Q) mutation analysis
questions.officialAnswer: Factor V Leiden (FV 1691G>A / R506Q) mutation analysis
questions.explanation: When a phenotypic APC resistance clot-based assay is abnormal (ratio < 2.0), DNA-based PCR testing for the Factor V Leiden mutation (a single G-to-A transition at nucleotide 1691 of the F5 gene, replacing Arg with Gln at cleavage site 506) definitively confirms whether the patient is heterozygous or homozygous for the mutation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 728–731, PDF pp. 741–744; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What therapeutic agent may occasionally provoke disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) or thromboembolic complications when administered in high doses?
choices: Prothrombin complex concentrates (PCC) containing activated coagulation factors
questions.officialAnswer: Prothrombin complex concentrates (PCC) containing activated coagulation factors
questions.explanation: Older unactivated and activated prothrombin complex concentrates (aPCCs/FEIBA) contain high concentrations of factors II, VII, IX, and X along with trace activated factors (FIXa, FXa). When administered repeatedly or in patients with impaired hepatic clearance, they can provoke systemic microvascular thrombosis and consumptive DIC. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 739–742, PDF pp. 752–755; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an endogenous plasma control or regulatory inhibitor of the fibrinolytic system?
questions.explanation: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) is an anticoagulant serpin that regulates the initiation of the coagulation cascade by inhibiting factor Xa and the TF-FVIIa complex; it has no direct role in inhibiting fibrinolysis. In contrast, PAI-1, alpha-2-antiplasmin, and TAFI are the three primary physiological inhibitors of fibrinolysis. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 736–739, PDF pp. 749–752; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the most clinically important diagnostic application of the quantitative D-dimer assay in the emergency department setting?
choices: Confirming the presence of antithrombin deficiency
Ruling out deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) in patients with low to intermediate pretest probability
questions.officialAnswer: Ruling out deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) in patients with low to intermediate pretest probability
questions.explanation: High-sensitivity quantitative D-dimer immunoassays have a negative predictive value approaching 99% to 100%. A normal (negative) D-dimer result (<500 ng/mL FEU) safely and reliably excludes active DVT or PE in outpatients with low to intermediate clinical probability, eliminating the need for expensive radiological imaging (ultrasound or CT angiography). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 741–744, PDF pp. 754–757; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the first mandatory laboratory test necessary to detect and monitor suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
choices: Platelet count monitoring to detect a relative drop of ≥50% from baseline
questions.officialAnswer: Platelet count monitoring to detect a relative drop of ≥50% from baseline
questions.explanation: Routine platelet count monitoring (every 2 to 3 days in patients receiving unfractionated heparin) is the essential first step to detect HIT. A relative platelet drop of ≥50% from baseline occurring 5 to 10 days after starting heparin warrants immediate clinical suspension of heparin and subsequent serological testing for anti-PF4/heparin antibodies. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 39, Book pp. 742–745, PDF pp. 755–758; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the target therapeutic INR range for Coumadin (warfarin) oral anticoagulant therapy in most standard clinical indications (such as treatment of DVT, PE, or nonvalvular atrial fibrillation)?
questions.explanation: For the vast majority of clinical indications—including prophylaxis and treatment of venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE) and stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation—the recommended therapeutic target INR is 2.0 to 3.0 (target 2.5). A higher target of 2.5 to 3.5 (target 3.0) is reserved for high-risk mechanical prosthetic heart valves. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 748–751, PDF pp. 761–764; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Laboratory monitoring of a patient taking Coumadin (warfarin) demonstrated that her INR was supratherapeutic (INR = 5.8) without active bleeding. What dietary change might have contributed to this exaggerated anticoagulant effect?
choices: Significantly decreased intake of vitamin K-rich green leafy vegetables (such as spinach, kale, and broccoli)
Significantly increased consumption of dark green salads
questions.officialAnswer: Significantly decreased intake of vitamin K-rich green leafy vegetables (such as spinach, kale, and broccoli)
questions.explanation: Dietary vitamin K directly antagonizes warfarin. A sudden reduction in dietary consumption of vitamin K-rich dark green leafy vegetables diminishes the available vitamin K substrate for hepatic carboxylase, intensifying warfarin's inhibitory effect and causing the PT/INR to become supratherapeutic. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 750–752, PDF pp. 763–765; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the greatest clinical advantage of point-of-care (POC) PT/INR testing using capillary fingerstick instruments in outpatient anticoagulation clinics?
choices: It has a lower coefficient of variation than central lab automated coagulometers
It measures direct oral factor Xa inhibitors accurately
It provides immediate results enabling immediate dosage adjustments and patient self-testing
It eliminates the need for thromboplastin international sensitivity index (ISI) calibration
questions.officialAnswer: It provides immediate results enabling immediate dosage adjustments and patient self-testing
questions.explanation: POC coagulometers require only a drop of capillary whole blood and deliver results within 1 to 2 minutes during the patient visit. This facilitates immediate real-time dosage counseling, improves patient adherence and time in therapeutic range (TTR), and allows home self-testing. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 752–754, PDF pp. 765–767; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: You collect a citrated whole-blood specimen to monitor unfractionated heparin (UFH) therapy. What specimen preparation step is critical before performing the PTT?
choices: Centrifuge within 1 hour at a speed sufficient to produce platelet-poor plasma (platelet count <10 × 10^9/L)
Incubate the tube at 37°C for 2 hours before centrifugation
Use platelet-rich plasma to enhance phospholipid activation
Refrigerate uncentrifuged whole blood for 24 hours
questions.officialAnswer: Centrifuge within 1 hour at a speed sufficient to produce platelet-poor plasma (platelet count <10 × 10^9/L)
questions.explanation: Residual platelets in plasma secrete platelet factor 4 (PF4) from their alpha-granules upon standing or refrigeration. PF4 strongly binds and neutralizes heparin in vitro, causing a spurious shortening of the PTT. Specimens must be centrifuged promptly to produce platelet-poor plasma (<10 × 10^9 platelets/L). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 754–756, PDF pp. 767–769; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What bedside point-of-care coagulation test is used to monitor high-dose unfractionated heparin therapy during percutaneous coronary interventions (PCI) and cardiopulmonary bypass surgery?
questions.explanation: The activated clotting time (ACT) uses celite or kaolin particulate activators to monitor high heparin concentrations (1.0 to 5.0 U/mL) used during cardiovascular surgery and catheterization where the standard PTT becomes unclottable (>150 to 200 seconds). Target ACT values typically range from 250 to 480 seconds depending on the procedure. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 755–757, PDF pp. 768–770; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What laboratory test is most widely utilized in hospital core laboratories to monitor standard therapeutic unfractionated heparin (UFH) infusions?
questions.explanation: The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) remains the standard hospital assay for monitoring intravenous unfractionated heparin, calibrated to a therapeutic target corresponding to a plasma heparin concentration of 0.3 to 0.7 U/mL by anti-Xa assay (or 1.5 to 2.5 times the patient's baseline clotting time). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 754–757, PDF pp. 767–770; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: When monitoring of low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) therapy is clinically indicated (e.g., in pregnancy, renal failure, or extreme obesity), what specialized assay is used?
questions.explanation: Because low-molecular-weight heparins have small polysaccharide chains that lack the length required to form a ternary complex with antithrombin and thrombin, they have minimal effect on the aPTT. LMWH preferentially inhibits factor Xa; therefore, therapeutic monitoring requires a chromogenic anti-factor Xa assay calibrated with an LMWH standard (peak target: 0.5 to 1.0 U/mL for twice-daily dosing). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 756–758, PDF pp. 769–771; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What major pharmacokinetic and clinical advantage does low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) possess over unfractionated heparin (UFH)?
choices: It is less expensive than UFH
It has a shorter plasma half-life
Predictable bioavailability and anticoagulant response allowing fixed weight-based subcutaneous dosing without routine laboratory monitoring
questions.officialAnswer: Predictable bioavailability and anticoagulant response allowing fixed weight-based subcutaneous dosing without routine laboratory monitoring
questions.explanation: LMWH binds far less non-specifically to plasma proteins, macrophages, and endothelial cells than UFH, resulting in nearly 90% bioavailability, a prolonged half-life (3 to 6 hours), predictable dose-response kinetics, lower incidence of HIT, and elimination of routine coagulation monitoring in uncomplicated patients. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 756–759, PDF pp. 769–772; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: In what critical clinical situation is an intravenous direct thrombin inhibitor (DTI), such as argatroban or bivalirudin, indicated as first-line therapy?
choices: Confirmed or strongly suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)
Any patient presenting with an elevated INR
questions.officialAnswer: Confirmed or strongly suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)
questions.explanation: Direct thrombin inhibitors (argatroban, bivalirudin) do not bind platelet factor 4 and do not cross-react with pathogenic anti-PF4/heparin antibodies. They are the drug of choice for immediate therapeutic anticoagulation when heparin is discontinued due to suspected or confirmed HIT. Argatroban is metabolized by the liver, making it preferred in patients with renal insufficiency. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 758–760, PDF pp. 771–773; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What routine central laboratory test is used to monitor intravenous argatroban therapy?
questions.explanation: Continuous intravenous argatroban infusions are titrated using the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), aiming for a therapeutic target of 1.5 to 3.0 times the patient's baseline value (not to exceed 100 seconds). Note that argatroban also prolongs the PT/INR, which must be accounted for during transition to warfarin. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 759–761, PDF pp. 772–774; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What gold-standard reference method is used in specialized hemostasis laboratories for detecting aspirin or clopidogrel resistance?
choices: Enzyme immunoassay for soluble GP IIb/IIIa
questions.explanation: Light transmission aggregometry (LTA) performed on platelet-rich plasma remains the gold-standard reference method for assessing antiplatelet therapy and drug resistance, using arachidonic acid to assess aspirin inhibition and ADP to assess P2Y12 receptor inhibitors (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 760–762, PDF pp. 773–775; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What stable urinary platelet activation metabolite is measured by immunoassay to assess in vivo aspirin antiplatelet efficacy?
questions.explanation: Thromboxane A2 has an in vivo half-life of 30 seconds and is rapidly hydrolyzed into thromboxane B2, which is metabolized by the liver into 11-dehydrothromboxane B2 and excreted in urine. Measuring urinary 11-dehydrothromboxane B2 (e.g., AspirinWorks test) reflects systemic in vivo thromboxane production and aspirin response. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 761–763, PDF pp. 774–776; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an intravenous glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor used during percutaneous coronary interventions?
questions.explanation: Eptifibatide (Integrilin) and tirofiban (Aggrastat) are intravenous small-molecule GP IIb/IIIa receptor antagonists administered during acute coronary syndromes and coronary stenting to prevent acute platelet thrombotic reocclusion. Clopidogrel is an oral P2Y12 antagonist, while dabigatran and warfarin are oral anticoagulants. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 760–762, PDF pp. 773–775; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Which of the following antithrombotic medications is classified as an oral direct factor Xa inhibitor (DOAC)?
questions.explanation: Rivaroxaban (Xarelto), apixaban (Eliquis), and edoxaban (Savaysa) are direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) that bind directly and reversibly to the active catalytic site of free and clot-bound factor Xa. Argatroban and bivalirudin are parenteral DTIs, whereas fondaparinux is a parenteral synthetic pentasaccharide indirect Xa inhibitor. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 40, Book pp. 759–762, PDF pp. 772–775; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What artifactual error occurs if a sodium citrate coagulation blood collection tube is underfilled (draw volume <90% of nominal fill volume)?
choices: Falsely decreased PT and PTT results caused by excessive calcium concentration
In vitro clot formation in the collection tube
Falsely prolonged PT and PTT results caused by excessive free citrate binding reagent calcium
questions.officialAnswer: Falsely prolonged PT and PTT results caused by excessive free citrate binding reagent calcium
questions.explanation: Standard coagulation tubes require a precise 9:1 blood-to-anticoagulant ratio (3.2% sodium citrate). When the tube is underfilled (<90%), the relative excess of unbound citrate chelates the calcium chloride added during the PT and PTT test assays, spuriously prolonging the clotting times. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 768–770, PDF pp. 781–783; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: If blood is collected into a multi-tube sequence during venipuncture, when in the CLSI order of draw should the sodium citrate coagulation tube be drawn?
choices: Second, immediately after blood cultures and before serum or heparin tubes
Immediately after the lavender-top EDTA tube
questions.officialAnswer: Second, immediately after blood cultures and before serum or heparin tubes
questions.explanation: Per CLSI standards, blood cultures are drawn first, followed second by the light blue sodium citrate tube (to prevent contamination with clot activators from serum tubes or EDTA/heparin from subsequent tubes). When drawing with a winged butterfly set, a discard tube must be drawn first to prime the tubing dead space and ensure complete filling. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 769–771, PDF pp. 782–784; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What is the primary effect of in vitro hemolysis on a hemostasis plasma specimen?
choices: In vitro activation of coagulation factors and platelets, release of intracellular clotting promoters, and interference with optical endpoint detection
questions.officialAnswer: In vitro activation of coagulation factors and platelets, release of intracellular clotting promoters, and interference with optical endpoint detection
questions.explanation: Hemolyzed specimens indicate cellular trauma during phlebotomy, which liberates red cell ADP and thromboplastic substances that prematurely activate clotting factors and platelets. Free hemoglobin also absorbs light at optical wavelengths (405–540 nm) utilized by photo-optical coagulometers, triggering spurious endpoint determinations. Hemolyzed specimens must be rejected. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 770–772, PDF pp. 783–785; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Except for platelet aggregometry, most routine diagnostic coagulation testing must be performed on:
choices: Platelet-poor plasma (PPP) with a platelet count <10 × 10^9/L
questions.officialAnswer: Platelet-poor plasma (PPP) with a platelet count <10 × 10^9/L
questions.explanation: Routine plasma clot-based assays (PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, factor assays, and lupus anticoagulant testing) require platelet-poor plasma (PPP, platelet count <10 × 10^9/L). Residual platelets provide uncontrolled phospholipid surfaces and release PF4, disrupting assay standardization. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 770–773, PDF pp. 783–786; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: You wish to collect a 5-mL citrated blood specimen from a polycythemic patient whose hematocrit is 65%. How must the volume of 3.2% sodium citrate anticoagulant be adjusted to maintain proper stoichiometry?
choices: Decreased using the CLSI formula C = (1.85 × 10^-3) × (100 - HCT) × V
Doubled because of high red cell mass
No adjustment is required for hematocrits up to 70%
questions.officialAnswer: Decreased using the CLSI formula C = (1.85 × 10^-3) × (100 - HCT) × V
questions.explanation: When the hematocrit exceeds 55%, plasma volume per unit of whole blood is markedly decreased, resulting in an excess of sodium citrate relative to available plasma. Anticoagulant volume (C) must be reduced using the standard CLSI formula C = (0.00185) × (100 - HCT) × V to avoid artifactual prolongation of the PT and PTT. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 769–771, PDF pp. 782–784; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: You perform whole-blood lumiaggregometry on a specimen from a patient with a bleeding tendency. Platelet aggregation curves demonstrate normal initial wave aggregation with low-dose ADP but completely absent ATP release and absent secondary aggregation. This pattern is diagnostic of:
choices: Storage pool deficiency or cyclooxygenase defect (secretion defect)
questions.officialAnswer: Storage pool deficiency or cyclooxygenase defect (secretion defect)
questions.explanation: Lumiaggregometry measures platelet aggregation impedance simultaneously with ATP luminescence (via firefly luciferin-luciferase). Impaired ATP release with absence of the irreversible second-wave aggregation curve reflects failure of dense granule secretion, characteristic of delta-storage pool deficiency or aspirin-induced COX-1 blockade. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 773–776, PDF pp. 786–789; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What gold-standard functional confirmatory assay is used to establish the definitive diagnosis of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
questions.explanation: While PF4/heparin ELISA has high sensitivity (>98%), it detects non-pathogenic antibodies and has poor specificity. The carbon-14 serotonin release assay (SRA) is the reference gold standard functional assay; it measures therapeutic- and high-dose heparin-dependent release of radiolabeled serotonin from donor platelets by patient antibodies, verifying true platelet-activating pathogenicity. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 776–778, PDF pp. 789–791; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What agonist is used in platelet aggregometry to assess VWF-dependent platelet agglutination and screen for von Willebrand disease?
questions.explanation: Ristocetin binds VWF and platelet GP Ib/IX, inducing platelet agglutination in vitro. Impaired or absent ristocetin-induced platelet agglutination (RIPA) at standard concentrations (1.2 to 1.5 mg/mL) that corrects upon adding normal plasma is the classic hallmark of von Willebrand disease (and fails to correct in Bernard-Soulier syndrome). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 774–777, PDF pp. 787–790; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Deficiency of which congenital single coagulation factor is indicated when the PT is markedly prolonged while the aPTT, TT, and fibrinogen levels are completely normal?
questions.explanation: Factor VII is the sole factor unique to the extrinsic pathway evaluated by the prothrombin time (PT). Isolated prolongation of the PT with a normal aPTT points specifically to congenital factor VII deficiency or the earliest stage of vitamin K deficiency/early warfarin initiation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 778–780, PDF pp. 791–793; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A prolonged PT, low factor VII level, but normal factor V level are most compatible with which clinical condition?
choices: Vitamin K deficiency or early warfarin therapy
questions.officialAnswer: Vitamin K deficiency or early warfarin therapy
questions.explanation: Factor VII is vitamin-K-dependent with the shortest half-life, so its activity drops first in vitamin K deficiency or early warfarin treatment. In contrast, factor V is produced by the liver independent of vitamin K. Normal factor V rules out severe hepatocellular liver disease and DIC. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 779–781, PDF pp. 792–794; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: A patient with deep vein thrombosis has a prolonged aPTT. A 1:1 mixing study with normal pooled plasma fails to correct the aPTT immediately and after incubation. The patient most likely has:
questions.explanation: In factor deficiencies, mixing patient plasma 1:1 with normal pooled plasma provides at least 50% activity of the deficient factor, completely normalizing (correcting) the clotting time. Failure of the 1:1 mix to correct indicates the presence of a circulating anticoagulant inhibitor, most commonly a lupus anticoagulant or factor-specific alloantibody. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 780–783, PDF pp. 793–796; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What acute clinical condition causes the most pronounced, dramatic elevation in plasma D-dimer levels alongside hypofibrinogenemia and thrombocytopenia?
questions.explanation: Acute uncompensated DIC involves widespread systemic microvascular fibrin clot generation with concurrent secondary hyperfibrinolysis, causing massive plasmin cleavage of cross-linked fibrin polymers. D-dimer levels typically soar to extreme values (>10,000 to >20,000 ng/mL) with marked consumption of fibrinogen and platelets. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 783–786, PDF pp. 796–799; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What type of specialized coagulation assay utilizes a synthetic oligopeptide substrate coupled to a p-nitroaniline (pNA) chromophore that releases yellow color upon enzymatic cleavage by an active serine protease?
questions.explanation: Chromogenic assays use synthetic peptide substrates tailored to mimic the cleavage sequence of a specific coagulation enzyme (e.g., thrombin or factor Xa) linked to p-nitroaniline (pNA). Free yellow pNA is cleaved proportionally to enzyme activity and measured spectrophotometrically at 405 nm. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 784–787, PDF pp. 797–800; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What primary physiological serine protease inhibitor circulates in plasma to bind and neutralize free plasmin in an instantaneous 1:1 stoichiometric complex?
questions.explanation: Alpha-2-antiplasmin (α2-AP) is the principal circulating physiological inhibitor of plasmin. It forms an immediate, irreversible covalent complex with any free plasmin that escapes the fibrin clot, preventing systemic proteolysis of circulating fibrinogen, factor V, and factor VIII. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 785–788, PDF pp. 798–801; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: What molecular sequencing technology is transforming the genetic diagnosis of complex congenital bleeding and thrombotic disorders by analyzing multiple target genes simultaneously?
questions.explanation: Targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) panels enable simultaneous high-throughput sequencing of dozens of bleeding and thrombophilia candidate genes (e.g., VWF, F8, F9, MYH9, GP1BA, PROC, PROS1) at high coverage, rapidly identifying causal variants that previously required laborious gene-by-gene Sanger sequencing. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 41, Book pp. 788–790, PDF pp. 801–803; Appendix C, PDF p. 864).

questions.prompt: Major technological advances in contemporary automated hemostasis analyzers include all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Pre-analytical specimen integrity checks (HIL: hemolysis, icterus, lipemia)
Primary tube cap piercing and automated barcode reading
Reflex testing and automated rerun rules
Elimination of the requirement for quality control testing
questions.officialAnswer: Elimination of the requirement for quality control testing
questions.explanation: Modern coagulation analyzers feature automated cap piercing, barcode scanning, optical pre-analytical HIL indexing, and reflex testing protocols. However, daily statistical internal quality control and periodic calibration verification remain strictly mandatory under regulatory standards (CLIA/CAP) to ensure accuracy and patient safety. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 42, Book pp. 796–798, PDF pp. 809–811; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.prompt: What is considered the chief advantage of mechanical (electromechanical) clot detection methods over photo-optical methods?
choices: Immunity to optical interference from lipemic, icteric, or hemolyzed specimens
Faster turnaround time for chromogenic assays
Ability to measure antigen-antibody agglutination directly
questions.officialAnswer: Immunity to optical interference from lipemic, icteric, or hemolyzed specimens
questions.explanation: Mechanical endpoint detection systems (such as electromagnetic steel ball movement or wire loop sensors) detect the physical change in plasma viscosity or impedance when fibrin strands form, making them completely insensitive to optical turbidity, severe lipemia, bilirubinemia (icterus), or free hemoglobin that confound photo-optical detectors. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 42, Book pp. 798–800, PDF pp. 811–813; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.prompt: What physical principle of clot detection is utilized in whole-blood viscoelastic testing devices such as the TEG (thromboelastograph) and ROTEM (rotational thromboelastometer)?
choices: Photo-optical light transmission through platelet-poor plasma
Capillary electrical impedance across a microfluidic channel
Viscoelastic pin-and-cup torsion resistance measuring the mechanical properties and shear elastic modulus of whole blood clotting
questions.officialAnswer: Viscoelastic pin-and-cup torsion resistance measuring the mechanical properties and shear elastic modulus of whole blood clotting
questions.explanation: Both TEG and ROTEM assess real-time viscoelastic clot formation in whole blood under low shear. As fibrin polymerizes and platelets cross-link via GP IIb/IIIa receptors between the oscillating cup and pin, mechanical torque is transmitted to the sensor, generating continuous tracing parameters: R/CT (clot initiation), alpha angle (clot propagation), MA/MCF (maximum clot strength), and LY30 (fibrinolysis). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 42, Book pp. 801–804, PDF pp. 814–817; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of semiautomated coagulation instruments?
choices: Automated pipetting of all patient plasma specimens and reagents
Manual pipetting of reagents and specimens by the operator, with automated instrument timer triggering upon final addition
questions.officialAnswer: Manual pipetting of reagents and specimens by the operator, with automated instrument timer triggering upon final addition
questions.explanation: Semiautomated coagulometers require the laboratory technologist to manually pipette patient plasma and reagents into the reaction cuvette. The instrument automatically starts a timer upon addition of the final reagent (electromechanically or optically) and senses clot formation to stop the timer. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 42, Book pp. 797–799, PDF pp. 810–812; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.prompt: When an automated coagulation analyzer with pre-analytical HIL indexing flags a plasma specimen as severely icteric (elevated bilirubin >20 mg/dL), what automated action is typically executed by advanced analyzers to prevent spurious results?
choices: The analyzer adds calcium chloride to clear the bilirubin
The analyzer automatically switches the optical measurement wavelength from 405 nm to 570 or 671 nm (or reruns on an electromechanical channel)
The plasma is diluted 1:100 with saline
questions.officialAnswer: The analyzer automatically switches the optical measurement wavelength from 405 nm to 570 or 671 nm (or reruns on an electromechanical channel)
questions.explanation: Bilirubin has high optical absorbance at 405 to 500 nm, overlapping with chromogenic and optical clot detection. Advanced multi-wavelength analyzers detect icterus and automatically reroute measurement to 570 nm or 671 nm (where bilirubin absorbance is negligible) or reflex to mechanical detection to deliver accurate results without manual intervention. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 42, Book pp. 800–802, PDF pp. 813–815; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.prompt: Which methodology is widely used on automated coagulation analyzers to quantify low concentrations of specific antigens (such as D-dimer, free protein S, and von Willebrand factor antigen)?
questions.explanation: Latex-enhanced immunoassays use submicron polystyrene latex beads coated with specific monoclonal antibodies against the target antigen (e.g., D-dimer). Antigen-antibody cross-linking causes agglutination of latex particles, increasing light absorbance/turbidimetry proportionally to antigen concentration. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 42, Book pp. 802–804, PDF pp. 815–817; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.prompt: All of the following are essential analytic performance characteristics to consider when selecting and validating a new automated coagulation analyzer EXCEPT:
choices: The geographic location of the instrument manufacturer
Within-run and between-run precision (coefficient of variation)
questions.officialAnswer: The geographic location of the instrument manufacturer
questions.explanation: Clinical validation standards (CLSI H57) require establishing assay precision, linearity, analytical measurement range, limit of detection, specimen carryover, reference intervals, and method comparison with existing instrumentation. Physical manufacturer location is not an analytical performance characteristic. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 42, Book pp. 804–806, PDF pp. 817–819; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.prompt: Platelet function is measured by the Platelet Function Analyzer (PFA-100 / PFA-200) by simulating in vivo primary hemostasis using:
choices: Electrical impedance aggregometry in a whole blood cuvette
Centrifugation through a dense oil gradient
A microscopic aperture coated with collagen and ADP (or epinephrine) under high-shear flow conditions
questions.officialAnswer: A microscopic aperture coated with collagen and ADP (or epinephrine) under high-shear flow conditions
questions.explanation: The PFA-100 aspirates citrated whole blood under high arterial shear stress (5,000–6,000 s^-1) through a 147-μm aperture in a membrane coated with equine collagen and epinephrine (Col/EPI) or ADP (Col/ADP). Activated platelets adhere, aggregate, and form a stable plug, reporting the time required to occlude blood flow as the "Closure Time" (CT). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 42, Book pp. 805–807, PDF pp. 818–820; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.prompt: A clinical hospital setting where point-of-care (POC) whole-blood coagulation testing is utilized in high volume to guide rapid, targeted transfusion algorithms is:
choices: Trauma resuscitation bays and cardiothoracic operating suites
questions.officialAnswer: Trauma resuscitation bays and cardiothoracic operating suites
questions.explanation: Trauma centers and cardiothoracic surgical suites utilize point-of-care viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) and ACT to obtain goal-directed coagulation assessment within 10 to 15 minutes, directing specific administration of tranexamic acid, cryoprecipitate, platelets, or fresh frozen plasma during massive hemorrhage. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 42, Book pp. 803–806, PDF pp. 816–819; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.prompt: Molecular genetic testing methods in the hemostasis laboratory are utilized to establish definitive diagnoses in patients with:
choices: Heritable thrombophilias such as Factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A mutations
questions.officialAnswer: Heritable thrombophilias such as Factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A mutations
questions.explanation: Molecular diagnostic techniques (real-time PCR, allele-specific amplification, and melt curve analysis) are standard clinical tests used to detect single nucleotide polymorphisms underlying heritable thrombophilias—specifically the Factor V Leiden (F5 1691G>A) and prothrombin (F2 20210G>A) mutations. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 42, Book pp. 807–809, PDF pp. 820–822; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.subtopic: Hematology and Hemostasis in Selected Populations
questions.prompt: The complete blood count (CBC) reference intervals for healthy children aged 3 to 12 years differ from those of adults in that children have:
choices: Higher hemoglobin and higher hematocrit levels
Lower hemoglobin levels, lower MCV, and higher relative lymphocyte percentages
questions.officialAnswer: Lower hemoglobin levels, lower MCV, and higher relative lymphocyte percentages
questions.explanation: Pediatric reference intervals reflect ongoing developmental hematopoiesis: normal hemoglobin and MCV values are physiological lower than in adults (mean Hb ~11.5–12.5 g/dL, MCV ~78–82 fL), and the differential leukocyte count exhibits a normal physiological lymphocytic predominance up to approximately age 4 to 6 years. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 43, Book pp. 816–818, PDF pp. 829–831; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.subtopic: Hematology and Hemostasis in Selected Populations
questions.prompt: Physiologic anemia of infancy (occurring around 8 to 12 weeks of postnatal life in term infants) results primarily from:
choices: Downregulation of erythropoietin production in response to increased tissue oxygenation after birth, coupled with rapid body growth
questions.officialAnswer: Downregulation of erythropoietin production in response to increased tissue oxygenation after birth, coupled with rapid body growth
questions.explanation: At birth, the shift from a relatively hypoxic in utero environment to atmospheric breathing dramatically increases tissue oxygen saturation. Renal sensors downregulate erythropoietin (EPO) synthesis, temporarily halting erythropoiesis while infant blood volume expands rapidly, producing a physiologic hemoglobin nadir (~9.5–11.0 g/dL) at 2 to 3 months of life. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 43, Book pp. 818–820, PDF pp. 831–833; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.subtopic: Hematology and Hemostasis in Selected Populations
questions.prompt: Morphologically and immunophenotypically, hematogones observed in newborn and infant bone marrow specimens represent:
choices: Malignant lymphoblasts requiring immediate induction chemotherapy
questions.explanation: Hematogones are benign, normal, polyclonal B-cell precursors found in high proportions (up to 10%–20%) in infant and regenerating bone marrows. Although they resemble lymphoblasts morphologically, flow cytometry demonstrates a characteristic continuous, ordered maturation antigen spectrum (CD34+ to CD10+ to CD19+/CD20+) without clonal light chain restriction. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 43, Book pp. 819–821, PDF pp. 832–834; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.subtopic: Hematology and Hemostasis in Selected Populations
questions.prompt: What is the single most common cause of anemia worldwide in childhood (particularly between 6 and 24 months of age)?
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency anemia is the most prevalent childhood anemia, peaking between 6 and 24 months of age when maternal neonatal iron stores become depleted and infants are fed unfortified cow's milk diets with inadequate bioavailable iron during rapid somatic growth. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 43, Book pp. 820–822, PDF pp. 833–835; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.subtopic: Hematology and Hemostasis in Selected Populations
questions.prompt: Which of the following are the two most common etiologies of anemia in the elderly population (aged 65 years and older)?
choices: Hereditary spherocytosis and sickle cell anemia
Aplastic anemia and pure red cell aplasia
Anemia of chronic inflammation (anemia of chronic disease) and iron deficiency anemia
questions.officialAnswer: Anemia of chronic inflammation (anemia of chronic disease) and iron deficiency anemia
questions.explanation: Anemia affects over 10% to 20% of adults aged 65 and older. The leading identifiable causes are anemia of chronic inflammation/disease (approx. 30%–35%, driven by inflammatory cytokines and elevated hepcidin) and iron deficiency anemia (approx. 15%–20%, commonly due to occult gastrointestinal blood loss). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 43, Book pp. 822–824, PDF pp. 835–837; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.subtopic: Hematology and Hemostasis in Selected Populations
questions.prompt: When iron deficiency anemia is recognized in an elderly individual, the underlying cause must always be presumed to be:
choices: Gastrointestinal blood loss (such as ulceration, angiodysplasia, or malignancy) until proven otherwise
Decreased duodenal absorption related to normal aging
questions.officialAnswer: Gastrointestinal blood loss (such as ulceration, angiodysplasia, or malignancy) until proven otherwise
questions.explanation: Adults and elderly individuals do not develop iron deficiency from simple dietary restriction under ordinary conditions. Unexplained iron deficiency in the elderly is considered a sign of chronic occult gastrointestinal bleeding (e.g., colorectal carcinoma, gastric ulcer, or vascular ectasia) and mandates prompt endoscopic evaluation. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 43, Book pp. 823–825, PDF pp. 836–838; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.subtopic: Hematology and Hemostasis in Selected Populations
questions.prompt: Which of the following hematologic conditions is LEAST likely to develop as a de novo primary disorder in an elderly individual?
choices: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) with hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes)
questions.officialAnswer: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) with hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes)
questions.explanation: Hyperdiploid ALL is characteristically a disease of young children (peak age 2 to 5 years). In contrast, CLL, MDS, and MGUS are diseases with incidence rates that increase dramatically with age, representing the most common hematologic neoplasms diagnosed in the geriatric population. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 43, Book pp. 824–826, PDF pp. 837–839; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.subtopic: Hematology and Hemostasis in Selected Populations
questions.prompt: The physiologic "anemia of pregnancy" observed in healthy pregnant women is primarily caused by:
choices: Increased destruction of maternal erythrocytes by placental macrophages
Disproportionate expansion of maternal plasma volume (up to 50%) relative to a smaller increase in red blood cell mass (hemodilution)
questions.officialAnswer: Disproportionate expansion of maternal plasma volume (up to 50%) relative to a smaller increase in red blood cell mass (hemodilution)
questions.explanation: During normal pregnancy, maternal plasma volume expands by approximately 45% to 50%, while total circulating RBC mass increases by only 20% to 30%. This physiological dilutional hypervolemia produces an apparent decrease in hemoglobin and hematocrit (physiologic anemia of pregnancy, normal lower limit ~10.5–11.0 g/dL). (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 43, Book pp. 826–828, PDF pp. 839–841; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.subtopic: Hematology and Hemostasis in Selected Populations
questions.prompt: Which of the following anticoagulant medications is recommended as the safe drug of choice for the prevention and treatment of venous thromboembolism (VTE) during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: LMWH (such as enoxaparin) is the anticoagulant of choice throughout pregnancy because its large, negatively charged molecules do not cross the placental barrier, posing zero risk of fetal embryopathy or fetal hemorrhage. In contrast, warfarin readily crosses the placenta and is teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy), and DOACs lack established safety data in pregnancy. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 43, Book pp. 828–830, PDF pp. 841–843; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).

questions.subtopic: Hematology and Hemostasis in Selected Populations
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 34 weeks of gestation presents to the emergency department with severe headache, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, hypertension, and marked peripheral edema. Laboratory results show a platelet count of 45 × 10^9/L, schistocytes on blood smear, elevated serum AST and ALT, and elevated LDH. Coagulation PT and PTT are within reference limits. What obstetric complication is indicated?
choices: HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets)
questions.officialAnswer: HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets)
questions.explanation: HELLP syndrome is a severe microangiopathic complication of preeclampsia characterized by microangiopathic Hemolysis (schistocytes, elevated indirect bilirubin, elevated LDH), Elevated Liver enzymes (AST, ALT), and Low Platelets (<100 × 10^9/L) in a pregnant third-trimester patient. Prompt delivery is the definitive treatment. (Rodak's Hematology, 6th ed., Ch. 43, Book pp. 829–831, PDF pp. 842–844; Appendix C, PDF p. 865).
